chapters.question_prompt: What is a tax lien certificate, how does the delinquent-tax-to-investor process work, and how does a beginner take their first steps?
chapters.title: Tax Lien Investing Foundations
chapters.subtitle: How Unpaid Property Taxes Become Interest-Bearing Certificates, Statutory Returns, Redemption Basics, AI-Assisted Research, and Step-by-Step Starts for Beginners
chapters.executive_summary: Sixteen practitioners agree on the core trade: a county sells unpaid property taxes as a certificate, the occupant stays put, and the county pays the buyer back plus a state-set rate when the owner redeems. Speakers peg redemption at 95 percent of the time, and Lien Ledger's D.C. data shows just 1 percent ending in foreclosure. The lien sits in first position above mortgages and, per Saen Higgins, even the IRS. Street mechanics center on statutory ceilings of 12 to 36 percent, bid-down versus premium auctions, Florida's 5 percent redemption floor, Dustin Hahn's county phone script, and over-the-counter leftovers bought without competition. The split: Ted Thomas, Dustin Hahn and The Economic Ninja sell the pennies-on-the-dollar house, while Lien Ledger, Julia M. Spencer and Real Estate Ninja frame liens as interest income where houses are rare.

key_metrics.value: 5% of face value; a $1,000 lien bid at 0.25% and redeemed in 3 months pays $50 (roughly 20% annualized)
key_metrics.context: Lien Ledger explains why Florida bids pile up just above zero: the 5% floor under section 197.472 applies to any bid above 0%, so quick redemptions beat the bid rate.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every speaker starts from the same funding gap: property taxes pay for police, fire, roads and schools, and when an owner skips the bill the county sells the debt instead of waiting. Sabrina of Tax Lien Bestie lays it out in under a minute: you step in and make the payment, you receive a tax lien certificate, and if the owner pays during the redemption period the county cuts you a check for your money plus interest, so you never deal with or bully the occupant [VH9CbLJ5Erk @ 00:00:35]. Ted Thomas calls the buyer a lender to the county and stresses that the occupant keeps possession but cannot refinance or sell until the certificate is paid [JcAwqIfK0vo @ 00:03:44]. Lien Ledger runs the same logic on a $2,000 delinquency: you pay the county, the owner still lives in the home, and clearing the debt now requires paying you back plus a rate set by state law rather than a bank, which can be surprisingly high [H9fPhqUYPfc @ 00:00:42]. Tax Lien Code explains why counties bother at all: roughly 20 to 30 percent of property taxes go unpaid each year, most eventually get collected anyway, and the certificate simply solves the county's real problem, which is needing the money now rather than in weeks, months or years [h-Q6weCN110 @ 00:01:29].

The second point of agreement is that redemption, not repossession, is the base case. Red Lotus Chic puts it at 95 percent: in 95 percent of cases the owner comes back and pays the back taxes, so the certificate buyer never takes ownership [ehSkuiHT060 @ 00:05:21]. Lien Ledger repeats the industry claim of more than 95 percent, then backs it with Washington, D.C.'s ten-year review of 9,395 properties: 70 percent redeemed, 16 percent canceled, 13 percent still in progress, and just 1 percent ended in foreclosure, concluding that a lien investor is basically a lender [H9fPhqUYPfc @ 00:03:33]. Tax Sale Secrets says liens are meant to pay off and that foreclosure is the more unusual outcome, though a necessary part of making the system work [fIPCLCdZlAU @ 00:02:07]. Invest with Wesley explains who actually lands on the delinquency list: owners who finally paid off a mortgage and lost the escrow account that used to cover their taxes, and heirs who inherited a house without realizing the tax bill came with it. Both groups usually pay or sell, and a sale pays the lien before the mortgage [n7l4w1FaXS4 @ 00:03:12]. The shared operator conclusion: underwrite every certificate as an interest trade first, and treat any house that falls out of it as the rare exception.

Priority is the third pillar. Tax Lien Code walks the lien stack: a mortgage, then a home equity line of credit, then a contractor's mechanic's lien normally get paid first in, first out, but the county ignores that order and drops its tax lien into first position over everybody [h-Q6weCN110 @ 00:03:33]. Saen Higgins goes further, calling the tax lien a phantom lien that has always sat on the parcel and pops up the moment taxes go unpaid; if the owner does not redeem in time, the buyer steps into the county's position and every other lien and encumbrance, including the mortgage, a second and the IRS, becomes junior [G44d74hIS_0 @ 00:05:45]. Tax Sale Secrets adds that this first-position status blocks any sale or refinance until the lien is cleared and is exactly what hands the holder foreclosure power [fIPCLCdZlAU @ 00:04:21]. The baseline prerequisite every speaker repeats is local homework. Bill Miller warns that each county runs its own auction rules, delinquency dates and redemption timelines, and that once the redemption period lapses the investor typically has to drive the foreclosure, ideally with an attorney guiding the process [PRTEvlETNdk @ 00:04:09]. Nobody in this group treats the rules as uniform across the country; the county is the unit of research, and the state statute sets the boundaries.

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The headline rates are statutory ceilings, and the bidding method decides what you actually keep. Lien Ledger lists Florida at 18 percent, Arizona at 16, New Jersey at 18 and Iowa at 24, then explains the split: New Jersey bidders pay a premium in cash on top of the lien, which cuts the return, while Florida opens at 18 percent and bids down in quarter-point steps until heavy competition collapses the rate toward zero [H9fPhqUYPfc @ 00:02:09]. The counterintuitive edge is Florida's 5 percent minimum under section 197.472: a $1,000 lien bid at a quarter of one percent and redeemed in three months still pays $50, roughly 20 percent annualized, while the same lien held two years earns only about 5 percent total, and a 0 percent bid forfeits the minimum entirely [H9fPhqUYPfc @ 00:04:40]. Saen Higgins describes a Chicago structure of 18 percent for the first six months, another 18 percent each following six-month block, running for three years until it tops 100 percent, which is why the buzz around liens exists [G44d74hIS_0 @ 00:05:06]. Tranquillity sums up the two auction formats operators will face: cash bids go to the highest bidder, rate bids go to the lowest, and bidding wars drive the interest rate and the profit down [VdRy2aZvV-Y @ 00:06:16]. Timing and format matter more than the advertised ceiling.

Dustin Hahn, who claims hundreds of deals across roughly 20 years, skips digging through the county website and calls the tax assessor directly with a fixed script: when and where the sale is held, what interest rate applies, what time it starts, where it is advertised, whether to pre-register, which payment forms are accepted and who checks are payable to, what happens to unsold liens, whether bids can be mailed in, how to decode the property codes, and how foreclosure works if a lien does not redeem [eNKIUQC6io0 @ 00:01:17]. The sharpest question is last year's lien count versus attendance: 30 liens and 50 bidders is a pass, while 200 to 500 liens and 20 bidders is the target, because the prior sale is a performance indicator for the next one [eNKIUQC6io0 @ 00:05:44]. Bill Miller adds that delinquent lists show up online, in the newspaper, or by request from the county office, sometimes for a fee, and that counties run sales once or several times a year, some online and some in person only [PRTEvlETNdk @ 00:01:44]. Ted Thomas shows the scale on newsprint: Hillsborough County's paper alone carries 25,000 to 40,000 certificates, with a couple of million certificates available nationally [JcAwqIfK0vo @ 00:10:13].

The leftover pile is where several operators hunt. Bill Miller says liens that fail to sell at auction can go over the counter with no bidding and no competition, often purchasable online and sometimes on credit, because counties want that inventory gone fast [PRTEvlETNdk @ 00:02:37]. Saen Higgins calls it assignment purchasing: ask what happens to unsold certificates, grab the second list that drops about 30 days after the sale, and look for aged paper, such as a 2021 lien bought in 2024, which becomes a foreclosable tax lien certificate the day you buy it [G44d74hIS_0 @ 00:09:40]. Dustin Hahn concedes that 90 percent of leftover liens are junk for a reason, but says the 10 percent of buyers willing to put in elbow grease find great deals, including certificates that have sat two years and can head into foreclosure within months [eNKIUQC6io0 @ 00:03:59]. On the back end, Tax Sale Secrets prices the rare foreclosure: one holder had just under $10,000 in delinquent taxes on a property worth just under $30,000, another just under $30,000 on a property valued around $650,000, each with an estimated $2,000 to $5,000 in attorney and foreclosure fees, which is where buying property for pennies on the dollar actually shows up [fIPCLCdZlAU @ 00:08:59].

callout.title: Edges the practitioners actually use
callout.body: These are the moves speakers say separate working investors from people who just read the auction list.
items: In Florida, a near-zero bid still collects the 5 percent floor if the owner redeems fast, but a 0 percent bid gets no minimum at all [Lien Ledger — H9fPhqUYPfc @ 00:04:40]
Ask the county how many liens sold last year and how many people attended; 200 to 500 liens with 20 bidders beats 30 liens with 50 [Dustin Hahn — eNKIUQC6io0 @ 00:05:44]
Work the unsold inventory list that appears about 30 days after the sale and target aged liens you can foreclose on immediately [Saen Higgins — G44d74hIS_0 @ 00:09:40]
When a foreclosed house needs to move, big ugly signs and Craigslist pull buyers; the exit is taught alongside the buy [Gerald Harris — nMj50Itu21Q @ 00:10:08]

sop_steps.title: Call the county with the full script
sop_steps.action: Google the county tax assessor phone number and call instead of browsing the website.
sop_steps.detail: Ask when and where the sale is held, the interest rate, start time, where it is advertised, and get on the mailing list for auction lists [Dustin Hahn — eNKIUQC6io0 @ 00:01:17]

sop_steps.title: Pull and decode the delinquent list
sop_steps.action: Get the list online, from the newspaper, or by request, and ask for the property code key.
sop_steps.detail: Request the delinquent list from the county office, paying a fee if required, and confirm whether the sale runs once or multiple times a year [realestatewealthguy — PRTEvlETNdk @ 00:01:44]

sop_steps.title: Look at every property and set an exit
sop_steps.action: Never bid on a number from the list without seeing the property and planning what you will do with it.
sop_steps.detail: Unseen bids land investors with chicken farms or hurricane- and fire-damaged property; decide the exit strategy before bidding [Ted Thomas — JcAwqIfK0vo @ 00:11:59]

sop_steps.title: Register, fund, buy and track deadlines
sop_steps.action: Confirm registration and payment form, buy at auction or over the counter, then calendar the expiration date.
sop_steps.detail: Miss the lien expiration date without getting paid or foreclosing and the deal is null and void and you lose the money [Invest with Wesley — n7l4w1FaXS4 @ 00:04:58]

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split among these operators is whether a lien is a loan or a back door into a house. Lien Ledger frames the investor as basically a lender, pointing to Washington, D.C.'s ten-year review of 9,395 tax-sale properties: 70% redeemed, 16% canceled, 13% still in progress, and just 1% ended in foreclosure [H9fPhqUYPfc @ 00:03:55]. The same channel flags Tyler versus Hennepin County, where a Minnesota county sold a condo for $40,000 over a $15,000 debt and the Supreme Court ruled unanimously that the surplus equity belongs to the owner, putting the back-taxes-for-a-house dream on shakier legal ground [H9fPhqUYPfc @ 00:06:34]. Dustin Hahn plays the opposite hand. He agrees 95% redeem, but calls the 5% that do not the life-changing home runs, describing a $100,000 house with $2,000 in back taxes where you end up in for about $5,000 after two more years of delinquent taxes and foreclosure costs [jwFVT7nCrg8 @ 00:01:47]. Ted Thomas goes further, arguing annual taxes run 1 or 2% of value, so two years of taxes puts you at roughly 4% of value with the mortgage wiped off the property [JcAwqIfK0vo @ 00:08:25]. Operators have to decide which model they are underwriting before they ever raise a bidder number.

Headline yields are the second fault line. Tax Lien Bestie Sabrina pitches state rates as flat numbers, Alabama at 12%, Florida 18%, Georgia 20% and Texas 25%, with the county cutting you a check for your money back plus that rate [VH9CbLJ5Erk @ 00:01:07]. Lien Ledger counters that those are ceilings: Florida bidding opens at 18% and drops in quarter-point steps, the lowest rate wins, and contested liens collapse toward zero. The play is Florida's 5% minimum on face value, which applies to any bid above 0%; a $1,000 lien bid at a quarter of 1% that redeems in three months pays $50, roughly 20% annualized, while the same lien sitting two years earns about 5% total [H9fPhqUYPfc @ 00:05:06]. Tranquillity sidesteps the auction entirely, claiming over-the-counter Florida liens are the way to assure the 18% rate because they are picked up without facing competition [VdRy2aZvV-Y @ 00:02:26]. Saen Higgins describes yet another structure, saying Chicago runs 18% for the first six months and another 18% for each following six-month block, stacking for three years until it is over 100% [G44d74hIS_0 @ 00:05:06]. The fight is less about whose number is right than about which statute, bid method and redemption clock sits behind it.

Leftover inventory and venue choice split the field too. Dustin Hahn admits that when commenters say over-the-counter liens are all junk, 90% of the time that is true, but argues the 10% of operators with elbow grease and grit land great deals, including certificates that may have sat about two years and can be pushed into foreclosure within a couple of months [eNKIUQC6io0 @ 00:03:59]. Saen Higgins flatly rejects the junk assumption, calling unsold liens assignment purchasing, or AP buying, released on a second list about 30 days after the sale, and hunting liens that sat in inventory two to four years as what he calls foreclosable tax lien certificates [G44d74hIS_0 @ 00:08:47]. On venue, Hahn wants the attendance ratio before he commits: 30 liens and 50 attendees is a pass, while 200 to 500 liens and 20 bidders is the target, because the previous year's sale is a performance indicator for the next one [eNKIUQC6io0 @ 00:05:44]. Julia M. Spencer ranks the whole field by risk instead of competition, starting with Florida certificates she buys in bulk at the May sale, moving to Georgia sheriff's deeds that work as liens with no co-holders, and ending with deed sales where nobody comes back to redeem [q7Fb-u0lpiY @ 00:02:45].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The costliest mistakes these operators describe happen before the gavel drops. Ted Thomas, who says he has spent 30 years in certificates and deeds, names two auction errors that hit newcomers and experienced investors alike. The first is getting excited and bidding on property nobody has looked at, which is how you end up with a chicken farm, a hurricane-damaged house or a fire job [JcAwqIfK0vo @ 00:11:45]. The second is bidding off a number on a list with no exit strategy, bidding high to win and then owning something at a high price you cannot sell [JcAwqIfK0vo @ 00:12:26]. Julia M. Spencer reports the aftermath from a tax sale Facebook group, where an investor had to tear down a building, shut off the gas and water, notify authorities and pull permits on a parcel he bought at the sale; her rule is simply not to buy those properties, because a dumpy property is one you may have to pay to get rid of [q7Fb-u0lpiY @ 00:06:05]. Invest with Wesley applies the same filter to land, warning against a random lot in the middle of nowhere that no one cares about and steering toward property in a municipality you could easily renovate, rent or sell [n7l4w1FaXS4 @ 00:02:27].

Deadlines and foreclosure costs are the second trap. Lien Ledger walks the Florida timeline: after about two years you can apply for a tax deed, but if you do not apply within seven years the certificate expires, and applying can mean paying off other liens on the parcel plus fees and a title search, with other bidders free to outbid you at the deed sale [H9fPhqUYPfc @ 00:05:50]. Invest with Wesley puts it bluntly: miss the expiration date without getting paid or foreclosing and the whole deal is null and void, and you truly lose out on all of your money [n7l4w1FaXS4 @ 00:04:58]. Tranquillity echoes that some states require you to initiate foreclosure within a set window after buying, or you may lose your right to collect your investment [VdRy2aZvV-Y @ 00:08:06]. Even the wins carry a legal bill. Tax Sale Secrets showed two foreclosed certificates, one with just under $10,000 in delinquent taxes on a property valued just under $30,000 and another with just under $30,000 in taxes on a property worth around $650,000, and estimated each carried roughly two to five grand in attorney and foreclosure fees [fIPCLCdZlAU @ 00:08:59].

The third failure mode is dead capital. Lien Ledger warns that your money is locked up, you cannot always cash out a lien whenever you want, bankruptcy can freeze the process and delay your payout for years, and the interest you earn is generally taxed as ordinary income [H9fPhqUYPfc @ 00:07:17]. Tranquillity goes further on bankruptcy, saying the IRS and other creditors with claims on the property can get involved and leave the tax lien useless because they get paid back before you, and tells investors to work with real estate lawyers on local law [VdRy2aZvV-Y @ 00:12:36]. That warning sits in direct tension with the first-position pitch Tax Lien Code and Saen Higgins make elsewhere. Dustin Hahn flags a process failure on the deed side: if the county never notified the mortgage company and the property goes to auction, that lien holder can come back and protest the sale, which he calls one of the big things people get hung up on [jwFVT7nCrg8 @ 00:03:47]. Tax Sale Secrets adds that redemption can land at any time and is outside your control, so the full redemption period has to be planned as the duration of the investment [fIPCLCdZlAU @ 00:10:02].

callout.title: Four Checks Before Capital Leaves the Account
callout.body: Every item below comes from a loss, reversal or bottleneck these practitioners described from the auction floor and the foreclosure file.
items: No bid on any parcel you have not looked at and have no exit strategy for, because bidding high just to win leaves you owning at a price you cannot sell [Ted Thomas — JcAwqIfK0vo @ 00:12:26].
Log every redemption and expiration date on the day you buy; in Florida, no deed application within seven years means the certificate expires [Lien Ledger — H9fPhqUYPfc @ 00:05:50].
Pass on demolition-grade structures where gas, water shutoffs, authority notices and permits stand between you and any profit [Julia M. Spencer — q7Fb-u0lpiY @ 00:06:05].
Reserve roughly two to five grand per file for attorney and foreclosure fees before counting any pennies-on-the-dollar acquisition [Tax Sale Secrets — fIPCLCdZlAU @ 00:08:59].

action_checklist: Google your county tax assessor phone number, call, and ask when and where the tax lien sale is held, what interest rate is offered, what time it begins and where it is advertised [Dustin Hahn — eNKIUQC6io0 @ 00:01:00].
Ask whether you register the day of the sale or pre-register, what forms of payment are accepted, and exactly who to make checks out to [Dustin Hahn — eNKIUQC6io0 @ 00:02:36].
Get the delinquent property list online, in the newspaper or by calling the office, and be ready to pay a fee in counties that charge for it [realestatewealthguy — PRTEvlETNdk @ 00:01:28].
Ask what happens to unsold certificates and pull the second assignment list that comes out about 30 days after the sale [Saen Higgins — G44d74hIS_0 @ 00:09:01].
Start small: attend an auction online or in person, which is free, and bid on lower-cost liens to gain experience [The Economic Ninja — I65EN8ypVwo @ 00:07:53].

Run remote diligence off county property appraiser records and online documentation, the way Deb Murphy bought from British Columbia without stepping foot on the property [Gerald Harris — nMj50Itu21Q @ 00:18:54].

chapters.question_prompt: Should I buy tax liens, tax deeds, redeemable deeds, or chase surplus funds, and how do those models differ in ownership, returns, and work?
chapters.title: Liens vs. Deeds vs. Redeemable Deeds
chapters.subtitle: Interest Versus Ownership, Redemption Deeds and Hybrid States, Surplus Overages, State Strategy Comparisons, and Choosing a Model on a Small Budget
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners converge on one dividing line: a tax lien buys a claim plus statutory interest, a tax deed buys the property, and a redeemable deed hands over the deed subject to a final owner buy-back paid as a flat penalty. Lien redemption estimates run from 90% to 98%, so lien buyers price for yield while deed buyers price for discount, with Ted Thomas citing 10 to 20 cents on the dollar. Street numbers include $1,000 at 12% returning $120, an 18% lien redeemed in month one netting about 1.5%, Georgia's 20% penalty inside 12 months, and Texas windows as short as six months from the foreclosure date. The sharpest split is budget: Dustin Hahn pushes anyone under $20,000 into over-the-counter deeds, while Casey Deon steers sub-$100 budgets into liens and Sean Higgins calls liens and deeds the same process at different stages.

sections.heading: 1. The Practitioner Consensus: Paper, Property, or a Deed With a Clock
paragraphs: Every practitioner opens with the same dividing line: a tax lien buys a claim, a tax deed buys the property. Cecil Jones strips it to one word for a live room, telling students that a deed is ownership and a lien is not, because the lien buyer is simply paying somebody else's property taxes and getting a government-backed return in exchange [Yq9tyhYQJGY @ 00:01:28]. Ted Thomas says the certificate buyer owns 'only a piece of paper' with no possession, earning 16%, 18%, or 24% while it stays outstanding, whereas deed counties confiscate the property, wipe out the mortgage and other liens, and auction it for back taxes plus fees because the county is 'in the tax business, not in the property business' [jWaS4Y2Z1Mg @ 00:00:49]. Dustin Hahn frames the operator role the same way: in a lien state 'you are the bank' lending the county money at a guaranteed rate, while in a deed state 'you are the buyer' and pretty much get the property day-of [akAZkzeH2PY @ 00:00:00]. Lien Ledger calls one product a loan and the other a project, warns that picking wrong means either earning almost nothing or inheriting a mess, and closes with the line most operators end up repeating: liens pay you to wait, deeds pay you to work [ul1onF24UbM @ 00:00:00].

The second consensus point is that the overwhelming majority of liens never turn into property. Dustin Hahn puts redemption at 95% and names the biggest redeemer: the mortgage bank, because on a $200,000 house carrying $2,000 a year in taxes, three unpaid years lets the lien holder foreclose, and if the bank does not redeem, the lien holder wipes the bank out [wemMjCnrX34 @ 00:01:09]. Casey Deon of Tax Sale Academy uses 90 to 95%, which is why the lien side gets described as a check in the mailbox once the research is done up front, with all the work front-loaded before the bid [oKQjnGAQlGs @ 00:02:28]. The Tax Sale Secrets hosts put lien redemption at 'more than 95%' [0adTzNpuLtk @ 00:03:51], then draw the contrast that defines the third system: redemption deeds, which they estimate redeem around 50% of the time or less [0adTzNpuLtk @ 00:11:13]. The Residential Buyer goes higher still, saying 98% of owners pay off the certificate with interest before the investor ever gets to file for foreclosure [2S4mkxCrOhM @ 00:01:22]. The shared operator takeaway: buy a lien expecting a yield, not a house, and treat the foreclosure as the rare home run rather than the plan.

The baseline prerequisite nobody skips is knowing the dirt under the paper, and knowing which system the target state runs. Ted Thomas holds up a Jacksonville, Florida newspaper listing 30,000 certificates with no pictures and mocks buyers who just point at one and buy, because a lot of certificates sit on worthless property; the fix is to go look at it, which on the lien side 'ends your work' [PSfIJ8cKE5I @ 00:04:41]. Casey Deon makes the same point from the collateral side: a lien not attached to valuable real estate 'does absolutely zero good,' so the research burden survives even on the passive product [FgLt0Zd5dxo @ 00:03:41]. On system choice, the Tax Sale Secrets hosts stress that state law decides whether a jurisdiction is a lien, deed, or redemption-deed state, and that once an operator understands those three fundamentals, property tax enforcement anywhere in the country becomes readable [0adTzNpuLtk @ 00:00:17]. Sean Higgins adds the scale: over 5,000 taxing jurisdictions, and every state plus Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, and Guam runs some form of lien or deed sale, with the county's position superseding the bank and even the IRS [IH1JGgxRwIg @ 00:01:41]. Casey also tells students that where they live should not dictate what they buy [FgLt0Zd5dxo @ 00:01:11].

sections.heading: 2. Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Lien math is simple interest on a small check, and the timing of redemption decides the real yield. Casey Deon's walk-through: $1,000 of back taxes in a 12% state returns $120 if the owner redeems at the end of year one, quality liens typically cost $300 to $1,000 even though some sell for $50 or $100, and 12 to 18-ish percent returns are 'not uncommon' [FgLt0Zd5dxo @ 00:02:42]. Lien Ledger runs a $3,000 lien at 12% simple for two years to $720 of interest, then flags the catch: redeem in month one and you earn one month of interest, and in competitive Florida counties bidders knock the 18% cap far lower, because 'competition eats the headline number' [ul1onF24UbM @ 00:04:18]. Cecil Jones makes the same point with Florida's 18%: a lien paid next month earns 18 divided by 12, about 1.5%, not the headline rate [Yq9tyhYQJGY @ 00:02:03]. On the ceiling, Ted Thomas quotes 16, 18, and 24 percent with Chicago paying up to 36% [x3XX9ysKcUA @ 00:04:16], and describes bidding $100,000 of back taxes on a huge shopping center because the certificate paid 16% against roughly 1% at Bank of America [x3XX9ysKcUA @ 00:05:53].

Deed economics run on discount, and redeemable-deed economics run on a flat penalty. Lien Ledger's deed model: buy a house for $20,000, add $10,000 in repairs and costs, sell for $60,000, and net $30,000, or 100% on cash, while noting that $20,000 buys either one house or about six $3,000 liens, a concentrated bet against a spread bet [ul1onF24UbM @ 00:04:42]. The Tax Sale Secrets hosts point to an Ohio auction where properties were back on the market within 30 days of acquisition, and recent deals showing about $100,000 of potential profit after estimated rehab [0adTzNpuLtk @ 00:07:58]. Cecil Jones paid $1,500 for a Lake Jackson waterfront parcel in Georgia, received the deed on the spot, and explains that a redemption inside Georgia's 12-month window pays a flat 20% penalty even if the owner comes back the next day [Yq9tyhYQJGY @ 00:03:17]. Casey Deon sizes the upside at as much as 25% within six months, so a $100,000 purchase redeemed at month six returns $125,000, but warns redeemable deeds cost much closer to deed prices than lien prices [FgLt0Zd5dxo @ 00:11:34]. The Tax Sale Secrets crew adds that when a Texas parcel opens at 10 and sells at 50, the owner owes 25% on the full high bid [0adTzNpuLtk @ 00:12:00].

Execution starts with a phone call and ends with a title company. Dustin Hahn's first move is to call the county and, if staff say they don't do tax liens, ask what happens when people don't pay their property taxes; 'tax defaulted list' or 'sheriff's sale' tells you the system [akAZkzeH2PY @ 00:01:01]. Mika Coleman relies on the Tax Sale Resources platform to flag whether a state is a redeemable-deed or straight-deed state, and warns that redemption periods often run longer on homesteaded properties than non-homesteaded ones [tMIwxs2U5JM @ 00:01:18]. William of Premier Wealth Builders says most California deed auctions run online on sites such as Bid4Assets, Clark County, Nevada sold in person, and Virginia winners must go to court for approval; because a tax deed is not a warranty deed and carries a cloud on title, a generic First American office quoted three years before insuring, so the play is the specific title company that insures right away plus a good real estate attorney [RvfjpH1PWxE @ 00:05:57]. On funding, Ted Thomas reports a Michigan student named Bill bought 60 properties in 60 months on a credit card, and Ted put 30% down by card on a $300,000 New York property [jWaS4Y2Z1Mg @ 00:05:52].

callout.title: How the pros tilt the odds before they bid
callout.body: Four edges practitioners use to steer redemption odds, penalty timing, and margin in their favor.
items: Buy liens further into the redemption period, or county-held leftovers, to start foreclosing quicker instead of waiting out the full clock [Tax Sale Secrets — 0adTzNpuLtk @ 00:02:55]
For pure yield, target occupied homes and businesses with a high likelihood of redeeming; to land property, target liens with a lower chance of redemption [Tax Sale Academy — oKQjnGAQlGs @ 00:08:22]

sop_steps.title: Identify the county's enforcement system
sop_steps.action: Call the county treasurer or tax office and ask what happens when owners don't pay.
sop_steps.detail: If staff say they don't do tax liens, ask what happens in the county when people don't pay their property taxes; 'tax defaulted list' or 'sheriff's sale' reveals the system [Dustin Hahn — akAZkzeH2PY @ 00:01:01]

sop_steps.title: Physically verify the collateral
sop_steps.action: Pull the published list and go look at every parcel before raising a hand.
sop_steps.detail: The Jacksonville list carried 30,000 certificates with no pictures; buyers who just point and buy end up with worthless property, so go look at it and confirm it has value [Ted Thomas — PSfIJ8cKE5I @ 00:04:58]

sop_steps.title: Run the three pre-bid checks
sop_steps.action: Check value, check what else is owed, check the state's redemption rules.
sop_steps.detail: Skip vacant lots and ruined buildings because cheap usually means cheap for a reason, and read each county's terms, deadlines, and deposits before bringing a dollar [Lien Ledger — ul1onF24UbM @ 00:07:18]

sop_steps.title: Price the exit, including foreclosure cost
sop_steps.action: Add the lien price to attorney foreclosure fees and compare against resale value.

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over which product a thin bankroll should touch first. Dustin Hahn tells anyone holding less than $20,000 to skip liens and start with over-the-counter tax deeds, because liens are 'not the fastest way to go' and Hahn's team likes speed [wemMjCnrX34 @ 00:02:51]. Casey at Tax Sale Academy runs the opposite playbook: with a budget under $100, buy liens as the entry point to get your feet wet, while conceding that deeds can still be had for a couple of grand or even less than a grand in some areas [oKQjnGAQlGs @ 00:09:46]. Ted Thomas backs the small-ticket lien route, citing certificates at $2,000 to $5,000 and even $500, while warning that most tax deeds do not sell for $5,000 [PSfIJ8cKE5I @ 00:01:56]. Tax Sale Secrets flips the framing again, calling liens a strategy 'for people that have money' who can park capital and collect a rate, and reserving tax deeds and redemption deeds for anyone trying to build wealth [0adTzNpuLtk @ 00:02:16]. The same dollar figure lands on opposite sides depending on which desk you sit at: Hahn optimizes for velocity and quick buys, while Casey and Thomas optimize for cheap entry and low effort. Pick the camp that matches your clock, not the one with the loudest pitch.

Every speaker agrees most liens redeem, but nobody agrees on the number, and the gap matters for anyone underwriting a foreclosure play. Ted Thomas puts payoff at 97 percent of certificates and describes the interest landing in your checking account with a phone notice [PSfIJ8cKE5I @ 00:03:42]. The Residential Buyer quotes 98 percent [2S4mkxCrOhM @ 00:01:22], while Casey at Tax Sale Academy uses a 90 to 96 percent band that shifts with where and what you buy [FgLt0Zd5dxo @ 00:03:04]. Lien Ledger brings city-level numbers that cut well below the headline: about 70 percent of sold properties redeemed in Washington DC with only about 1 percent going to foreclosure, and roughly 80 percent of certificates paid back in Baltimore [ul1onF24UbM @ 00:01:48]. Yield is just as contested. Thomas sells 16, 18 and 24 percent, but Lien Ledger warns that Florida's 18 percent cap gets bid down at auction until competition eats the headline number, and that a month-one payoff earns one month of interest. The practical split: Thomas frames the certificate as predictable, certain and secure money, while Lien Ledger calls it a slow state-backed loan that is boring on purpose, with a catch. Underwrite to the realized rate and the realized redemption timing, not the ceiling the state sets by law.

Redeemable deeds draw the widest spread of opinions. Tax Sale Secrets estimates that if 95 percent of liens redeem, probably 50 percent or less of redemption deeds do, and says chances run pretty low in Delaware's 60-day window or in Texas, where the six-month clock starts at foreclosure rather than the sale [0adTzNpuLtk @ 00:11:13]. Cecil Jones prefers Georgia and Texas outright because the 20 percent Georgia penalty is owed even if the owner redeems the next day, which beats a lien paying 18 divided by 12 for a one-month hold [Yq9tyhYQJGY @ 00:03:41]. Mika Coleman calls the redeemable deed a win-win, either the property or a return like 25 percent on a six-month redemption, but flags that homesteaded properties often carry longer windows [tMIwxs2U5JM @ 00:00:58]. Casey at Tax Sale Academy agrees on the 25 percent upside yet gates it behind staying power, since you pay much closer to tax deed prices and tie up capital for six or 12 months [FgLt0Zd5dxo @ 00:12:16]. The operator split is about liquidity: Jones and Coleman chase the fixed penalty, while Casey warns that anyone who needs every penny all the time should not wait a property out. Tax Sale Secrets also notes counties never use the term; the hosts coined the redemption deed label back in 2004 and 2005.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most common lien loss is buying paper secured by dirt nobody wants. Ted Thomas holds up a Jacksonville, Florida newspaper with 30,000 certificates and no pictures, and describes buyers who just point at one and buy it; a lot of tax lien certificates sit on worthless property, so you have to go look at it [PSfIJ8cKE5I @ 00:04:58]. Casey at Tax Sale Academy runs the math on what happens next: pay $1,500 for a lien, pay an attorney roughly $2,500 to foreclose, and you have $4,000 in a landlocked vacant lot that might be worth three or four grand, while unresearched code violations can turn the deal into a negative return [FgLt0Zd5dxo @ 00:04:14]. Lien Ledger names the same risk bluntly: if the house is a condemned shack or an empty lot, foreclosure gets you nothing worth having [ul1onF24UbM @ 00:05:06]. Tax Sale Secrets adds the hybrid-state version of the trap, where a lien that ends up at a county deed sale with no bidder is probably a property you never wanted anyway [0adTzNpuLtk @ 00:05:17]. The rule across all four: the rate is irrelevant when the collateral is junk, so value the land before you price the certificate, and walk from anything cheap for a reason.

Deed buyers get hurt after the gavel, not before it. The Residential Buyer warns that prior mortgages usually clear at foreclosure, but municipal liens and code violations ride through the sale to the new buyer, and since no one lets you into the home, you may be buying a literal meth lab [2S4mkxCrOhM @ 00:03:06]. Casey at Tax Sale Academy says the moment you win, it is yours good or bad; if somebody burns the house down that morning you need to know, and you inherit occupants and code violations immediately [oKQjnGAQlGs @ 00:09:12]. The same trainer reports new investors who haphazardly buy and only discover at resale that they own junk land, landlocked parcels, or lots too small to build on [FgLt0Zd5dxo @ 00:09:44]. Premier Wealth Builders flags the exit bottleneck: a tax deed is not a warranty deed, the cloud on title has to be cleared, and the local First American Title office may refuse title insurance for three years unless you use a title company that will insure now [RvfjpH1PWxE @ 00:05:57]. Price every deed bid as acquisition plus surviving municipal liens, code fines, occupant removal and title clearing, then confirm access or drive-by condition before the auction, or the discount evaporates on the first invoice.

The economics breaks are quieter but just as costly. Cecil Jones warns that a Florida lien advertised at 18 percent and redeemed next month pays roughly 1.5 percent, which is why Jones routes lien-style money into Georgia redeemable deeds where the 20 percent penalty is owed even on a one-day redemption [Yq9tyhYQJGY @ 00:04:13]. Lien Ledger runs the deed side: buy at $20,000, add $10,000 in repairs and costs, sell at $60,000 and net $30,000, but if repairs double and the house sits for a year that profit shrinks fast, and on the lien side a $3,000 certificate at 12 percent simple returns $720 after two years of locked cash [ul1onF24UbM @ 00:04:42]. Casey at Tax Sale Academy tells the surplus story as a cautionary benchmark: a $3,000 overage drew about a dozen chasers quoting 25 to 60 percent fees, and the paperwork took five or six minutes to file solo [FgLt0Zd5dxo @ 00:15:31]. Premier Wealth Builders adds a jurisdiction trap: in Virginia a winning bid has to go to court for approval, while in California you own it right now [RvfjpH1PWxE @ 00:04:06]. Model hold time, court approval time, competition and fee drag before the bid goes in, not after the gavel.

callout.body: Every one of these gates comes from a loss, a near-miss or a hard warning reported by the practitioners. Clear all four or do not raise your hand.
items: Look at the property and confirm value before buying any certificate, because a lot of tax lien certificates sit on worthless property [Ted Thomas — PSfIJ8cKE5I @ 00:04:58].

chapters.question_prompt: How do the rules, rates, and sale procedures differ across the major tax lien states?
chapters.title: The State-by-State Lien Playbook
chapters.subtitle: Florida 18% Certificates, New Jersey Sales, Arizona Law Changes, Illinois and Cook County 36% Penalties, Maryland 6–20%, Indiana, Georgia, and Kentucky's 11-Year Liens
chapters.executive_summary: Operators working Florida, New Jersey, Illinois, Arizona, Indiana, Maryland and Georgia converge on one rule: there is no national lien playbook, only state and even municipal rulebooks. Bob Diamond, Dustin Hahn and Ted Thomas agree liens are an interest play where 90 to 97 percent redeem, with Chicago's south and west sides dropping to about 70 percent. Street mechanics vary sharply: Florida and New Jersey bid down from 18 percent, Arizona from 16 with no penalty floor, Illinois offers 12 percent subsequent taxes, Indiana pays flat 10 and 15 percent penalties, Maryland stacks interest-free premiums, and Georgia's redeemable deeds escalate from 20 to 50 percent. Paperwork such as New Jersey recording and the Illinois 22-5 notice decides whether a lien holds. The fights center on zero-percent bidding, Florida's foreclosure path, and whether the Texas 25 percent redemption penalty is ever actually collected.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator here starts from the same premise: there is no national tax lien game, only state-by-state rulebooks. Ted Thomas hammers that the legislature writes the rules and pushes them down to the counties, so Texas plays differently than Indiana and Indiana differently than Pennsylvania, which means you read the auction rules every single time [LsEFs7uqzbA @ 00:00:39]. Dustin Hahn sorts the map into buckets: red tax deed states where you are the buyer, green tax lien states where you are the lender collecting a government-set rate, redeemable deed states such as Texas, Georgia, South Carolina and Tennessee, and hybrids like California that now do a little of both [VK7ChKB-gNU @ 00:02:14]. Saen Higgins calls Florida a dual state for exactly that reason: an 18 percent lien with a two-year redemption that, if unpaid, gets pushed through the county into a tax deed sale where the lienholder is the opening bid [z3AT7UeX52o @ 00:00:12]. Sabrina of Tax Lien Bestie adds that New Jersey breaks even the county model, because sales run at the municipality level across more than 500 independent jurisdictions, each free to set its own percentages and bidding style [G8iotxNSgRg @ 00:00:38]. The first job, before any capital moves, is classifying the state and then the specific jurisdiction running the sale.

The second point of agreement is blunt: buy liens for the yield and treat the property as a rare bonus. Bob Diamond tells Cook County bidders not to think of the general sale as an acquisition strategy, because 96 percent of the time the owner pays and you never get the house, and when a valuable parcel does slip through unredeemed Diamond calls it a lottery play you cannot build a plan around [B0WBR5swuac @ 00:00:50]. Dustin Hahn puts the Illinois redemption rate at 97 percent and says the only way to lose money is to screw up and buy a totally wrong piece of land [rYcTmrny9JQ @ 00:05:45], while in Maryland Hahn uses 95 percent and frames the occasional non-redeemer as the home run that pays for the patience [hK5QVUgFulI @ 00:03:46]. Ted Thomas lands in the same zone for Indiana, estimating that 90 or 95 percent of owners come forward, pay the taxes and then pay the investor all of the penalty [LsEFs7uqzbA @ 00:09:00]. The shared operating logic follows directly: size every position for interest income, assume the check comes back, and underwrite the deed scenario only as upside that must still be worth owning if it actually lands in your lap.

Every speaker who addresses bidding mistakes names the same one: buying a parcel number you never looked at. Ted Thomas calls it the biggest mistake at any lien or deed auction, asking what happens when the house burned down or sits next to a chicken farm or pig farm, and insisting on boots on the ground or a stand-in who goes and looks [LsEFs7uqzbA @ 00:12:05]. Working an Illinois question, Thomas holds up a raw county list and points out that bidders grab item 777 at 18 percent simply because it costs 500 dollars, without ever seeing what they bought [QQ4bx7vLNS4 @ 00:10:58]. Sabrina pushes the same discipline in New Jersey: never buy what you have not seen, because the lot could be burned down, beyond repair, or a former gas station with something buried underground, and the county only cares about the parcel ID, not whether it includes half of someone's garage [G8iotxNSgRg @ 00:06:26]. Bob Diamond closes the loop for Cook County, telling bidders to put eyes on each property because the money is ultimately backed either by an owner who wants it back badly enough to redeem or by a parcel you genuinely want to own [B0WBR5swuac @ 00:08:05]. Research is the price of admission.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The dominant lien mechanic is the bid-down, and every speaker flags the same pressure point at the bottom of it. In Florida, Saen Higgins watches bidders drive the 18 percent rate down through 17, 16 and 14 until some take it to zero, banking on an early-payment penalty Higgins believes is 5 percent; Higgins and the CFO call that smoking hopium, and Higgins refuses to play it [Lcz3UJEz_oM @ 00:07:21]. Brian of Tax Sale Resources warns that Arizona copies the Florida bid-down from a 16 percent ceiling but strips out the floor: no automatic 5 percent, so a zero bid earns nothing, and some market reports show average winning rates sinking below 1 percent [46pI-T2mHZs @ 00:02:00]. New Jersey pays a flat redemption penalty of 2 percent on liens over 200 dollars, 4 percent at 5,000 and 6 percent at 10,000, which is why Tax Sale Secrets sees bidders drop to zero chasing that penalty plus a shot at owning the property [-1glwzvZBoQ @ 00:01:55]. Bob Diamond explains why Illinois bidders also go to zero: whoever holds the first lien can pay the following years' unpaid taxes at 12 percent without competing against Fred at 10 percent or Lisa at 8 percent on the auction floor [bFO7QIn_w3U @ 00:01:53].

Not every lien state plays the bid-down, and operators working premium and penalty states run different math. Casey Diamond of Tax Sale Academy lays out Indiana's overbid auction: the minimum bid is taxes, penalties and interest, bidders compete upward, and the investor earns a flat 10 percent penalty on the taxes and fees if redeemed in the first six months and 15 percent from months six through twelve, while the overbid itself earns only 5 percent per year [K4wAHGQcqzQ @ 00:00:50]. Dustin Hahn walks Maryland's premium bid with real numbers: a 1,000 dollar tax lien on a 100,000 dollar house, a 10,000 dollar premium on top, interest paid only on the 1,000, the premium returned flat on redemption, and if one of twenty liens fails to redeem the house lands for roughly 16 to 17 thousand all-in after back taxes and foreclosure [hK5QVUgFulI @ 00:04:22]. In Illinois, Hahn frames the 36 percent ceiling as roughly 3 percent per month stacked in multiples [rYcTmrny9JQ @ 00:04:03]. Ted Thomas pitches Georgia's redeemable deed as the escalator: 20 percent whenever the owner pays inside 365 days, then 30, 40 and 50 percent if it rolls into years two, three and four [DPKvfqp7T9g @ 00:02:26].

Winning the lien is only half the job; the paperwork decides whether it holds. Sabrina tells New Jersey buyers they have 90 days to record the tax certificate with the county clerk and must fill out the county's index page correctly, or it gets mailed back unrecorded [G8iotxNSgRg @ 00:06:08]. In Illinois, Bob Diamond calls the 22-5 notice the hinge of the deal: it goes to the last assessee within four months and 15 days of the sale, Cook County demands strict compliance, and a botched notice means you just paid someone else's taxes, which is why Diamond wants an experienced Illinois tax-sale attorney preparing and serving it [bFO7QIn_w3U @ 00:03:36]. Florida runs the other direction: after two unredeemed years, Saen Higgins calls the county, pays its fee, brings the taxes current, and the county forecloses into a deed sale where the lienholder's roughly 5,000 dollar stake becomes the opening bid; if someone bids it to 50,000, the lienholder walks with principal plus interest [Lcz3UJEz_oM @ 00:05:13]. In Arizona, Brian adds a post-auction play: liens that sold at auction but were never funded drop onto the over-the-counter list at the full 16 percent, first come first served [46pI-T2mHZs @ 00:04:31].

callout.title: Edges the Lien Operators Actually Use
callout.body: Four plays the practitioners run to squeeze yield out of crowded bid-down auctions and post-sale lists.
items: Pull Arizona's over-the-counter list as soon as it posts after the auction, timing it with the county so it includes liens that sold but never funded, and collect the full statutory 16 percent [Tax Sale Resources — 46pI-T2mHZs @ 00:04:50].

In Illinois, hold the first lien and pay each following year's unpaid taxes at 12 percent with no competing bidders, which can make up for a near-zero first-year rate [Bob Diamond - America's Tax Sale Attorney — bFO7QIn_w3U @ 00:02:28].

Write your minimum rate on the list before the auction starts, such as 8.5 percent, and walk the moment bidding hits 8.49 percent instead of catching ego-based auction fever [Bob Diamond - America's Tax Sale Attorney — B0WBR5swuac @ 00:05:05].

On RealAuction in New Jersey, the platform only lets you spend up to your deposit, so you can bid across many liens hunting your target rate without over-winning [Tax Sale Secrets — -1glwzvZBoQ @ 00:07:55].

sop_steps.title: Classify the state and lock the calendar
sop_steps.action: Confirm lien, redeemable deed or hybrid status, then pull each jurisdiction's sale dates and registration rules.
sop_steps.detail: Indiana sales are handled by the county treasurer's office, typically in the fall; search the county name plus 'treasurer's office' and read its tax sale section [Tax Sale Academy — K4wAHGQcqzQ @ 00:02:36]. In Arizona, start looking in January because auctions run in early February and bids may need to be loaded ahead of time [Tax Sale Resources — 46pI-T2mHZs @ 00:13:51].

sop_steps.title: Screen lien-to-value and parcel boundaries
sop_steps.action: Run an online first-pass review of every target parcel's value and verify exactly what the parcel includes.
sop_steps.detail: Tax Sale Secrets flagged a 6,000 dollar lien on a property valued at 551,000, roughly 1 percent of value, as a highly secured lien [Tax Sale Secrets — -1glwzvZBoQ @ 00:06:52]. Sabrina checks each Parcel Dream property profile to confirm the photo matches what the parcel actually contains [Tax Lien Bestie | Sabrina — G8iotxNSgRg @ 00:07:21].

sop_steps.title: Set rate floors and carry fee cash
sop_steps.action: Fix a minimum acceptable rate per lien before the sale and bring money beyond the exact bid amounts.
sop_steps.detail: Decide your floor beforehand and stop bidding the instant the rate drops below it [Bob Diamond - America's Tax Sale Attorney — B0WBR5swuac @ 00:05:05]. Ted Thomas had a client lose a won property because the client lacked an extra 40 dollars for transfer fees, so never write the check for the exact amount [Ted Thomas — QQ4bx7vLNS4 @ 00:08:53].

sop_steps.title: Perfect the lien after the sale
sop_steps.action: Record the certificate and serve every required notice on the statutory clock.
sop_steps.detail: New Jersey buyers have 90 days to record the certificate with the county clerk and must file the index page correctly [Tax Lien Bestie | Sabrina — G8iotxNSgRg @ 00:06:08]. Illinois buyers must send the 22-5 notice within four months and 15 days of the sale, with strict compliance in Cook County [Bob Diamond - America's Tax Sale Attorney — bFO7QIn_w3U @ 00:03:36].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Florida splits the bench. Saen Higgins runs it as a two-lane state: buy the lien at the late-May sale, ride out the two-year redemption, then have the county foreclose and push the parcel to a deed sale where the lien holder is the opening bid. Higgins frames the payoff bluntly: buying the lien does not insure you the property, but it does insure the interest rate, because if someone bids the deed up to $50,000 the lien holder still walks with principal plus interest [Lcz3UJEz_oM @ 00:05:32]. In the shorter Florida breakdown, Higgins calls this the dual component and notes that anyone who wants dirt can skip the lien entirely and buy deeds at the monthly county sales [z3AT7UeX52o @ 00:02:26]. Dustin Hahn reads the same structure as a weakness: Florida is one of the only states where an unpaid lien cannot be foreclosed and taken outright, so Hahn's team does not love Florida liens and points to the plentiful weekly deed sales as the cooler play [VK7ChKB-gNU @ 00:02:51]. Casey Diamond of Tax Sale Academy points out that Arizona's new excess-proceeds rules now push lien holders into a nearly identical structure, where the holder recovers money plus interest and a deed buyer takes the parcel, so the Florida argument is spreading into other lien states [mwdmkHEw0Rc @ 00:06:43].

The zero-percent bid is the sharpest split on the floor. Higgins watches Florida bidders drive rates to zero, calls them knuckleheads, and says they are chasing a roughly 5% early-redemption penalty; in Higgins's words, hope isn't a plan, and the CFO calls it smoking hopium [Lcz3UJEz_oM @ 00:07:21]. Bob Diamond argues zero can be rational in Illinois, because the first-lien holder gets to pay the subsequent years' taxes at a flat 12% without bidding against Fred or Lisa, and the owner has to redeem every year at once, so the subsequent taxes can make up for earning nothing on year one [bFO7QIn_w3U @ 00:01:36]. The Tax Sale Secrets hosts report New Jersey bidders dropping past zero on purpose, because the redemption penalty of 2% to 6% is paid regardless of when the lien redeems, and the bidder keeps a shot at owning the property [-1glwzvZBoQ @ 00:01:55]. Brian, the Tax Sale Resources CEO, says that logic dies in Arizona: there is no fast five, the bid rate is prorated, and a bid to zero earns nothing at all, which is the exact pit beginners fall into after learning the Florida bidding procedure and assuming Arizona runs the same way [46pI-T2mHZs @ 00:02:00]. The operator read: zero only pays where a flat penalty or a subsequent-tax lever sits behind it.

Redeemable-deed states trigger the next fight. Ted Thomas pitches Georgia as a passive play: the owner can redeem anytime inside 365 days and must pay a 20% penalty, and Thomas tells students to prefer not getting the property, letting the deed roll to 30% in year two, 40% in year three and 50% in year four [DPKvfqp7T9g @ 00:02:26]. Hahn calls the parallel Texas pitch a myth: an owner who could not cover $10,000 in taxes now owes 25% on a $20,000 bid, so the buyer is generally always going to end up with the property, a point Hahn backs with the 50 or so Texas deals the team has done [VK7ChKB-gNU @ 00:03:45]. On straight lien states, the split is about what you are really buying. Bob Diamond tells Cook County bidders to stop treating the general sale as a property-acquisition strategy, since 96% of liens redeem and a valuable unredeemed parcel is a lottery play you cannot count on [B0WBR5swuac @ 00:00:34]. Diamond goes further, saying the scavenger sale, with no competition, no notices and no redemption periods, beats fighting it out with the hoi polloi at the lien auction, even after Diamond duked it out at auctions for many years before switching [bFO7QIn_w3U @ 00:09:46].

Whether to chase the biggest county or the small ones
Hahn says Cook County's 5.2 million people bring more competition and smaller counties can play better
Diamond says Cook County, being largest and containing Chicago, is where the most opportunity sits despite stricter rules

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Paperwork kills more returns than bidding does. Bob Diamond's Illinois warning: the 22-5 notice has to reach the last assessee within four months and 15 days of the sale, Cook County demands strict compliance while other counties allow only substantial compliance, and a botched or skipped notice means no deed, so the bidder has simply paid someone else's taxes; Diamond's fix is an experienced Illinois tax sale attorney who prepares, serves and defends the notice [bFO7QIn_w3U @ 00:03:36]. In New Jersey, Sabrina of Tax Lien Bestie says the buyer has 90 days to record the certificate with the county clerk, and an index page filled out wrong gets mailed back unrecorded [G8iotxNSgRg @ 00:06:08]. The Tax Sale Secrets hosts state a tighter clock of 60 days to record with the tax collector, so the two practitioners do not agree on the deadline, and that gap is itself the trap for anyone buying across dozens of municipalities [-1glwzvZBoQ @ 00:02:16]. Ted Thomas adds a cash trap from the auction floor: clients have won properties, then could not cover the transfer charges, the auctioneer stopped the auction, and the buyer lost out over something like an extra 40 dollars, so Thomas says never to write checks for the exact amount and always carry extra money for fees [QQ4bx7vLNS4 @ 00:08:37].

Blind bidding is the second recurring loss. Ted Thomas names it the single biggest mistake at both lien and deed auctions: bidders who never look at the parcel end up owning a burned-down house or a lot next to a chicken or pig farm that will be hard to sell, and Thomas says to put boots on the ground or send someone else to look [LsEFs7uqzbA @ 00:12:05]. Bob Diamond layers in Chicago-specific risk: on the south and west side only about 70% of liens redeem versus 96% overall, and a house can land on the city demolition list while you hold the lien, leaving you with a vacant lot instead of the fix-up you thought you bought after a two-and-a-half-year wait [B0WBR5swuac @ 00:07:06]. Dustin Hahn warns against liens on swamp land or an old landfill, tells bidders to use Landglide so they know what they are buying, and says that with 97% of liens redeeming, the only way to lose money is to buy some totally wrong piece of land [rYcTmrny9JQ @ 00:05:45]. Sabrina adds a boundary check inside Parcel Dream, because the government only sees a parcel ID, and the photo may show half of someone's garage or backyard that is not actually included in what you are buying [G8iotxNSgRg @ 00:07:39].

The economics checks are state-specific, and several practitioners report the math breaking. Brian of Tax Sale Resources lays out why Arizona lien returns collapsed: no penalty, a three-year redemption before you can even file for a tax deed, three to four years before seeing any positive return, and institutional buyers willing to bid tiny rates because they are waiting on REO, with average rates in some counties falling below 1% [46pI-T2mHZs @ 00:06:28]. Casey Diamond reports the Arizona change that followed Tyler versus Hennepin County: when a lien holder moves to foreclose, the owner can request court review, and if the parcel should sell for at least $2,500 above everything owed, it goes to an excess-proceeds sale where the certificate holder gets capital plus interest instead of the property [mwdmkHEw0Rc @ 00:03:35]. Bob Diamond says the same case started a groundswell of changes and Illinois is one of the places shifting, so old information may be out of date [B0WBR5swuac @ 00:06:37]. In Maryland, Hahn flags dead money: the premium earns no interest, so a $10,000 premium stacked on a $1,000 lien only comes back as principal, and even the unredeemed home run lands around $16,000 to $17,000 all-in on a $100,000 house [hK5QVUgFulI @ 00:03:31].

callout.title: Four checks before any bid gets funded
callout.body: Every item below comes from a loss or near-miss the practitioners describe on the auction floor or in the post-sale paperwork. Clear all four before committing capital to a lien.
items: Write down your minimum acceptable rate before the auction starts and walk the second the bidding drops below it, because ego-driven auction fever is where bidders hand away their profit [Bob Diamond - America's Tax Sale Attorney — B0WBR5swuac @ 00:04:36].
Physically inspect the parcel or send someone to look, and know what you would sell it for before raising your hand [Ted Thomas — LsEFs7uqzbA @ 00:12:32].

Calendar the Illinois 22-5 notice deadline of four months and 15 days from the sale and have experienced tax sale counsel prepare and serve it [Bob Diamond - America's Tax Sale Attorney — bFO7QIn_w3U @ 00:03:36].

Confirm you are buying the first-position lien, because that priority is what lets you foreclose, and check whether the county only lets second- or third-year holders foreclose [Dustin Hahn — rYcTmrny9JQ @ 00:04:41].

chapters.pull_quote: Hope isn't a plan. Me and my CFO call that smoking hopium. — Saen Higgins (Lcz3UJEz_oM @ 00:07:35).
action_checklist: Call each Arizona county to learn when unfunded auction liens hit the over-the-counter list, then pull that list as soon as it is available to buy at the statutory 16% [Tax Sale Resources — 46pI-T2mHZs @ 00:04:50].

In Illinois, hold the first lien and pay the subsequent years' taxes yourself at a flat 12% so another investor cannot get in front of you [Bob Diamond - America's Tax Sale Attorney — bFO7QIn_w3U @ 00:02:28].

Register once on the New Jersey real auction platform, bid across multiple municipal sales, and let the deposit cap stop you from winning more liens than you can fund [Tax Sale Secrets — -1glwzvZBoQ @ 00:07:55].
Compute the lien-to-value ratio on every New Jersey lien and favor liens at roughly 1% or less of the property's value [Tax Sale Secrets — -1glwzvZBoQ @ 00:06:35].

Print the Kentucky county directory and call every county to find any that sell over-the-counter properties instead of sending them to the land bank [Tax Lien School Highlights - Dustin Hahn — VK7ChKB-gNU @ 00:01:44].

For Indiana, search the county name plus treasurer's office, read the tax sale section, and confirm whether the county runs the sale itself or through a third-party auction company [Tax Sale Academy — K4wAHGQcqzQ @ 00:02:36].

chapters.question_prompt: How do tax lien auction formats work, and how do bid-downs and premiums change my actual return?
chapters.title: Auction Formats and the Real Yield
chapters.subtitle: Interest Bid-Downs to 0.25%, Premium and Overbid States, Ownership-Interest Bidding, Interest Versus Penalty Rates, Premium Formulas, Colorado's 13%, and the Worst States for Returns
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners agree the statutory rate is only a ceiling and the auction format decides the real yield. Florida and Arizona bid interest down from 18% and 16%; New Jersey runs 18% to 0% and then flips into dollar premiums at 0% interest; Colorado and other overbid states fix the rate and auction the premium; Louisiana and Utah bid down ownership percentage instead. Institutional money and online platforms grind popular counties toward zero, yet a 0.25% Florida bid still collects a 5% penalty on fast redemption, Colorado pays about 13%, and Arizona proxy engines can award the full 16% to a lone bidder. Operators split on whether quarter-point fast-five plays and 1% ownership bids are smart bets or traps when liens sit unredeemed for years, and on whether to fight New Jersey institutions or pivot elsewhere.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner on this beat agrees on one thing first: the statutory rate printed in the law is a ceiling, and the auction format decides how much of it survives to your pocket. Casey Demmon of Tax Sale Academy lays out the bid-down engine plainly: the sale opens at the highest allowable rate set by statute, bidders call it down in steps, and whoever accepts the lowest rate takes the lien, with Florida opening at 18% and sliding through 16, 14, 12, 10, nine, eight [0XlgBwC8tog @ 00:00:49]. Julia M. Spencer frames it against a normal auction: the price is set and does not change, so competitors are not bidding the price up, they are bidding the interest down to the lowest number they can live with [NAHQ-7eWR_c @ 00:01:25]. Olivia at Smart Capital hammers the same point from the yield side, calling the 18%, 16%, and 24% headlines ceilings set by law rather than promises, because in a competitive county the 18% routinely gets bid down to a small fraction of the ceiling [TL6AIsoe5m0 @ 00:07:14]. Realauction's New Jersey walkthrough shows the extreme version: interest bids run from 18% to 0%, and once bidding passes zero it flips into dollar premiums tied to 0% interest [hKsLdKqVOE0 @ 00:00:54].

The second consensus point: premium, or overbid, formats invert the auction while freezing the rate. Casey Demmon describes premium states as ones where the interest rate is set by state statute and never changes, and the lien goes to whoever pays the most above the face value of the back taxes, with the gap between what is owed and what is paid called the premium or overbid [0I_mhnrF0So @ 00:01:05]. Brian Seinsticker of Tax Sale Resources says that whatever the local label, high bid premium, true bid premium, bid up, it is the traditional auction most people already picture, live or online, outbidding the other bidders in dollars [6hRZuHmCM0M @ 00:01:10]. The Tax Sale Secrets hosts put Colorado in this camp: a 3-year redemption under a premium bid system where a $1,200 lien gets bid to 1,201, 1,202, 1,203, and paying $5 or $10 over is effectively how you bid down your interest [stFlmSmpP3Q @ 00:01:43]. Smart Capital's Olivia adds that some counties run round-robin or rotational systems instead, and insists you know which system your county uses before you show up, because the winning strategy is completely different under each [TL6AIsoe5m0 @ 00:17:46]. Misread the format and you misread the yield before placing a single bid.

The third agreement is about who is on the other side of the paddle. Josh, on Dustin Hahn's Tax Lien School panel, says New Jersey makes their worst-states list because large investors scoop up everything and are willing to bid it down to 0%, which makes it very hard for anyone to be scrappy when institutions or hedge funds show up [mHvzzGVcYdI @ 00:01:36]. Julia M. Spencer reports the same pattern: institutional investors like banks bid the interest down to almost zero or half a percent because they do not care about keeping properties and have a very high amount of money to park in liens on valuable properties [NAHQ-7eWR_c @ 00:02:17]. The SKW Central trainer quotes an article on Pima County, Arizona, where banks bought nearly 6,000 tax liens totaling at least $15.8 million after the 2008 bailout, earning up to 16% with a three-year foreclosure trigger, and concludes that if they recognize the value, so should individual investors [e-CuINE8x-g @ 00:00:48]. Smart Capital's Olivia names the mechanism behind the compression: online platforms like Real Auction opened the market to out-of-state money, which increased competition and pushed winning rates down in popular counties [TL6AIsoe5m0 @ 00:16:39]. Big money and easy access both grind the rate toward the floor.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The mechanics start inside the bidding software. Realauction's New Jersey walkthrough runs the click path: Place Bids on the left, the batch summary screen, click a batch number, then work the bid menu where each ADV number opens item details and the face amount sits in the center; a page-fill tool drops one rate across every item, but you still must click Bid or Submit Bids, and it only covers the page you are looking at, not later pages in the batch [hKsLdKqVOE0 @ 00:02:10]. The Arizona module adds the setting that silently changes your yield: in a proxy bid county, if you bid 5% and nobody else bids, the engine wins you the 16% maximum, while in a direct bid county 5% is what you get even as the only bidder [cleRXY7vybQ @ 00:02:20]. Smart Capital's Olivia layers on session discipline: big online sales run in batches with hundreds of liens each over several days, bidders in every batch make worse decisions in the last one, and experienced bidders pre-rank targets and set automated maximums so the plan executes when attention fades [TL6AIsoe5m0 @ 00:18:18]. They also flag Florida's cash clock: 10% at the auction and the balance within 48 hours, or you can lose the deposit and the certificate [TL6AIsoe5m0 @ 00:17:12].

Real yield math splits into interest and penalty. Dustin Hahn explains interest states accrue monthly, so a 12% certificate pays 1% a month, and a lien redeemed one month after sale returns 1.33% at Arizona's 16% or 1.5% in Florida at the full rate, adding that much again for every month it sits [Ip2V3ixjk4k @ 00:03:52]. Penalty states charge the full amount on day one: Hahn's Texas example has the owner owing 25% on top of what you paid whether they redeem on day one or day 179, and Georgia charges 20% the day after the sale plus another 10% past the one-year mark [Ip2V3ixjk4k @ 00:02:28]. Brian Seinsticker connects the two inside Florida: the 'fast five' model works because a 5% penalty applies even if the lien redeems the next day, so a bidder at a quarter percent technically still earns 5% [XbThUArmcIE @ 00:01:24]. Seinsticker frames it as a way of deploying capital for a quick 5% and moving it somewhere else, not a strategy for earning interest over a multi-year period. Casey Demmon reports seeing liens sell at 1% or 1.5% for exactly that reason, since many states add a penalty of maybe five or six percent on top [0XlgBwC8tog @ 00:01:38]. The bid rate and the realized rate are two different numbers.

For pricing, Casey Demmon refuses a one-size premium formula for individuals, noting institutions with tens of millions in liens can run one because everything averages out; instead, call the county for redemption stats, get a figure like 1.8 years or two years, and model a fake $1,000 lien with a given premium against the return you need [cnd7EM15dyk @ 00:00:40]. The stacking angle changes that math: in some states, Casey Demmon says, the first-year holder gets first option on years two, three, and four, so a bidder can take year one at 1% and buy the later liens at 15% or 16% [0XlgBwC8tog @ 00:01:55]. Dustin Hahn confirms the New Jersey version, where you bid the rate down but subsequent liens added on top earn the full interest rate amount, calling it very powerful if done right [Ip2V3ixjk4k @ 00:04:58]. Smart Capital's Olivia runs a straight interest play for scale: an $8,000 lien won at a 12% bid-down rate with a two-year redemption collects roughly $1,900, about 24% total over two years, with a $200,000 house as collateral the whole time [TL6AIsoe5m0 @ 00:21:03]. Every model starts from expected hold time, not from the auction-day rate.

callout.title: Where the yield hides from the crowd
callout.body: Operators find rate where the institutional bidders and auction-day tourists are not looking.
items: Sort big lien lists by face amount: the Montezuma County, Colorado list opens with $25 and $26 liens on lots and acreage, and the well-secured $900 to $128,000 liens on homes and hotels only start showing about 11 pages in [Tax Sale Secrets — stFlmSmpP3Q @ 00:04:24].

Pull the county's past auction results first: if downtown condo liens get bid to near zero while suburban single-family liens clear at double-digit rates, the market is telling you where the crowd is not [Smart Capital — TL6AIsoe5m0 @ 00:14:44].

Chase liens too big for most bidders: the hosts flagged a $128,000 lien on a Best Western valued at 5.7 million and about $250,000 in liens tied to one hotel operator, noting only so many people have that money to bid against you and you could probably still get them close to 10% [Tax Sale Secrets — stFlmSmpP3Q @ 00:10:01].

In New Jersey, dodge the institutions by sticking to smaller-population counties, or pivot to Pennsylvania and New York where Josh says you will find better opportunities [Dustin Hahn — I9YP4P0-OM0 @ 00:00:44].

sop_steps.action: Know whether the state pays a flat penalty on early redemption before deciding how low to bid.

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The first fault line is whether a bid cap should come from a fixed formula at all. Olivia at Smart Capital teaches a hard walk-away number set before the gavel drops: conservative value times 0.65, minus every surviving lien, minus quiet title costs, minus holding costs, with no exceptions once bidding passes it. On a $200,000 Florida house carrying an $8,000 lien, that math lands at $115,000 of maximum total exposure [TL6AIsoe5m0 @ 00:19:24]. Casey at Tax Sale Academy refuses to hand out a one-size formula for individuals, conceding only that institutions sitting on tens of millions of dollars in liens can run one because they play the long average and everything evens out [cnd7EM15dyk @ 00:00:15]. Casey's alternative is a personal formula: call the county for redemption stats, take the typical 1.8 or 2 years as the starting number, model a fake $1,000 lien at a given premium, and solve for the return required, folding in suit and quiet title costs whenever foreclosure is on the table [cnd7EM15dyk @ 00:00:40]. Brian Seinsticker of Tax Sale Resources adds that high bid premium, true bid premium and bid up are all names for the same traditional bid-up auction, so the formula fight is really about how far to chase a familiar price war [6hRZuHmCM0M @ 00:01:10].

The second split is whether a near-zero rate is a smart play or a slow bleed. Brian Seinsticker explains the Florida 'fast five': bidders drive the rate to a quarter point because a 5% penalty pays even if the lien redeems the next day, which turns the certificate into a way to deploy capital, grab a quick 5%, and move the money somewhere else [XbThUArmcIE @ 00:01:24]. Casey at Tax Sale Academy reports liens selling at 1% or 1.5% for the same reason, because many states stack a penalty of five or six percent on top, and lays out a second angle: take the first-year lien at 1% to hold the first option on years two, three and four, then buy those later liens at 15% or 16% [0XlgBwC8tog @ 00:01:38]. Dustin Hahn's crew runs identical logic in New Jersey, where the initial lien gets bid down but subsequent liens bought on top carry the full interest rate, a move Dustin calls very powerful when done right [Ip2V3ixjk4k @ 00:04:58]. Julia M. Spencer reads the floor differently: banks and other institutions bid toward zero or half a percent because they do not care about keeping properties and have huge sums to park against high-value collateral [NAHQ-7eWR_c @ 00:02:17].

The third split is about which arena to enter in the first place. Josh, on Dustin Hahn's panel, ranks New Jersey among the worst states because hedge funds and large institutions sweep the sale and bid it to zero, so a scrappy buyer should stick to smaller-population areas or pivot to Pennsylvania's over-the-counter tax deeds or to New York [I9YP4P0-OM0 @ 00:00:44]. The Tax Sale Secrets hosts argue the opposite end of the size curve in Colorado: a $128,000 lien on a Best Western valued near $5.7 million, and roughly $250,000 in liens tied to one hotel operator, are buys for a millionaire because few bidders can bring that cash, and even rate-minded big fish might leave them close to 10% [stFlmSmpP3Q @ 00:10:01]. On ownership bid-down sales, Brian Seinsticker says the ownership percentage is irrelevant to redemption earnings in Louisiana, where 95 to 97 percent of liens redeem, so the odd format alone is no reason to stay away [3thEKo1DOwU @ 00:03:36]. Casey treats the same format as a co-ownership fight waiting to happen: a 30% winner who forecloses must negotiate a buyout with the 70% delinquent owner or sue to force a partition sale, usually with a hired attorney [YMBhKuuupDc @ 00:03:07].
