sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive trap the practitioners report is a cheap rate or a fat premium colliding with the wrong redemption clock. Brian Seinsticker warns that the quarter-point Florida play burns the buyer who lands a lien that never redeems: hold it two years and the effective return falls to about two and a half percent a year, a figure Brian says does not even keep pace with inflation [XbThUArmcIE @ 00:02:11]. Casey at Tax Sale Academy walks through the premium-side version using a real certificate with a $293.57 face value and a $28.82 overbid: in states where the overbid is not reimbursed or earns no interest, paying too much and getting redeemed before enough months accrue to cover the premium means losing money outright [0I_mhnrF0So @ 00:02:27]. Olivia at Smart Capital lists the same timing wound from the opposite direction, budgeting for a two-year hold only to watch the owner redeem in month three at a pro-rated minimum return while the capital sat idle [TL6AIsoe5m0 @ 00:28:49]. The Realauction New Jersey walkthrough shows why premium pain lands so hard there: once bidding moves past rate and into dollars above face, every premium bid associates with 0% interest on redemption [hKsLdKqVOE0 @ 00:02:28]. The economics check is identical across all four: the redemption timeline, not the headline rate, decides whether the bid made money.

The second failure pattern is showing up where the capital in the room is far bigger than yours. Josh, on the Tax Lien School panel, says most New Jersey sales get scooped up by large investors willing to bid to 0%, leaving more competition there than even in big California cities [mHvzzGVcYdI @ 00:01:53]. The host adds that desirable California counties such as Santa Barbara, San Luis Obispo and Ventura see little action at all, because a bank carrying a million-dollar mortgage will simply pay several thousand in back taxes rather than risk getting eliminated [mHvzzGVcYdI @ 00:00:15]. The SKW Central trainer reads an article reporting that bailed-out banks bought nearly 6,000 Pima County liens totaling at least $15.8 million, chasing up to 16% with a three-year path to foreclosure, and turns the initial anger into a signal that the asset class is worth pursuing [e-CuINE8x-g @ 00:00:48]. Olivia at Smart Capital explains why the crowd keeps growing: online platforms opened the market to out-of-state investors, which increased competition and pushed winning rates down in popular counties, the trade-off of convenience [TL6AIsoe5m0 @ 00:16:55]. The fix the practitioners report is geographic rather than tactical: smaller counties, over-the-counter leftovers, and states where the heavy money is not parked.

The third cluster is pure execution failure, where the bid or the paperwork breaks rather than the deal itself. The Realauction New Jersey tutorial flags that the fill tool types a number only across the page being viewed, not every item in a multi-page batch, and that bids still need the bid key or the submit bids click to register at all [hKsLdKqVOE0 @ 00:02:10]. Olivia at Smart Capital names fatigue as a real cost in multi-day batch auctions, noting that investors who bid in every batch make worse decisions in the last one, so experienced bidders pre-rank targets and set automated maximums wherever the platform allows it [TL6AIsoe5m0 @ 00:18:18]. Olivia also calls missed notices the single most common way investors lose a valid claim: a wrong address or a filing one day late has led courts to throw out entire foreclosures, taking the legal fees, the time, and sometimes the investment position with them [TL6AIsoe5m0 @ 00:25:09]. Brian Seinsticker supplies the endgame trap for ownership bid-down states: bid ownership down to 1% and a foreclosure leaves the investor sharing the property with a 99% previous owner who is unhappy about it, a setup Brian expects to breed confusion and disputes [3thEKo1DOwU @ 00:02:48]. Every one of these losses hit after the hard work of finding the lien was already done.

callout.title: Four Checks Before Any Bid Goes In
callout.body: Every loss the practitioners reported traces back to a format rule, a redemption clock, or a deadline the bidder did not price in. Clear all four gates before entering a rate, a premium, or an ownership percentage.
items: Price every sub-1% bid against a no-redemption scenario, because a quarter-point lien held two years yields only about 2.5% a year [Tax Sale Resources — XbThUArmcIE @ 00:02:11]
Confirm whether the state returns the overbid and pays interest on it before bidding any premium above face value [Tax Sale Academy — 0I_mhnrF0So @ 00:02:42]
Read the county bidding rules for proxy versus direct bid before entering a low rate as a possible sole bidder [Realauction — cleRXY7vybQ @ 00:02:43]
Calendar every foreclosure notice and filing deadline, since one day late has gotten entire foreclosures thrown out [Smart Capital — TL6AIsoe5m0 @ 00:25:09]

action_checklist: Call the county for its average redemption time, such as 1.8 or 2 years, and build a personal premium formula from that starting number [Tax Sale Academy — cnd7EM15dyk @ 00:00:40]
Write down a walk-away cap before the auction: conservative value times 0.65 minus surviving liens, quiet title costs and holding costs [Smart Capital — TL6AIsoe5m0 @ 00:35:11]
In New Jersey, accept a low rate on the initial lien, then buy subsequent liens that carry the full interest rate [Dustin Hahn — Ip2V3ixjk4k @ 00:04:58]
In Florida, reserve quarter-point bids for capital meant to come back fast through the 5% penalty, not for multi-year holds [Tax Sale Resources — XbThUArmcIE @ 00:01:41]

chapters.question_prompt: How do I find, register for, and bid in online tax deed and tax lien auctions, and what does a cheap-property deal actually look like?
chapters.title: Online Auctions and Cheap-Property Deed Plays
chapters.subtitle: RealAuction, LienHub County-Held Liens, ZeusAuction, Duval County Walkthroughs, Texas Deed Results, $50 Land Buys, and the $500-to-$50,000 Flip
chapters.executive_summary: The operators converge on one thesis: county tax sales, now mostly run online through RealAuction, Grant Street Group, Bid4Assets, SRI, CivicSource, LienHub and ZeusAuction, sell property and liens at a fraction of value, and the leftovers sold over the counter are cheaper still. Tax Sale Secrets says tax-sale foreclosures open at 10-20% of value versus 90-100% for mortgage foreclosures, and their students buy OTC land at 5-15%. Dustin Hahn documents a $500 Indiana commissioner-sale house resold for $50,000. The street mechanics are free registration, roughly 10% deposits, a parcel-ID click-through to the appraiser, Regrid and Street View checks, a predetermined max bid, and $50 Craigslist photos. The operators disagree on Texas redemption odds (95-97% redeem per Ted Thomas versus 75%+ ending in ownership per Tax Sale Secrets) and on whether to buy sight-unseen.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The baseline every operator agrees on is that the county only wants its back taxes, so the opening bid tracks delinquency, not market value. Dustin Hahn says that in a deed state you own the property free and clear and 'the opening bid is always going to be the back taxes owed on that property.' Owners get three to five years of nonpayment before it reaches the block [ES5ZPyHRFMM @ 00:00:53]. Tax Sale Secrets quantifies the spread. Mortgage foreclosures start at 90 to 100% of value, while tax-sale foreclosures start at about 10 to 20% [IMGzMnzQiZQ @ 00:23:32]. A deed opening bid of roughly 5 to 10% of value usually represents three to five years of taxes. Tax Sale Support applies the same math on Bid4Assets: the opening bid is typically the total delinquent taxes, and the buy zone is 10 to 20% of fair market value [0TBV3XkrRmo @ 00:04:14]. The instrument split is settled too. Liens are an interest play paying 18 to 36% in Hahn's telling, and deeds are ownership. Jackie Jackson compresses it to 'tax liens are a rate of interest tax deed is when you actually get the property' [XaihRHU__R4 @ 00:17:30]. Every operator builds the buy box on that single gap between what the county is owed and what the parcel will fetch on the open market.

The second point of agreement is that the sale has moved online, and the unsold leftovers are the cheapest inventory in the system. Tax Sale Secrets says counties are replacing the courthouse auctioneer with vendor software that runs highest bid for deeds and lowest interest rate in bid-down lien states. Roughly 80% of volume now runs through Bid4Assets, RealAuction and Grant Street Group [IMGzMnzQiZQ @ 00:15:26]. The operators use different words for what happens after the gavel, but the play is identical. Hahn defines an over-the-counter deed as one 'that does not sell at the tax deed auction.' The move is to call the county, ask what happens to unsold properties and request the list [ES5ZPyHRFMM @ 00:07:35]. Ted Thomas describes the same leftover pool on the lien side: struck-off certificates bought at the county with no bidding. With 30,000 liens and only three or four dozen bidders, many are left over [KoANRHO6Uko @ 00:07:44]. Tax Sale Secrets lists the alternate names a county may use: assignment, county-owned, tax-forfeited, repository and struck-off. Their students buy OTC land at 5 to 15% of value, while counties generally run 5 to 20% [RgLErVu5_Kk @ 00:23:45]. The county, they stress, does not care about price beyond the opening bid.

The third consensus is that cheap only pays when the parcel has use and the buyer has done the homework. Jackie Jackson says flatly, 'It's not okay to purchase anything blindly.' Even before buying a $79 certificate, Jackson checks the usage code, flood map, zoning and frontage/depth [fbdN21IB-I0 @ 00:13:25]. Ted Thomas names skipping title searches and skipping property inspection as the two big no-no's. Discovering a bad neighborhood after paying is too late, so Thomas pushes boots on the ground [KoANRHO6Uko @ 00:03:38]. Tax Sale Secrets eliminates landlocked parcels first, 'even if we can get it for cheap the problem is is that use factor' [RgLErVu5_Kk @ 00:29:54]. They steer buyers toward lots of roughly 0.2 to 0.25 acre that can hold a single-wide, and they avoid side lots with a single possible buyer. Land is the shared favorite. The same team says land draws fewer bidders than homes, and improved deeds make up only about 30% of available inventory. The Tax Lien School Highlights channel notes 'a lot of people actually overlook land' and pegs 2x to 4x upside when comparable lots sell for $20,000 to $50,000 [prp5x8F5I60 @ 00:02:14]. Temperament lines up too: Hahn's effort target is an hour a day, five days a week, for a year.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Registration is free on every platform the operators walk through, but funding is where bidders trip. Tax Sale Secrets says registration takes minutes. One account works per vendor, though each auction needs its own registration. The deposit runs about 10%, for example $1,000 to bid on $10,000 of liens [IMGzMnzQiZQ @ 00:11:42]. They keep every username and password in one document. Jackie Jackson confirms RealAuction asks only for first name, last name, email and phone, with a company name optional. One login covers every county, with a different bidder number in each [Pz2ZCMuIox4 @ 00:07:59]. Loren Brown's Duval County walkthrough adds the funding friction. ACH deposits need four full working days to clear the national ACH system, and ACH may be unavailable from money-market, brokerage or trust accounts. Refunds take about 20 business days. Brown recommends a counter deposit in certified funds, money order or cash by 4 pm the day prior, then ACH for the final payment [gamhQuWz38o @ 00:06:56]. For county-held lien sales, the Realauction training shows that bank details may need re-entry daily. Certificates sit locked and pending until the ACH clears [_Ge3YGeNsFg @ 00:02:33]. The rates are capped at Florida 18% and Arizona 16% upon redemption.

The valuation workflow is consistent across channels: never trust the vendor's assessed figure; click through to the county. The Tax Lien School Highlights channel shows a RealAuction Florida lot assessed at $2,900 that sold for $9,100. Clicking the parcel ID on the county site shows 0.5 acres, a county market value near $10,000 and prior sales of $15,000 and $25,000. Running the parcel number through Regrid then catches landlocked or irregular lots [prp5x8F5I60 @ 00:00:52]. Jackie Jackson notes the vendor's assessed value 'isn't 100% accurate' and flags a 2007 listing photo on what the appraiser calls vacant residential land [Pz2ZCMuIox4 @ 00:11:05]. Tax Sale Support pulls Bid4Assets lists as Excel or PDF, then checks an appraisal site, since county photos may be one to two years old [0TBV3XkrRmo @ 00:06:26]. Tax Sale Secrets closes the loop with a comparative market analysis and a predetermined maximum bid. When Street View dates to 2007, they pay someone about $50 via Craigslist for current photos [AO4ZqaMio7s @ 01:13:42]. Condition moves the ceiling: on a $100,000 property they cite a $35,000 to $40,000 maximum in good shape versus $20,000 to $25,000 in bad. They also say land bought at 20% of value still makes money even if sold at half price.

Bidding tactics center on reading competition and refusing to chase. Dustin Hahn screens ZeusAuction by bidder count versus item count. Hahn avoids a 48-bidders-for-2-items sale and calls zero bidders on many items 'the dream.' The target is sales like the Lake County, Indiana commissioner sale, whose registration closed months early: 380 bidders against more than 6,000 parcels [M8AxkDXoffk @ 00:03:24]. On Grant Street, Tax Sale Secrets prefers live bidding in $100 to $500 steps over proxy. A $10,000 proxy against a rival sitting at $8,000 still wins at around $8,100, so a proxy ceiling buys nothing [AO4ZqaMio7s @ 00:21:50]. Loren Brown found that a $90,000 proxy bid went through without a deposit, where 5% would have been $4,500. Removing it reset the proxy to $0 [gamhQuWz38o @ 00:11:16]. Once an auction officially commences, bid retractions are not accepted. The exit is planned before the bid. Tax Sale Secrets buys near 10% of value and wholesales at 30 to 40%, prizing speed over margin. They flipped 27 New York acres assessed near $200,000 on an $80,000 offer within 30 days. A quiet title would have meant six months plus $12,000 to $13,000 a year in taxes [RgLErVu5_Kk @ 01:01:26].

callout.title: Edges the operators use on sale day
callout.body: These are the small timing, funding and venue moves that separate the bidders who win at a fraction of value from the ones who overpay or miss the sale.
items: Run the heavy due diligence one to two weeks before the auction so the property is still likely to be available on sale day [Tax Sale Secrets — AO4ZqaMio7s @ 01:41:13].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Texas is the sharpest split on whether a redemption deed lands property or just yield. Ted Thomas says 95 to 97 percent of owners come in and redeem, so the bidder mostly collects the price back plus a flat 25 percent inside a 180-day window [41UuQtBLiBo @ 00:06:15]. Tax Sale Secrets runs the clock differently: six months on most properties but up to two years on homesteads [7lyUS9FiWeM @ 00:00:37], and because that six months starts at foreclosure, roughly three months are often left by sale day, which is why they estimate 75 percent of properties, if not higher, end in ownership [7lyUS9FiWeM @ 00:02:18]. Dustin Hahn lumps Texas in with California, New York and Georgia as redemption-period deed states paying 25 percent over six months [ES5ZPyHRFMM @ 00:04:13]. This is a real split, not a rounding difference: one camp sees a few deeds per hundred convert, the other sees three in four. The two playbooks follow directly. A Thomas-style bidder prices a Texas deed as a short-dated 25 percent penalty play, expects to be paid off, and walks from heavily mortgaged homes. A Tax Sale Secrets-style bidder treats the same deed as a discounted acquisition, expects the keys, and budgets rehab and resale from the day the hammer falls, as their Cherokee County and Galveston wins show.

The bid-to-value ceiling is the second open fight. Tax Sale Secrets wants over-the-counter land at 10 percent of value or less, noting counties run 5 to 20 percent and students buy at 5 to 15 [RgLErVu5_Kk @ 00:23:45]. On their online-auction session the same channel loosens the leash by price band: 10 to 20 percent on a $10,000 lot, but up to 50 percent on a $1.2 million home opening at $27,000 [AO4ZqaMio7s @ 01:19:28]. Tax Sale Support teaches 10 to 30 percent of fair market value, stretching to 40 percent only when the buyer knows the property well [0TBV3XkrRmo @ 00:08:38]. Dustin Hahn's pitch frames the win far more modestly, as purchases 30 to 60 percent below market value, mortgage-free, even while showing a $500 Gary, Indiana shell resold for $50,000 [SwH4FFj8oZc @ 00:02:10]. Thirty to 60 percent below market means paying 40 to 70 percent of value, a band Tax Sale Secrets only tolerates on high-dollar homes. Operators splitting the difference set a written maximum per parcel before bidding opens, tied to a comparative market analysis, and refuse to chase past it, the discipline Tax Sale Secrets calls not getting emotionally involved once the bottom line is set.

Channel choice and exit split the room as well. Tax Sale Secrets says that in Florida they would look only at the auction and would not even look at over-the-counter inventory, calling Florida OTC junk [RgLErVu5_Kk @ 00:37:17]. Jackie Jackson works the opposite end of the same state, pulling the lands-available list across Florida's 67 counties to buy unsold parcels directly for the delinquent taxes, and buying county-held certificates year-round [XaihRHU__R4 @ 00:10:15]. On exit, Dustin Hahn says most deed states carry no redemption so you can sell the same night, and recounts a Troy, New York winner signing the deed over to a latecomer for $5,000 cash [ES5ZPyHRFMM @ 00:04:50]. Ted Thomas insists the county is not going to warranty your property and that a quitclaim tax deed means you will have to do a quiet title [41UuQtBLiBo @ 00:08:14]. Tax Sale Secrets lands in between: decide quiet title versus as-is wholesale before buying, then flip fast at 30 to 40 percent of value, as on 27 New York acres where an $80,000 offer inside 30 days beat six months of quiet title and $12,000 to $13,000 a year in taxes. Speed over margin is their stated rule.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most repeated failure is trusting county data that is stale or flat wrong. Tax Sale Secrets shows a 2017 photo against the 2020 reality of the same structure and says condition is unknown without boots on the ground [RgLErVu5_Kk @ 00:15:14]; on an over-the-counter vacant-land lien, Google Maps pinned the wrong parcel entirely, forcing a check against aerials [IMGzMnzQiZQ @ 01:06:02]. On a Texas list they caught a county map mislabeling the lot, which they call the reason you always got to do due diligence [7lyUS9FiWeM @ 00:13:31]. Tax Sale Support warns county photos may have been taken a year or two earlier [0TBV3XkrRmo @ 00:06:26], and Jackie Jackson flags a Cocoa listing carrying a 2007 photo while the description says vacant residential land. Assessed values mislead in both directions: Dustin Hahn's team watched a parcel assessed at $2,900 sell for $9,100 because the assessment is generally not correct, while Tax Sale Secrets notes Texas counties often list values high. Hahn's parcel turned out to be half an acre with prior sales of $15,000 and $25,000. The fix they converge on is a second source: parcel-ID click-through to the appraiser, Zillow and comps, Regrid for access, and a $50 Craigslist hire for current photos.

The second trap is buying a parcel that is cheap because it is useless or encumbered. Tax Sale Secrets warns that an over-the-counter home still unsold at about 10 percent of value likely has issues, and eliminates landlocked parcels first even when they can be had for cheap, because the problem is use [RgLErVu5_Kk @ 00:29:54]. On their auction session they flag a $1,300 lien at 18 percent that may sit in a lake and has cycled through tax deed sales repeatedly [AO4ZqaMio7s @ 01:54:28]. Jackie Jackson reads a frontage and depth of 00 as a speck of land that may not be buildable, and one such parcel was possibly a retention pond [fbdN21IB-I0 @ 00:14:11]. Liability hides off the parcel too. Ted Thomas says the two big no-nos are skipping the title search and skipping inspection; a search for hidden liens, code violations and municipal liens costs 300 or 500 and very few people do one [KoANRHO6Uko @ 00:03:58]. Thomas adds that in Texas the deed of trust is not wiped out, so an unredeemed buyer becomes responsible for it, and Tax Sale Secrets tells beginners to avoid IRS-lien properties and to check the total roll-up, such as five liens totaling $20,000 on a $100,000 home.

The third failure mode is operational: money, timing and competition. Tax Sale Secrets lost seven or eight Florida properties before winning one [IMGzMnzQiZQ @ 01:30:17], and warns against sinking $10,000 into a single $10,000 property because it ties up capital. Funding rails bite on deadline. Loren Brown found ACH deposits need four full working days through the national system, refunds take about 20 business days, and ACH may be unavailable from brokerage, money-market or trust accounts, so Brown recommends a counter deposit by 4 pm the day prior [gamhQuWz38o @ 00:06:04]; Realauction locks a purchased certificate as pending until ACH clears. Brown also watched a $90,000 proxy bid post without any deposit behind it, then reset to zero when removed. Competition kills spreads: Dustin Hahn's ZeusAuction screen rejects a sale with 48 bidders on 2 items and targets far more items than bidders, noting registration often closes near or months before auction day [M8AxkDXoffk @ 00:00:31]. Ted Thomas runs the economics check on Texas: a $300,000 value carrying a $200,000 mortgage plus a $100,000 bid is retail, and retail is not profitable [41UuQtBLiBo @ 00:06:34]. Jackie Jackson adds that bank minimum thresholds make these low prices unmortgageable, so the bid has to be cash or pooled partner funds.

callout.title: Do Not Bid Until All Four Clear
callout.body: Every item below maps to a loss, near-miss, or trap a named practitioner hit firsthand. A parcel that fails any one of them gets struck from the bid sheet, no matter how low the opening bid.
items: Current photo or boots on the ground: no bid on a parcel without a current image, because county and Street View shots run years stale [Tax Sale Secrets — IMGzMnzQiZQ @ 01:29:27].

Parcel verified on the property appraiser site for usage and description, not the vendor's assessed value or listing photo [The Jackie Jackson | Tax Deed & Real Estate Coach — Pz2ZCMuIox4 @ 00:12:04].
Encumbrances cleared: title search for hidden, municipal and IRS liens, plus any surviving deed of trust on Texas redemption deeds [Ted Thomas — 41UuQtBLiBo @ 00:03:04].
Exit and maximum fixed before the auction: quiet title or as-is wholesale chosen and a CMA-based ceiling written down [Tax Sale Secrets — RgLErVu5_Kk @ 00:48:38].

action_checklist: Call the county, ask what happens to properties that do not sell at the tax deed auction, and request the over-the-counter list (Dustin Hahn, ES5ZPyHRFMM @ 00:08:09).

Screen online auctions by bidder-to-item ratio, skip sales like 48 bidders on 2 items, and register before cutoffs that can close months ahead (Tax Lien School Highlights - Dustin Hahn, M8AxkDXoffk @ 00:03:08).
Click every parcel ID through to the county site, then run the parcel number through Regrid to catch landlocked or irregular lots (Tax Lien School Highlights - Dustin Hahn, prp5x8F5I60 @ 00:01:32).
Pull a comparative market analysis, set a predetermined maximum bid, and hire someone off Craigslist for current photos before bidding (Tax Sale Secrets, IMGzMnzQiZQ @ 01:35:08).
Run the daily RealAuction practice auctions until the bidding process is familiar, then do major due diligence one to two weeks before the sale (Tax Sale Secrets, AO4ZqaMio7s @ 00:15:56).

Fund the deposit at the counter with certified funds, money order or cash by 4 pm the day prior, and save ACH for the final payment (Loren Brown - The 5am Reinvention Project, gamhQuWz38o @ 00:06:56).

chapters.question_prompt: Where do leftover liens and deeds go after the auction, and how do I buy them over the counter from home?
chapters.title: Over-the-Counter Liens and Deeds
chapters.subtitle: Finding County Leftover Lists, Maryland OTC Liens, Top OTC Deed States, No-Redemption Deed States, and Verifying Struck-Off Parcels Before Paying
chapters.executive_summary: Over-the-counter tax liens and deeds are the leftovers: parcels that went to a county tax sale, drew no winning bid, and now sit on a list the treasurer will sell directly, usually for back taxes with no bidding. Ted Thomas, Dustin Hahn, Saen Higgins and the Tax Sale Support hosts agree the edge is asking the county what happens to properties that did not sell, because each state brands the list differently: scavenger, strike off, lands available, forfeited lands, repository. Reported buys run from $36 lots to a $5K Arkansas funeral home, with Florida OTC liens paying the full 18% and Maryland liens paying 20%. The split is over quality: Tax Sale Support calls the garbage label a misperception, while John Lane and Tax Deed Wolf say most leftovers carry major problems or are overpriced.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner defines the play the same way: a parcel goes to the county tax sale, nobody takes it, and it lands in inventory the treasurer will sell straight across the counter. Ted Thomas says unsold auction properties go onto an unsold list held at the treasurer's office, and that a Los Angeles sale might offer 2,000 properties and move only 1,500, leaving a deep pool for anyone who asks [g0bsPf3Jwo4 @ 00:02:24]. Saen Higgins frames it as a property that went to sale, did not sell, and went into inventory, adding that roughly half the states sell liens and half sell deeds, and that nothing survives a deed [nbHUraglUQo @ 00:02:30]. Steve and Shade at Tax Sale Support widen the definition to anything left after a sale that can be bought directly from the county, and they pin down the core pricing hook: buyers pay back taxes only and bid against no one, with no travel and no bidding up a $5,000 opener [5t3VbtPlElc @ 00:10:27]. The baseline prerequisite, per Dustin Hahn, is confirming whether you sit in a lien state or a deed state before calling anyone, because the leftover product changes completely depending on that answer [uiH28IFKgC4 @ 00:01:43].

The second consensus point is linguistic: the list exists, but the clerk may not recognize your name for it. Thomas catalogs roughly a dozen labels by region, including the Illinois scavenger list, the Texas strike off list, the Florida lands available list and the Carolinas forfeited lands list, and tells buyers to simply ask for properties that did not sell [g0bsPf3Jwo4 @ 00:03:24]. Hahn hears the same complaint constantly, county workers swearing they have no over-the-counter tax liens, and fixes it with one reframed question: what happens to the leftover properties that don't sell at the tax lien or tax deed sale, naming the specific county and state [2M5EFWdf-is @ 00:00:46]. Higgins drops the OTC jargon entirely, using the script 'if you did have a sale and one didn't sell, where would I find that,' because there are 5,000-plus jurisdictions down to townships [nbHUraglUQo @ 00:03:08]. Tax Sale Support adds county owned, tax forfeited, land bank, struck off, upset bid and the Pennsylvania repository to the vocabulary, and the hosts say their state guides decode each term, so a buyer working a new county is translating, not guessing, when the clerk answers with a local label [5t3VbtPlElc @ 00:21:21].

Across every camp, the non-negotiable is seeing the parcel and checking title before money moves, because the county sells as-is. Ted Thomas calls it caveat emptor, with no warranty on condition or title, and insists you still walk the property and check the title for defects [g0bsPf3Jwo4 @ 00:03:50]. On the lien side, Thomas names the ghetto, the dump, and the chicken or pig farm as the kind of parcel that will neither redeem nor sell, so inspection comes first [rmXwIKKIDiw @ 00:05:39]. Dustin Hahn openly concedes that most of any leftover list is going to be crap and will not dispute it, telling buyers to accept that going in [uiH28IFKgC4 @ 00:03:46]. Saen Higgins has watched buyers land a garbage dumpster, a strip four feet wide and a hundred yards long, and a median between subdivisions, and the rule is blunt: whatever the case is, you got to do your research [nbHUraglUQo @ 00:05:19]. The consensus is not that leftovers are gold or garbage, but that the list is a raw feed: price is low, competition is thin, and the screening burden shifts entirely onto the buyer, who gets no county warranty and no realtor holding their hand.

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Pulling the list is a phone job, not a search-engine job. Dustin Hahn's call to the treasurer has three questions: when is the sale, what happens to properties that don't sell, and where does the inventory list live, whether that is an email, a website or a fax [uiH28IFKgC4 @ 00:02:38]. The Over The Counter Tax Deeds channel boils it down to two questions, where is the list of unsold properties and how do I buy them, and as a fallback it Googles tax lien list, tax deed list or tax delinquent list near me, clicks contact us and calls the number [RxbJj9wFJXI @ 00:01:26]. Tax Deed Wolf starts with the county clerk of court and falls back to the contact page, and lists land banks, lands available, surplus, scavenger, upset bid and sheriff sale as names the inventory may hide under [sY8o7KeLptY @ 00:00:47]. Hahn's sharpest filter is friction itself: older, smaller counties and hard-to-get information beat easy ones, and hidden or paid lists, at 15 cents a page or roughly $30 total, are better across a 3,300-county field [YVYW5E5cTUI @ 00:16:14]. Friction keeps casual buyers out, which is the whole point.

Screening is a sort-and-strike exercise run against hard numbers. Tax Sale Support's Polk County, Florida demo opened a 592-page list holding about 29,500 liens, sorted by face amount from $2 to $18,000, and starred only the promising rows while scanning roughly 50 at a time; on a $93 lien on vacant residential land assessed at $4,100, a $1,173 prior-year roll-up meant Shade would probably just keep moving on [5t3VbtPlElc @ 00:55:48]. Hahn's title research sorts by property type and amount owed, confirms the price covers taxes to date, confirms chain-of-title parties were notified, and kills anything with IRS liens or buried gas tanks [uiH28IFKgC4 @ 00:04:31]. Higgins checks whether the IRS was notified and the 120-day window, then checks improvements like sewer and power, because Higgins's own $1,500 lot needed $20,000 to bring power from the end of the street [nbHUraglUQo @ 00:07:11]. In Georgia, Hahn and guests trust the parcel ID over the street address, since a $2,800 minimum bid on a roughly $1M property does not make sense, and they note counties may still list improvement value on demolished houses [YVYW5E5cTUI @ 00:03:22]. Every one of these checks happens before a dollar goes to the county.

Closing is where OTC beats the auction floor: there is no clock and no bidding war, just paperwork. Higgins's version is the simplest, give the county the parcel number and the money and receive the deed, then make the first move clearing title through an attorney [nbHUraglUQo @ 00:07:59]. Thomas describes the deed-side cadence as making an offer and waiting a few days; if nobody makes a better offer, the county sells to you with no auction [g0bsPf3Jwo4 @ 00:09:35]. Alabama runs a quote-and-accept queue: Tax Deed Wolf pulls from a state list of more than 20,000 parcels dating to the 1990s, the county quotes a price such as $550, and the buyer has a 10-day window before the parcel moves to the next person in line [sY8o7KeLptY @ 00:03:15]. Maryland liens add a timing twist Hahn flags hard: the six-month redemption runs from the auction date, not your purchase date, so a June sale bought in September is already halfway home, but the lien expires after two years, and waiting until year two to foreclose is too late [Ayjol9fgpNg @ 00:02:15]. The takeaway across all four: the price is set, so the edge lives entirely in timing and paperwork.

callout.title: Cheap Edges the OTC Operators Actually Use
callout.body: Small, low-cost moves that separate a disciplined leftover-list buyer from someone mailing a check on a guess.
items: Get eyes on a remote parcel for pocket change: send someone through wegowlook.com for $20 to $50 in pictures, or hire a Craigslist gig driver, after a first pass on Google Earth [Dustin Hahn — uiH28IFKgC4 @ 00:06:06].
Pay for the list nobody else bothers to buy: hidden or paid lists at 15 cents a page, roughly $30 total, are the better hunting ground [Dustin Hahn — YVYW5E5cTUI @ 00:16:14].
Skip the site visit on deeds under $1,000 and run desk diligence instead: county records, tax records, maps, Google Maps, and sold and for-sale comps [Tax Sale Support — 5t3VbtPlElc @ 00:50:20].

On Maryland OTC liens, count the six-month redemption from the auction date, not your purchase date, so many are foreclosable the day you buy [Tax Lien School Highlights - Dustin Hahn — Ayjol9fgpNg @ 00:02:15].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split in the OTC game is whether the leftover list is a landfill or a vault. Tax Deed Wolf is blunt: if a deed failed to sell, “chances are it's crap or it's overpriced,” and those parcels are typically not the best properties to get [sY8o7KeLptY @ 00:02:13]. John Lane of Tax Sale Lists, who reports acquiring 77,000+ properties over 20 years, attacks the guru story that bidders simply ran out of money. If that were true, OTC liens would cluster at the tail end of the sale, and Lane says, “I have never found that to be the case,” warning that most OTC liens carry major problems [ymnkPFHPY40 @ 00:01:04]. Ted Thomas pushes the opposite read: unsold parcels are “not necessarily bad properties,” because snow on auction day or bidders short on cash can strand good inventory [g0bsPf3Jwo4 @ 00:01:39]. Steve and Shade of Tax Sale Support call the garbage belief a misperception outright, pointing out that live auctions draw thin crowds, counties hold more property than investor money, and sales fall through or winning bidders walk away [5t3VbtPlElc @ 00:13:59]. The operator takeaway: both camps scan the same list, but the skeptics expect to reject nearly everything while the believers mine it for the outliers that slipped past the room.

The second fault line is how much physical diligence a cheap parcel deserves. Ted Thomas names buying unseen as mistake number one and insists, “You need boots on the ground,” paired with a defined exit plan before any money moves [rmXwIKKIDiw @ 00:13:06]. Saen Higgins splits the difference: 95% of the work happens from home, yet Higgins disagrees with pure remote buying because you make “a lot more money” when you actually show up [HjwUaTY_CAk @ 00:08:27]. Steve and Shade at Tax Sale Support run a tiered rule instead, working county records, tax records, maps, Google Maps, and sold plus for-sale comps on everything, but skipping the on-site visit entirely on deeds under $1,000 [5t3VbtPlElc @ 00:50:20]. Dustin Hahn offers the outsourced middle path: Google Earth first, a drive-by if you are close, otherwise pay wegowlook.com $20 to $50 for photos or hire a Craigslist gig driver to walk the lot [uiH28IFKgC4 @ 00:06:06]. The real disagreement is the price threshold where a site visit stops paying for itself. Thomas treats it as mandatory at every price point, while the Tax Sale Support crew lets sub-$1,000 deeds ride on desk research alone, provided both value and use check out before payment.

Practitioners also split on whether OTC liens or OTC deeds are the right instrument. Ted Thomas sells liens as a passive play: no bidding, the state maximum rate, and the claim that “95 to 97 percent of all the people will come in and pay the tax” [XLUuBoGUOj8 @ 00:08:01]. Tax Sale Support agrees most liens end in interest earned rather than property, puts the chance of acquiring through a lien at only 5% climbing toward 20%, and tells operators who want dirt to buy deeds instead [5t3VbtPlElc @ 00:32:00]. Tax Deed Wolf flips the quality argument by instrument: leftover deeds are distrusted, but lien leftovers are different because auctions can run three weeks and plenty of liens slip through untouched [sY8o7KeLptY @ 00:02:30]. Dustin Hahn adds a timing wrinkle with Maryland OTC liens: the 6-month redemption clock runs from the auction, so many leftovers can be foreclosed immediately, and if they redeem the downside is 20% interest. The catch is that the liens expire after 2 years, summed up as “Quicker foreclosure turnaround time, but shorter lifespan” [Ayjol9fgpNg @ 00:03:18]. Pick the instrument by goal: yield seekers ride redemptions at the maximum rate, while acquirers buy deeds outright or target short-clock lien states like Maryland.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive OTC losses are physical, not paperwork. Saen Higgins bought a $1,500 lot and only then realized “the power's at the end of the street,” a $20,000 bill to bring electricity to a parcel that looked like a steal [nbHUraglUQo @ 00:07:11]. Higgins has also watched buyers land a garbage dumpster site, a strip 4 feet wide by 100 yards long, and a median between two subdivisions, parcels that sit on the county list precisely because nobody else wanted them [nbHUraglUQo @ 00:05:19]. Ted Thomas tells operators to inspect before paying because the list hides ghetto blocks, dumps, and chicken or pig farms, and a worthless property will neither redeem nor sell, leaving the buyer holding a lien nobody pays off and dirt nobody buys [rmXwIKKIDiw @ 00:05:39]. John Lane narrows the realistic target: “You may find decent vacant land on an otc list but it is unlikely you will find any decent improved parcels,” so a cheap house on a leftover list deserves suspicion rather than excitement, and Lane closes with a flat “be very careful” [ymnkPFHPY40 @ 00:01:28]. The pattern across all three operators: the sticker price on the leftover list is the smallest number in the deal, while utilities, access, and resale demand decide whether the money ever comes back.

Title and identification errors are the second kill zone. Dustin Hahn's research checklist sorts the list by type and amount owed, confirms the price covers taxes to date, and checks that every party in the chain of title was notified, while flagging IRS liens and buried gas tanks as walk-away items [uiH28IFKgC4 @ 00:04:31]. Saen Higgins drills into the federal angle specifically: check whether the IRS was notified and whether the 120-day window applies before treating a deed as clean [nbHUraglUQo @ 00:06:09]. Ted Thomas reminds buyers that OTC deeds are sold caveat emptor, with no warranty on condition or title, which is exactly why Thomas tells them to walk the property and check the title for defects themselves or hire someone to do it [g0bsPf3Jwo4 @ 00:04:35]. The Dustin Hahn panel adds a data trap: trust the parcel ID, never the street address, because a $2,800 minimum bid on a roughly $1M property doesn't make sense, and counties may still carry improvement value on houses that were already demolished, as the panel saw in Philadelphia [YVYW5E5cTUI @ 00:03:22]. Higgins's first move after any purchase is the same every time: clear title through an attorney, because wholesale buyers will ask for clear title and an inspection report before they pay.

The economics failures come from bad roll-ups, over-buying, and blown clocks. Tax Sale Support walks away from upside-down structures: a $100K property carrying $70K in taxes is out, and in the Polk County demo a $93 lien on vacant land that sold in 1997 for $30,000 looked tempting until the roll-up showed $1,173 in prior-year taxes, at which point Shade “would probably just keep moving on” [5t3VbtPlElc @ 01:02:25]. Ted Thomas tells the story of a student who bought 40 properties before selling a single one, and caps new investors at one or two liens and only one deed under the rule “buy and learn to sell” [XLUuBoGUOj8 @ 00:09:47]. Dustin Hahn's Maryland warning is about the calendar: the 6-month redemption runs from the June auction rather than your September purchase, and the liens expire after 2 years, so waiting until year two to foreclose is too late [Ayjol9fgpNg @ 00:02:30]. Saen Higgins confesses an admin blunder from about 14 years ago: online sales run through third parties require two separate registrations, one with the county and one with the platform, a mistake Higgins made firsthand [HjwUaTY_CAk @ 00:09:24]. Each of these failures is cheap to prevent upfront and expensive to discover after the money clears.

callout.title: Four kill-checks before any OTC check clears
callout.body: Every item below is a loss or near-miss practitioners reported firsthand. A parcel that fails any one of them gets dropped, no matter how low the county price is.
items: Confirm power, sewer, and access before paying; a $1,500 lot needed $20,000 just to bring power from the end of the street [Saen Higgins — nbHUraglUQo @ 00:07:11].
Match every parcel by parcel ID, never the street address, and kill any minimum bid that doesn't make sense against value [Dustin Hahn — YVYW5E5cTUI @ 00:03:22].
Screen for IRS liens, buried gas tanks, and chain-of-title notification failures before money moves [Dustin Hahn — uiH28IFKgC4 @ 00:04:31].
Cap first buys at one or two liens and one deed, and sell before buying more, after a student stacked 40 unsold properties [Ted Thomas — XLUuBoGUOj8 @ 00:09:47].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I research a parcel before I bid so I know what I am actually buying?
chapters.title: Pre-Bid Due Diligence and GIS Research
chapters.subtitle: County GIS and Parcel Viewers, Google Street View Checks, Assessor and Tax Records, Research Platforms, Live County Research, and County-Records-to-CMA Valuation
chapters.executive_summary: Operators converge on one rule: never bid off the county list alone. Pull the parcel number, run it through the free county GIS or parcel viewer, and verify the structure still exists with dated Street View and historical aerials. Tax Sale Secrets frames research as elimination scaled to cost, a $300 lien is not a $30,000 deed, and warns counties never refund. The hard numbers: avoid parcels under 0.1 acre, pay 10 cents on the dollar or less for over-the-counter land, screen opening bids at 10 to 15 percent of assessed value, and value within plus or minus 10 percent using the cheapest comps. The split is over imagery and tooling: Ted Thomas distrusts five-to-ten-year-old Street View while onlinetaxsales rates Google Maps accurate within one to two years.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator starts from the parcel number, not the street address. Dustin Hahn pulled an over-the-counter lien off the Coconino County, Arizona list that carried account number, parcel number, owner, online pay and legal description but no address, and told buyers not to worry: copy the account number, Google the county name plus GIS or parcel viewer, accept the disclaimer, and paste it into search [eJhR4GkZ7Qo @ 00:02:26]. Tax Sale Secrets calls the parcel number the property's social security number and runs the assessor record, tax history and court records by full owner name off it [GxMaS0YFT1Y @ 00:08:29]. Jason Porter goes further on the address itself: the county property profile is free, so never pay for it, and never trust the situs address until it matches the GIS, which counties link 9.9 times out of 10. Porter watched Google pin the wrong address on a 2-bed, 1-bath tax deed property [bnQAJL9-zo0 @ 00:00:17]. Ted Thomas, through five-year associate Linda, adds the hunting rule: there is no single GIS, most of the 3,000-plus counties run their own, so the search string is always the county name plus GIS [a81g1szr71Y @ 00:02:12]. The shared baseline is simple: parcel number in, county viewer confirms location, owner and address before anything else gets money.

The second point of agreement: GIS kills the old plat-map grind. Tax Sale Academy describes the old-school method as transposing a legal description such as Jones subdivision lot one block one onto Bing or Google, with metes-and-bounds descriptions landing in good-luck territory and plats dating to 1902 with no reference points and renamed streets, where Smith A is now 14th Street. GIS transposes the plat automatically and stacks an aerial layer plus school zones, water lines, wells or septic and voting precincts; in the demo the parcel sat in flood zone X, not AE, with dimensions, acreage and qualified sales for comps on the same screen [2B3hCb362oA @ 00:03:23]. Tax Sale Secrets relied on plat maps for 20 years and now checks road access, size, zoning and water in GIS, using 2004 to 2017 historical imagery to catch demolitions [GxMaS0YFT1Y @ 00:16:54]. Ted Thomas pulls floodplain, elevation and boundaries for vacant land, plus soil and vegetation data to plan the exit strategy [a81g1szr71Y @ 00:01:23]. Even IAAO, speaking from the assessor's side, says assessor offices pair street-level and aerial collection with CAMA data and run QC maps that flag waterfront miscoding [1rrID1N_BEY @ 00:02:29]. Operators read the same layers the county uses to set value.

Third, nobody bids until the structure and the land are confirmed with dated imagery, because the county will not bail anyone out. Tax Sales Rebels pulled an over-the-counter parcel that went unsold at auction: 0.29 acre, $1,082 owed, county estimate of $19,000 split $4,000 land and $15,000 building, a 25-year-old wood single-family home with asphalt shingle. The county photo was undated, an old van sat in the frame, and the house may already be gone, so the next move was Google Maps and working on redundancy before bidding [dO80b3ivtWM @ 00:02:05]. Tax Sale Academy uses the top-left date stamp in Street View to click through history, tracking one building from September 2007 through heavier graffiti in 2009 and 2011 to demolition by July 2017, and flags any residential parcel vacant 10 to 20 years as serious serious issues [yUKmyPRuIsY @ 00:00:36]. Dustin Hahn's golf-course parcel pencils at roughly $50k to buy and $800k to build, but only after confirming it is buildable, its hazards and restrictions, and its look in Google Maps [eJhR4GkZ7Qo @ 00:05:11]. Tax Sale Secrets closes the loop: counties never refund, buyer beware, and the one dispute in 20 years ended with the property deeded back [GxMaS0YFT1Y @ 00:29:04].

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Inside the viewer, the mechanics are tool-by-tool. Tax Sale Academy searched Dallas County by owner name Jones and read lot 19 straight off the GIS: 50 ft right-of-way, 75 ft frontage, 120 ft depth. They warned that the aerial angle can draw the house off the lot because the lines are inexact, and that stacking flood, subdivision, utilities and topo layers at once turns the map into an unreadable mess [Mp1_eOyha6A @ 00:01:35]. In Miami-Dade the same channel searched by address, flipped the base map to aerial, and worked the measure and draw tools alongside education and land layers [Mp1_eOyha6A @ 00:03:00]. In the paper-to-property walkthrough, they used the measure tool to clock 106 ft to the target lot so it could be found in the field [_nIeKBXnmws @ 00:03:12]. Dustin Hahn's Coconino lookup shows how to read the value fields: the viewer returned the address, the owner's mailing address and a $3.156M last sale they called aggressive, while the assessor value moved from $47k in 2014 to $107k in 2018. Hahn trusts the $107k because the $3.156M sale likely covers the whole golf course [eJhR4GkZ7Qo @ 00:04:54]. Read assessor history and sale scope together, never one number alone.

The bid math is about elimination and hard caps. Tax Sale Secrets matches research depth to cost, since a $300 lien is not a $30,000 deed, and sets a budget band such as $10k for each round [GxMaS0YFT1Y @ 00:02:56]. Valuation only needs to land within plus or minus 10 percent, using the cheapest comps: their worked example puts an 1,800 sq ft home against comps at $105k to $110k and lands at $55 to $62 per sq ft, with the warning don't cheat yourself [GxMaS0YFT1Y @ 00:34:52]. Tax Sale Academy ran the same discipline on a Marion County vacant 0.17-acre lot with a $5,800 opening bid. Vacant-sale comps ranged from $12.5k to $125k; they threw out a $1.2M outlier, valued the lot at $12,500, capped the max bid near $6,000, and told buyers to drive the comps [_nIeKBXnmws @ 00:09:30]. onlinetaxsales, through Skyler of Tax Sales Solutions, modeled rental exits on Lake County deeds: the Paisley property was assessed at 41k, opened at 5,100, sold at 7,100 against a 54k Zestimate, with $900 rent modeled down to $700 for a 10-month payoff and 10 percent property management [OU-LqZt4nCs @ 00:42:50]. Every number above is a ceiling, not a target.

For screening at volume, the practitioners split between paid platforms and public-web stacks. Tax Sale Resources walks from the Auctions hub to auction details to access data, with raw and over-the-counter lists downloadable by subscription tier. Filters cover deed, redeemable deed and next week, a red icon marks an active filter, and the demo stacked SFR with market value above $50k; saved searches fire weekly Monday emails [HU2epaRqEZE @ 00:02:32]. Parcels can be tagged, graded, grouped and annotated, but export only includes parcels already viewed, and arrow navigation steps parcel to parcel once roughly 2,000 parcels are cut to 5 to 10 [HU2epaRqEZE @ 00:10:15]. Skyler's public-web stack at onlinetaxsales runs propertytaxlist.com for the calendar, then the county files, then lake.realtaxdeed.com on RealAuction, then Zillow and Trulia for comps, history and rent estimates, with Google Voice and a headset to call agents. Then come Google Maps and Google Earth, which Skyler rates accurate within one to two years, sometimes three. Their Quick Glance screen wants the opening bid at 10 to 15 percent of assessed value, up to 20 percent [OU-LqZt4nCs @ 00:47:15]. Ted Thomas adds that building a custom Google map for a county such as Broward cut research time in half [a81g1szr71Y @ 00:03:30].

callout.body: Small workflow habits that keep the parcel count shrinking fast and stop bad data from leaking into a bid [Tax Sale Academy — Mp1_eOyha6A @ 00:05:24].
items: Every county GIS differs, so be patient and click every single button, but toggle layers sparingly because flood, subdivision, utilities and topo stacked together turn the map unreadable [Tax Sale Academy — Mp1_eOyha6A @ 00:05:24].

Keyword search on Tax Sale Resources is broad: 'South Carolina' also hits '500 South Carolina Avenue,' so lean on structured filters instead of free-text search [Tax Sale Resources — HU2epaRqEZE @ 00:03:25].
Build a custom Google map per county, Broward County in the demo, to cut research time in half [Ted Thomas — a81g1szr71Y @ 00:03:30].

sop_steps.title: Pull and Re-Check the List
sop_steps.action: Download the county or over-the-counter list, then re-pull it right before the sale.
sop_steps.detail: Coconino County's downloadable list carries account number, parcel number, owner, online pay and legal description, often with no address [Dustin Hahn — eJhR4GkZ7Qo @ 00:00:32]; availability is step one of the six L&R steps because properties redeem right before the sale [Tax Sale Secrets — GxMaS0YFT1Y @ 00:05:41].

sop_steps.title: Locate the Parcel on County GIS
sop_steps.action: Google the county name plus GIS or parcel viewer, accept the disclaimer, and paste the account or parcel number.
sop_steps.detail: Paste the account number into the county viewer search [Dustin Hahn — eJhR4GkZ7Qo @ 00:02:26], then confirm the situs address against the GIS instead of trusting the list or a Google pin [Jason Porter — bnQAJL9-zo0 @ 00:00:17].

sop_steps.title: Verify Structure, Flood and Hazards
sop_steps.action: Cross-check the county photo with Google Maps, read the flood layer, and scan the hazard panel.
sop_steps.detail: Run Google Maps for redundancy before bidding [Tax Sales Rebels — dO80b3ivtWM @ 00:02:25], confirm flood zone X versus AE on the GIS [Tax Sale Academy — 2B3hCb362oA @ 00:03:23], and read the hazard panel, which showed 5 nearby hazards, medium risk and minimal flood risk in the demo [Tax Sale Resources — HU2epaRqEZE @ 00:09:04].

sop_steps.title: Value Conservatively and Cap the Bid
sop_steps.action: Value within plus or minus 10 percent off the cheapest comps, drop outliers, set a max bid and hold it.
sop_steps.detail: Use the cheapest comps and a $/sq ft check [Tax Sale Secrets — GxMaS0YFT1Y @ 00:34:52], discard outliers like the $1.2M vacant-lot comp and cap near $6,000 on a $12,500 valuation [Tax Sale Academy — _nIeKBXnmws @ 00:09:30], and stick to the max bid with about a year of holding costs budgeted [Tax Sale Secrets — GxMaS0YFT1Y @ 00:55:40].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Tooling is the first split. Jason Porter [bnQAJL9-zo0 @ 00:00:17] is blunt that the county property profile is free, so nobody should pay for it, and that the county GIS is linked to that profile 9.9 times out of 10. Ted Thomas associate Linda [a81g1szr71Y @ 00:00:36] builds the whole stack from three free sources: the property appraiser for assessed value, zoning, land use and owner name, the county GIS, and Google Maps with Street View. Linda adds that a custom Google map built for one county, such as Broward, "cut your research time in half," a free speed hack that requires no subscription. Tax Sale Resources [HU2epaRqEZE @ 00:08:16] runs the opposite playbook: a subscription hub where raw and over-the-counter lists download by tier, and title search, property scope, inspection and AVM or MLS comps cost $0 with credits or about $0.99 after. Tax Sale Academy [2B3hCb362oA @ 00:04:44] adds the coverage reality behind the debate: GIS is an expense for counties, only about 50% have it, so check for GIS before committing research hours to a county. The split comes down to cost versus speed: the county tools are free, while the hub's parcel-to-parcel arrow navigation is built for narrowing a list of about 2,000 parcels down to 5 to 10 serious targets.

Practitioners split hard on how far to trust dated street-level and aerial imagery before bidding. Linda [a81g1szr71Y @ 00:02:30] says Google Street View updates roughly yearly and warns that photos 5 to 10 years old are unreliable for judging a parcel. Skyler of onlinetaxsales [OU-LqZt4nCs @ 00:49:04] is more confident, calling Google Maps and Google Earth accurate within 1 to 2 years, sometimes 3, and folds them straight into the address workflow after Zillow and Trulia. Tax Sale Academy [yUKmyPRuIsY @ 00:00:23] flips the staleness problem into an asset: the date stamp at top left and the clickable history let an operator watch a building go from September 2007 to more graffiti in 2009 and 2011 to demolished by July 2017, and a residential parcel sitting vacant for 10 to 20 years signals serious serious issues. Tax Sales Rebels [dO80b3ivtWM @ 00:02:05] treats imagery as a single point of failure, flagging an undated county photo with an old van in it and refusing to bid until the house is confirmed through Google Maps, a process they call working on redundancy. The three alternative playbooks are therefore current-snapshot trust, timeline reading for trend direction, and multi-source cross-checking before any deposit money goes down.

Valuation and target selection split the room further. Tax Sale Secrets [GxMaS0YFT1Y @ 00:34:52] says valuation within plus or minus 10% is enough, insists on the cheapest comps, and caps over-the-counter land at 10 cents on the dollar, while Tax Sale Academy [_nIeKBXnmws @ 00:09:30] values a vacant 0.17 acre Marion County lot at the $12,500 bottom of a $12.5k to $125k comp range, throws out a $1.2M outlier, and sets a max bid near $6,000 against a $5,800 opener. Skyler's Quick Glance screen instead keys off assessed value, wanting an opening bid at 10 to 15% of assessed, up to 20%. On asset type, the Tax Sale Secrets lien session [dI48opW6bWQ @ 00:13:35] targets land over the picket-fence home because it pays about 16 to 17% versus about 3% at equal value, and land is more likely to reach foreclosure. Cal Ewing [rDGjWMwISOY @ 00:05:36] counters the rate optimism with Maricopa data: bidding opens at 16% and gets bid down to an average of about 5%, and there is no real general formula, so every county gets its own research. Skyler's pitch of 10 to 25% guaranteed returns following their system sits at the opposite pole of that spread.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: A recurring trap is bidding on a structure that is not where, or what, the record says. Tax Sales Rebels [dO80b3ivtWM @ 00:01:22] walked an over-the-counter parcel owing $1,082 with a $19,000 county estimate, a 25-year-old wood single-family home, and still called it not a go because the only county photo was undated and the house might be gone. Tax Sale Secrets [GxMaS0YFT1Y @ 00:16:54] reports that historical imagery from 2004 to 2017 reveals demolitions, after relying on plat maps for 20 years. Address errors compound it: Jason Porter [bnQAJL9-zo0 @ 00:00:52] watched Google pin the wrong address on a 2-bed, 1-bath property and refuses to trust the situs address until the GIS confirms it, and Tax Sale Academy [Mp1_eOyha6A @ 00:01:20] warns that aerial angle can make the house appear off its own lot because the lines are inexact. Skyler adds a mechanical failure, noting addresses can split when pasted into search tools. Tax Sale Academy's Miami-Dade walk-through likewise compares 2005 imagery with current aerials before a $35,000 opening bid. The fix is the redundancy the Rebels describe: parcel number into GIS, aerial plus Street View history, then a second map source like Google Maps before the max bid is locked.

Land is where practitioners report the most traps on cheap lists. Jason Porter [bnQAJL9-zo0 @ 00:01:27] found 1.14 acre parcels with $1,500 opening bids that looked worth $25,000 but sit underwater half the year, making them worthless. Tax Sale Secrets [dI48opW6bWQ @ 00:23:09] calls a $36 lien on a 0.7 foot strip of land junk, and the same channel [GxMaS0YFT1Y @ 00:46:21] names useless land the biggest risk, avoids anything under 0.1 acre, and says to call the HOA before buying. Dustin Hahn [eJhR4GkZ7Qo @ 00:05:11] floats a buy-for-about-$50k, build-for-about-$800k play on the Coconino parcel, but only after verifying the land is buildable, its hazards and restrictions, and a Google Maps check. Government liens found through court records are the second trap: Tax Sale Secrets plans around the 120-day IRS window on IRS liens but treats city and state liens as payoffs, and Skyler warns Florida HOAs may try to collect from the new owner even after a mostly free-and-clear deed purchase. Flood layers need reading, not glancing: one Tax Sale Academy demo confirmed zone X rather than AE, while All Things Spatial flags a zone AE floodway hit on a Livonia parcel and notes the official determination is a separate document.

The economics checks are where cheap paper turns into dead money. Tax Sale Secrets [GxMaS0YFT1Y @ 00:29:04] warns that counties will never refund a buyer, buyer beware, and that their one dispute in 20 years was settled by deeding the property back; the same masterclass says to re-check the county list because properties redeem right before the sale, budget about one year of holding costs such as $100 to $150 weed cutting, and stick to the max bid. On liens, the Tax Sale Secrets auction review [dI48opW6bWQ @ 00:55:02] reminds that a small lien carries the exact same foreclosure cost as a big one, that redemption happens 95 plus percent of the time, that roll-up risk concentrates in Arizona and Florida, and that an unpurchased 2019 lien on a $9.2M property is a caution flag. Platform mechanics bite too: Tax Sale Resources [HU2epaRqEZE @ 00:06:38] warns that exports include only parcels already viewed and that keyword search is broad enough for South Carolina to match 500 South Carolina Avenue. Skyler [OU-LqZt4nCs @ 00:34:19] adds that an investor renting out or living in a Texas redemption-deed property must write in a redemption clause and be ready to move out if it redeems.

callout.title: Do Not Bid Until These Four Clear
callout.body: Every item below comes from a loss, a near-miss, or a hard rule the practitioners report from their own parcels. If any one fails, the parcel stays off the bid sheet.
items: Structure confirmed on current and historical imagery, never on an undated county photo alone [Tax Sales Rebels — dO80b3ivtWM @ 00:02:05].
Location verified in the county GIS by parcel number, never by the situs address or a Google pin [Jason Porter — bnQAJL9-zo0 @ 00:00:17].
Land checked for flooding, buildability and minimum size, skipping anything under 0.1 acre and calling the HOA [Tax Sale Secrets — GxMaS0YFT1Y @ 00:46:21].
Parcel re-confirmed on the county list right before the sale, owner name run through court records for government liens, and max bid fixed [Tax Sale Secrets — GxMaS0YFT1Y @ 00:05:41].

action_checklist: Download the county or over-the-counter list and copy the account or parcel number, even when no address is listed [Dustin Hahn — eJhR4GkZ7Qo @ 00:01:53].
Google the county name plus GIS or parcel viewer, click through the county's entry screen, and paste the parcel number into search [Dustin Hahn — eJhR4GkZ7Qo @ 00:02:26].
Toggle aerial, flood and other layers one at a time, then pull dimensions, acreage and qualified sales for comps [Tax Sale Academy — 2B3hCb362oA @ 00:04:16].
Click through Street View history by date stamp to judge area direction and the specific parcel's history [Tax Sale Academy — yUKmyPRuIsY @ 00:02:29].
Run the owner name from the property appraiser through county records to find liens and mortgages [Ted Thomas — a81g1szr71Y @ 00:01:08].
Value off the cheapest comps within plus or minus 10%, set the max bid, and do not cheat yourself [Tax Sale Secrets — GxMaS0YFT1Y @ 00:34:52].

chapters.question_prompt: When a lien doesn't redeem, how do I foreclose and turn the deed into insurable title?
chapters.title: Foreclosure and Quiet Title
chapters.subtitle: Tax Lien Foreclosure Steps, Judicial vs. Nonjudicial Processes, Suit to Quiet Title, Tax Foreclosure Certification, DIY Quiet Title, Timelines and Costs, and Why 'Pay the Taxes, Get the House' Is False
chapters.executive_summary: Tax lien foreclosure practitioners agree the non-redeeming lien is the payday: the lienholder steps into the county's first-position strength, notices every interest holder, and wipes out mortgages and junior liens once the window closes. They equally agree the resulting county deed is a bare quitclaim whose clouded title no insurer will cover until it is cured, and that experienced counsel should drive both the foreclosure and the cure. Street numbers run from $500 to $4,000 for foreclosure counsel, a $1,400 flat-fee Michigan quiet title in roughly 120 days, $3,000 to $5,000 over three to six months per Ted Thomas, and $1,950 to $3,000 certification audits turning in three to six weeks. Practitioners split on suit versus certification, pro se filing, IRS lien survival, and installment sales that let time quiet the title.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator on this foreclosure track agrees on the same engine: the tax lien sits in first position, and pushing it through foreclosure strips the encumbrances that sit behind it. Saen Higgins frames the lienholder as stepping into the county's shoes, saying that position carries the power to wipe out Bank of America, Wells Fargo, the mechanic's lien, Aunt Sally and even the IRS, and that if nobody steps up inside the prescribed window the property is theirs free and clear [EXkUbWWenl0 @ 00:06:28]. Dustin Hahn calls the non-redeeming lien the home run of the business precisely because the tax lien is the priority lien and foreclosure wipes out the mortgage [tXVBp8vbkT4 @ 00:05:05]. Tax Sale Secrets ranks judicial tax foreclosure as the most powerful foreclosure a property can go through, telling buyers they are always better off taking a parcel that has just run through that process than one that has not [rQco9s4XodM @ 00:07:57]. The baseline economics are the same across the room: most owners redeem, so the deed is the exception, and Hahn models it as roughly one property out of every 20 certificates when 95 percent redeem [tXVBp8vbkT4 @ 00:04:12].

The second point of agreement is that the deed coming out of a tax foreclosure is a bare quitclaim and the title behind it is clouded. Ted Thomas says whatever the county calls it, whether a county deed, tax deed, treasurer's deed or commissioner's deed, it is always a quitclaim, the county takes no responsibility for condition or title defects, and a quitclaim alone is worthless to a commercial title company [O8MWhOJE6Oc @ 00:04:12]. Darren Findlay of Quiet Title Michigan puts it in chain-of-title terms: the county hands over a quitclaim sale deed, so if there is a defect, a tenant or an undischarged interest, the buyer receives it [7yD_brKdgXk @ 00:14:38]. Findlay adds that a title issue is inherent in every tax sale parcel because the title industry has watched former owners sue counties over notices and win, so insurers treat these properties as higher risk [7yD_brKdgXk @ 00:22:28]. Casey Dimmon of Tax Sale Academy lands in the same place, explaining that high-volume counties overlook steps and some sales get challenged in court, so title insurers simply refuse to insure; the options are selling as-is at a discount, which Dimmon has done many times, or removing the cloud [7BP12s9Jn2c @ 00:03:45].

Third, the practitioners agree the paperwork belongs with a specialist and that the courtroom fight is usually a formality. Saen Higgins says don't do this on your own over and over, telling lienholders to let the county run the foreclosure where it is required to and otherwise hire a real estate attorney in that particular jurisdiction who understands the local rules [EXkUbWWenl0 @ 00:05:39]. Ted Thomas says a buyer can legally run a quiet title solo but refuses to, insisting on an attorney who has already done quiet titles, because an inexperienced one gets paid to learn how on your file [TRZbdE4y2sc @ 00:07:14]. On the other side of the docket, Darren Findlay reports that the vast majority of named defendants never respond or simply consent to the relief requested, which keeps most quiet title actions procedural in nature [kJRxvYeK_eU @ 00:06:08]. Casey Dimmon confirms that challengers rarely show up because litigating is expensive and time-consuming for a defendant, so the overwhelming majority of suits end in a default judgment after the statutory response window closes, and the same title company that refused coverage is then more than happy to insure [7BP12s9Jn2c @ 00:06:15].

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Executing the lien foreclosure starts with one question: who drives it. Tax Sale Secrets splits states into self-executing systems, where the lienholder fills out a form or gives the county the go-ahead and the county sends every notice, and non-self-executing systems, where the burden sits on the lienholder and the move is to hire a real estate attorney and bake that cost into the deal [rQco9s4XodM @ 00:16:31]. They flag Florida as self-executing with a twist: the county runs the parcel through a tax deed sale, pays lienholders from the proceeds, and only hands over the property if nobody bids [rQco9s4XodM @ 00:18:02]. Saen Higgins describes the notice blast going to everyone with a financial interest, a response window of roughly 60 days in some counties and 100 in others, and attorney fees of about $500 on simple files up to $3,000 to $4,000 on complicated ones, which the owner must also pay if they redeem mid-process [EXkUbWWenl0 @ 00:07:50]. Dustin Hahn budgets one to two thousand dollars for the foreclosure attorney, roughly another thousand for the follow-on quiet title, plus a year or two of subsequent taxes [tXVBp8vbkT4 @ 00:05:34].

The quiet title suit itself follows a fixed sequence that Darren Findlay of Quiet Title Michigan lays out step by step: run an independent title search even if a title company already did one, stack the deeds into a chain, then cast a wide net of defendants because missing one fish means the judgment fails to clear title and the process starts over [kJRxvYeK_eU @ 00:03:19]. The complaint is filed in the circuit court where the property sits, fees are paid, and service of process begins, using personal service where possible, certified mail, or a court order for alternate means such as publishing in the legal news and mailing last known addresses for missing owners, defunct entities and probate estates [kJRxvYeK_eU @ 00:04:56]. Findlay calls service the most time-consuming step, then files the default, re-serves it, obtains the default judgment, waits out the appeal period and records the perfected judgment at the Register of Deeds [kJRxvYeK_eU @ 00:08:02]. Casey Dimmon times the same track: a good attorney files within a week or two, defendants get 30 or 45 days to respond, and backed-up courts can add eight months to a year before a judge even sees the file [7BP12s9Jn2c @ 00:13:14].

Pricing spreads wide. Findlay quotes about 120 days and a flat $1,400 plus costs on tax reversion or very procedural files, with more complicated matters priced differently [kJRxvYeK_eU @ 00:09:55]. Ted Thomas plans on three to six months and $3,000 to $5,000 for a normal quiet title [MzL0xEaYnUI @ 00:01:31]. Casey Dimmon cites $2,000 to $5,000 as common suit figures, then lays out the faster lane: a tax foreclosure certification, where a third-party firm audits every document in the foreclosure file against state statute and, if it checks out, tells its partner title insurer to issue a policy. Dimmon names Tax Title Services out of California at four to six weeks with a paid rush option under a month, Clear to Sell in Florida at around three weeks, fees of $1,950 to $3,000, and an uncertifiable rate the companies put under 5 percent [7BP12s9Jn2c @ 00:15:10]. In an earlier Tax Sale Academy episode, the quoted ranges were $600 to $5,000 and a couple of months to a full year for a suit, against 45 to 60 days and $1,500 to $3,000 for certification [2g2qJcuuey4 @ 00:02:22].

callout.title: Compressing Time and Cost from Lien to Insurable Title
callout.body: Four moves practitioners use to speed up foreclosure and shave the title-cure bill.
items: Buy foreclosable liens straight out of county inventory: certificates already past redemption let you start foreclosure immediately, which Higgins likens to taking 20 shots on goal now instead of waiting two years [Saen Higgins — EXkUbWWenl0 @ 00:08:53].
Buy the first-year lien, not the second or third, so you hold the priority to foreclose; Hahn warns that a third-year lien buyer cannot foreclose [Dustin Hahn — tXVBp8vbkT4 @ 00:05:49].
Batch your files: Dimmon's cheapest quiet titles came from handing one attorney ten properties at once, which gave leverage to back the price down [Tax Sale Academy — vMMozg0xaSA @ 00:05:22].

Cast the defendant net wide, because one missed claimant leaves the title unresolved and forces the whole suit to start over to remove that one interest [Quiet Title Michigan — kJRxvYeK_eU @ 00:03:19].

sop_steps.title: Confirm Who Drives the Foreclosure
sop_steps.action: Determine whether the state runs self-executing or non-self-executing foreclosure before buying any lien.
sop_steps.detail: In self-executing states the lienholder fills out a form and the county sends all notices; in non-self-executing states the lienholder carries the process and should plan on hiring a real estate attorney and pricing that into the investment [Tax Sale Secrets — rQco9s4XodM @ 00:17:06].

sop_steps.title: Trigger the Foreclosure and Notice Blast
sop_steps.action: After redemption expires, call the county as lienholder of record and elect to foreclose.
sop_steps.detail: Notices go to every party with a financial interest, from the owner to Bank of America to the IRS; if nobody pays inside the county's 60-day or 100-day style window, the property transfers free and clear of liens and encumbrances [Saen Higgins — EXkUbWWenl0 @ 00:06:10].

sop_steps.title: Build the Chain and the Defendant List
sop_steps.action: Run an independent title search and name every undischarged interest in a circuit court complaint.
sop_steps.detail: Findlay's firm re-runs its own title search even when a title company supplies one, builds the chain person A to B to C, flags gaps and defects, and names every claimant before filing where the property sits [Quiet Title Michigan — kJRxvYeK_eU @ 00:02:02].

sop_steps.title: Serve, Default, Record, Insure
sop_steps.action: Serve all defendants, enter defaults, obtain the judgment, let the appeal period run, and record it.
sop_steps.detail: The perfected judgment is recorded at the Register of Deeds like any deed or mortgage [Quiet Title Michigan — kJRxvYeK_eU @ 00:08:02], then taken to the same title company, which will issue title insurance against it [Tax Sale Academy — 7BP12s9Jn2c @ 00:06:33].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over who files the paper. Saen Higgins is absolutist. They call a do-it-yourself tax lien foreclosure 'just ridiculous' and compare it to swapping the batteries on a Tesla. Their play is to let the county run it where it is required to, or to retain a local real estate attorney for roughly $500 on simple files and up to $3,000 to $4,000 on complicated ones. A redeeming owner who comes in during the window pays those attorney fees [EXkUbWWenl0 @ 00:07:38]. Dustin Hahn concedes the lienholder can foreclose solo, but still budgets one to two grand for an attorney plus roughly another thousand for the quiet title afterward [tXVBp8vbkT4 @ 00:05:19]. Casey Dimmon of Tax Sale Academy draws the legal line operators miss. Pro se filing only works when the deed sits in the investor's personal name. An LLC or corporation cannot be represented without a license to practice law, and that filing will likely be rejected or worse [vMMozg0xaSA @ 00:02:46]. Ted Thomas lands in the middle: yes, a quiet title can be done yourself, but their own answer is no. The proceeding turns adversarial when fences, easements, or encroachments surface. The move is an attorney who has already done quiet titles, not one who learns on your dime [TRZbdE4y2sc @ 00:04:24].

On how to cure the cloud, the playbooks fork. Casey Dimmon calls the suit to quiet title 'really the complete solution,' because the judgment alone gets the policy issued. The tax foreclosure certification is faster and usually cheaper, but it carries strings. The certifier's partner title insurer may be mandatory at closing. The tax-deed history may have to be disclosed. The certification can also expire and need paid re-certification if the asset sits for three, four, or five years [7BP12s9Jn2c @ 00:09:00]. In an earlier breakdown, the same operator is openly skeptical of the vendors' 'faster and cheaper' pitch. Quiet titles run $600 to $5,000 over a couple of months to a year, against certifications advertised at 45 to 60 days and $1,500 to $3,000. The instruction is to collect attorney quotes, compare them, and take the cheapest route [2g2qJcuuey4 @ 00:02:05]. Darren Findlay of Quiet Title Michigan rejects workarounds outright. Short of getting prior owners to deed off, which is very uncommon, the lawsuit is the only actual way to correct the title [7yD_brKdgXk @ 00:23:13]. Any strategy that merely lets a title agency close 'just kicks the can down the road,' because a title issue runs with the land and resurfaces with the next purchaser [7yD_brKdgXk @ 00:26:42].

The exit side splits too. Ted Thomas teaches advanced students to skip the lawsuit on certain deals. They sell on a contract of sale or installment note and keep legal title while the buyer makes payments for two or three years. Time then clears the title, and the title company says there have been no claims for three years and writes the policy. Brand-new investors are told to plan for the experienced attorney instead [MzL0xEaYnUI @ 00:07:50]. Casey Dimmon's cheaper alternative is to sell as-is at a discount without title insurance. They have done that 'many many times' over the years [7BP12s9Jn2c @ 00:04:03]. On the lien side, the foreclosure regime itself rewrites the playbook. Tax Sale Secrets separates self-executing states from non-self-executing states. In a self-executing state, the lienholder fills out a form and the county sends every notice. In a non-self-executing state, the lienholder carries the process and should plan on hiring a real estate attorney. Florida adds a layer: it runs the lien through a tax deed sale and pays lienholders from the proceeds, and hands over the property only if nobody bids [rQco9s4XodM @ 00:16:12]. Saen Higgins shortcuts the clock instead. They buy already-foreclosable liens out of county inventory, so 20 purchases become 20 immediate 'shots on goal' instead of a two-year redemption wait [EXkUbWWenl0 @ 00:08:53].
