sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Time is the bleed nobody prices in. Ted Thomas bought a tax-defaulted property online with a credit card for $140,000 and planned a $350,000 to $400,000 exit. Real estate dropped substantially the following winter, and they ultimately sold at $280,000. That sale came only after a retiring judge spent 13 months of diligent work getting the quiet title issued. Buyers could not get a mortgage until the title cleared. So Thomas ate 13 months of taxes, heat, cleaning, landscaping, snow removal, and security bills on an ownership period they did not want [O8MWhOJE6Oc @ 00:07:42]. Casey Dimmon flags where those months hide: an attorney who lets the file sit on the desk for a month or longer, 30 to 45 day defendant response windows, and court systems backed up eight months or even a year before a judge sees the case. The investor carries maintenance the whole time [7BP12s9Jn2c @ 00:13:14]. Ted Thomas's own baseline for a normal quiet title is three to six months and $3,000 to $5,000 [MzL0xEaYnUI @ 00:01:31]. Darren Findlay quotes about 120 days, and a $1,400 flat fee plus costs, only on procedural tax-reversion files. They warn that the judge's schedule and the defendant count set the real clock [kJRxvYeK_eU @ 00:09:18].

The second trap is a judgment that does not hold. Casey Dimmon warns that a pro se filer who blows a single stipulation can have the case thrown out by the judge. That burns hundreds of dollars in filing fees and hours of preparation. Worse, the filer can win a signed order whose language still fails the title insurance company's requirements, which forces the whole process to start over [vMMozg0xaSA @ 00:04:02]. Darren Findlay calls the defendant list a net. Miss one fish, meaning one undischarged interest holder, and the judgment of quiet title does not resolve the title. The process then starts all over again just to get rid of that one party [kJRxvYeK_eU @ 00:03:19]. Findlay says the office regularly gets called to fix judgments that other law firms obtained or started. The title company reviews every step behind the order. A judgment built on work that was not done correctly is suspect and can be overturned by a subsequent court [kJRxvYeK_eU @ 00:08:20]. Even the certification route has a failure branch. Vendors report hitting uncertifiable tax sale files less than 5 percent of the time. When the defect cannot be solved, the investor needs a suit to quiet title after all, and the time spent on the certification attempt is gone [7BP12s9Jn2c @ 00:11:48].

The third cluster detonates before the gavel. Darren Findlay has watched clients buy what they thought was a structure plus the land at tax sale, only for the city or county to demolish it shortly afterward. Any dilapidated or unsafe-looking parcel gets checked against the demolition list before money goes down [7yD_brKdgXk @ 00:04:36]. Findlay also flags IRS liens. Those are governed by federal law, while the tax forfeiture runs under state law, and there is some question whether the county has the power to wipe them out. That pushes those files into a quiet title action [7yD_brKdgXk @ 00:25:11]. This directly undercuts Saen Higgins's street pitch that the foreclosing lienholder inherits the county's strength and extinguishes everything, 'including, yes, even the IRS' [EXkUbWWenl0 @ 00:06:28]. Dustin Hahn's trap is buying the wrong year and running the wrong math. Only a first-year lien carries the priority to foreclose, and a third-year purchase cannot be foreclosed. The viral 'pay the back taxes, own the house' hustle ignores two numbers. With roughly 95 percent redemption, an operator needs about 20 certificates to land one property. That operator still pays subsequent taxes, an attorney, and the quiet title [tXVBp8vbkT4 @ 00:05:34].

callout.title: Clear These Four Gates Before Funding Any Foreclosure or Tax Deed Bid
callout.body: Each gate below traces to a delay, loss, or restart that a practitioner hit personally or watched clients hit. A file that fails any one of them gets repriced or passed.
items: Carry-cost gate: underwrite three to six months and $3,000 to $5,000 for a normal quiet title. Then stress-test a 13-month hold that includes taxes, heat, snow removal, and security, because buyers cannot get a mortgage until the title clears [Ted Thomas — O8MWhOJE6Oc @ 00:08:01].

Entity gate: decide on individual, LLC, or joint ownership before bidding. Re-deeding afterward can trigger property tax uncapping or gift conveyance issues [Quiet Title Michigan — 7yD_brKdgXk @ 00:13:04]. An LLC-owned parcel also cannot be quieted pro se [Tax Sale Academy — vMMozg0xaSA @ 00:02:46].

Defendant-net gate: build the full chain of title, name every undischarged interest, and serve each one properly, because one missed party forces a full restart [Quiet Title Michigan — kJRxvYeK_eU @ 00:03:19].

Lien-priority gate: confirm the certificate is the first-year lien that carries the right to foreclose. Model roughly 20 certificates per property acquired at about 95 percent redemption [Dustin Hahn — tXVBp8vbkT4 @ 00:05:34].

chapters.pull_quote: "Our quiet title action is only as good as the net that we cast." — Darren Findlay, Quiet Title Michigan (kJRxvYeK_eU @ 00:03:19).
action_checklist: Physically inspect every target parcel and its neighborhood instead of relying on photos. Check whether it is on the demolition list and whether it is occupied before bidding [Quiet Title Michigan — 7yD_brKdgXk @ 00:02:34].
Set your exit price before the auction and derive your maximum bid from that exit strategy [Ted Thomas — TRZbdE4y2sc @ 00:11:50].

Confirm whether the state runs self-executing or non-self-executing foreclosure. In a non-self-executing state, retain a real estate attorney for the first file [Tax Sale Secrets — rQco9s4XodM @ 00:17:28].
Get quiet title referrals from local tax sale investors and price-shop attorneys. Bundle multiple properties into one engagement to lever the fee down [Tax Sale Academy — vMMozg0xaSA @ 00:05:22].

Compare attorney quotes against tax foreclosure certification vendors on both price and turnaround, then take the cheapest route that still gets title insurance [Tax Sale Academy — 2g2qJcuuey4 @ 00:02:38].

After the judgment, let the statutory appeal period expire. Then record the perfected judgment at the Register of Deeds so the title is quieted of record [Quiet Title Michigan — kJRxvYeK_eU @ 00:08:02].

chapters.question_prompt: What risks, title traps, and competing liens can wipe out a tax sale investment, and what do real outcomes look like?
chapters.title: Risks, Title Traps, and Field Case Studies
chapters.subtitle: Skeptical Takes and Pros/Cons, Supplemental Taxes, HOA Liens, Code Enforcement Lien Clearing, Removing Parties From a Deed, Burned-Down and Negative-Value Parcels, and Lien Case Studies
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners across lien, deed, title, and HOA channels converge on one reality: roughly 90-95% of tax liens redeem, so the lien is mostly an interest play (8-36% maximum rates, bid down by banks and funds), while the property is the rare outcome that drags in title trouble. Dustin Hahn, Ted Thomas, and TaxLienLady all hammer county-by-county rules, physical inspection, and paying subsequent taxes. Alex Goldovsky puts 25% of title issues on unrecorded municipal liens, and Jennifer Felton prices quiet title from a grand or two uncontested to $100K+ disputed, over one to four years. The split is sharp: Dustin Hahn models $50k into 100 liens yielding about 5 properties, while The Ramsey Show host calls two lien buys "a freaking nightmare" and puts the odds of success "really close to zero."

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Redemption is the base case, and every serious operator prices it that way. Dustin Hahn puts redemption at about 95% and names the mortgage bank as the biggest redeemer, because a county foreclosure would wipe its loan [iCR-rdsQrUg @ 00:02:31]. Ted Thomas and coach Bill Williams land in the same band, with 90-95% of liens paying off, and flag non-owner-occupied or out-of-state owners as the files most likely to end with the investor holding the property [sXKw09ndbYg @ 00:09:03]. The Ramsey Show host frames the same mechanic from the skeptic side: the owner gets one to two years to redeem and pays back the taxes plus "10% or 15% interest" [KytTy1-RC5I @ 00:04:55]. Dustin Hahn adds the cash-flow reality that capital sits tied up for two to three years, so the money in a lien is not working money in the short run [vA4ImBMyenY @ 00:03:02]. The operating takeaway is blunt: the lien is an interest instrument first, and property acquisition is a low-percentage tail outcome. Anyone underwriting a lien purely as a cheap path to a house is fighting the core math that both bullish and bearish practitioners agree on, and needs a deliberate filter for the small slice that will not redeem and the extra cost that slice triggers.

The second point of agreement is that there is no national tax lien game, only thousands of local ones. Dustin Hahn counts roughly 3,300 counties, split about half lien and half deed, each running different rules [iCR-rdsQrUg @ 00:04:18], and tells bidders to learn each county's rules before posting a dollar [vA4ImBMyenY @ 00:09:10]. TaxLienLady (Joanne Musa), who learned by trial and error in New Jersey, reduces every jurisdiction to four essentials: interest rate, bidding procedure, redemption period, and lien life [7ybooMbrE58 @ 00:07:10]. Those four variables swing hard: New Jersey caps at 18% with a two-year redemption and a 20-year lien life, Iowa caps at 24% with a three-year lien life that means starting foreclosure right away, Arizona caps at 16% with three years to redeem, and Florida caps at 18% with a seven-year lien life. Ted Thomas maps the deed side the same way: South Carolina's county issues the deed, Georgia requires a private attorney, Florida runs two auctions, and California and Washington sell deeds directly [sXKw09ndbYg @ 00:07:47]. The consensus prerequisite is a county rulebook built before bidding, because the same lien dollar earns a different rate, waits a different period, and dies on a different clock depending on where it sits on the map.

The third consensus is that title, not the interest rate, is where operators get hurt. The Ramsey Show host states that tax foreclosures "in zero States clean the title," warning that a buyer can inherit mortgages and IRS liens, and puts Texas redeemable tax deeds in the same bucket [KytTy1-RC5I @ 00:06:06]. Ted Thomas reports government liens surviving the sale, including a lot worth $156K that carried a $145K lien, and reminds bidders that everything sells as-is under caveat emptor [sXKw09ndbYg @ 00:22:36]. Alex Goldovsky of ProTitleUSA, who founded the firm in 2008 after taking losses from a bad search, says "25% of the issues are related to unrecorded municipal liens," such as code violations and permits that can run $100 per day in Arizona, plus utility debt attaching to the property in roughly half the country [O6HhpnnQADM @ 00:16:00]. A Florida title attorney with about 20 years in practice reports that in blighted neighborhoods, code enforcement, special assessment, and municipal liens blocked rehabbers "almost every time," alongside unclear title from absentee owners, defunct corporations, and multi-generation estates [zPDMr-7eAOc @ 00:00:33]. The shared rule: the recorded index is incomplete, and the debt that never hits it is what kills the deal after the auction.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: On the lien side, the execution loop is simple and the money is in the follow-through. TaxLienLady lays out the cycle as buy the lien, record it, pay the subsequent taxes, and collect, noting some Arizona counties require the subsequent-tax payments and that foreclosure "rarely happens" [7ybooMbrE58 @ 00:10:33]. Premier Wealth Builders says the lienholder holds first right to pay supplemental taxes in every state the speaker knows except Mississippi, naming Alabama, Arizona, and Florida, and warns that skipping a year lets another party buy the subsequent-year lien and either sit as a second lienholder or pay the original holder off: "If you don't pay the supplemental, that's your fault" [AYiTxfuCWHk @ 00:01:36]. Kyra at Rent To Retirement runs the operator sequence as learn the auctions, pick a county, scout properties from the outside, set a maximum bid, check payment rules, notify homeowners, and collect, with 12-18% returns as the target band [iOoZ743spRo @ 00:02:55]. Dustin Hahn's portfolio math shows why scale matters: $50k buys about 100 liens, and at roughly 5% non-redemption that yields about five properties, or around $500k in property, the same model Hahn says big funds run [iCR-rdsQrUg @ 00:03:19].

Deed and post-foreclosure diligence is a physical job with hard numbers attached. Dustin Hahn's rule is "drive the property," because Google Earth misses fires, floods, and demolitions, and title company research runs $20-30 per report, or $2-3k to clear a list of 100 deeds [vA4ImBMyenY @ 00:07:24]. Ted Thomas and Bill Williams push trained boots on the ground with a checklist covering roof, windows, green pools, and oak roots under the driveway; a popped Houston pool, roughly $30K, went straight into Bill's maximum bid [sXKw09ndbYg @ 00:31:26]. That crew pays 20-50 cents on the dollar and wins only "several percent" of the bids it places, which is selectivity by design [sXKw09ndbYg @ 00:33:48]. Tax Lien Bootcamp's Georgia instructor shows the exterior-only workflow on a live deal: no key, estimate the AC at about $5k plus paint, then buy a 3-bed, 2-bath for $4,500 against a $2,300 opening bid. Repairs ran $55k for about $60k all-in, against a $130k after-repair value and $70k of equity, held as a rental at $1,200 per month with a cash-out refinance of up to 80% to fund the next buy [wyAiYLlWM6A @ 00:03:31].

Clearing whatever survives the sale is its own playbook. Alex Goldovsky's rule is "if it's not municipality, everything is negotiable," and Goldovsky reports partial IRS releases are achievable by presenting a sale to a homebuyer [O6HhpnnQADM @ 00:10:47]. ProTitleUSA prices curative work at $150-175 per release and says replacement title policies lift note value by 20-30% [O6HhpnnQADM @ 00:25:57]. For strangers stuck on title, Jennifer Felton of ReLaw gives two paths: locate the person and get a deed signed back, or file a quiet title lawsuit that runs through lawyer databases, then private investigators, proof of a diligent search before service by publication, a default, and a mandatory prove-up hearing. Felton's timeline is one year best case, two to three realistically, with one case in year four; cost runs a grand or two uncontested, $10-15K in court, and $100K+ when disputed, and one client paid $25K to get people off title [B0yvMIdmaaQ @ 00:23:16]. The episode's buyout math is direct: "if you can get the guy to sign off now and you give him 20 grand it's probably a good deal" versus litigating. Dustin Hahn builds a quiet title into the plan on deed acquisitions from day one [vA4ImBMyenY @ 00:10:04].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is whether the game is worth playing at all. The Ramsey Show host has owned about 2,000 properties, bought exactly two tax-lien plays, called both “a freaking nightmare,” and said “never again,” rating the odds of success “really close to zero” and telling a 24-year-old TikTok recruit he would be better off delivering pizza [KytTy1-RC5I @ 00:05:35]. Dustin Hahn runs the opposite math: about 95% of liens redeem, the bank is the biggest redeemer because a county foreclosure would wipe its mortgage, and $50k spread across 100 liens should shake loose about five properties worth roughly $500k, the model he says big funds run [iCR-rdsQrUg @ 00:03:19]. Even Hahn splits by bankroll: with only $5–10k he calls liens “not really worth it” and steers students to deeds, where he says they bought up to ninety percent below market [iCR-rdsQrUg @ 00:05:24]. Joanne Musa of TaxLienLady plays a third game entirely, treating liens as a compounding interest engine rather than a property grab: foreclosure “rarely happens,” and $5k a year for 10 years at 10% projects to $361,662 after 25 years, close to $1M at 15% [7ybooMbrE58 @ 00:11:56]. Same instrument, three incompatible theses: avoid it, farm it for properties, or farm it for yield.

Title is the second fault line. George on The Ramsey Show says Texas sells “redeemable tax deeds,” and the host goes further: tax foreclosures “in zero States clean the title,” so the buyer inherits mortgages and IRS liens [KytTy1-RC5I @ 00:06:06]. Dustin Hahn pitches the reverse on over-the-counter deeds, available “as fast as today” and arriving mortgage-free because the tax deed is the priority lien [bsVbyBCB2sA @ 00:00:00]. Alex Goldovsky of ProTitleUSA sits between the two camps with hard mechanics: second-lien foreclosures stay subject to the first, a Nevada HOA can wipe both, and a $10k tax-sale bid can yield clear title after redemption, but in Texas tax loans and some HOAs jump priority, and a deed-in-lieu leaves second liens intact [O6HhpnnQADM @ 00:05:46]. Ted Thomas and coach Bill Williams land closer to Ramsey on the deed side, warning that government liens can survive the sale, citing a lot worth $156K that carried a $145K lien, with everything sold as-is under caveat emptor [sXKw09ndbYg @ 00:22:36]. The working read for an operator is that “clean title” is never a blanket promise; it swings on the state, the lien type, and who holds the senior position, so each camp’s claim gets tested county by county before money moves.

Federal liens and timing split even the people who agree on title risk. Goldovsky insists that “if it’s not municipality, everything is negotiable,” and says partial IRS releases are achievable when you present a sale to a homebuyer, while his own host Logan simply avoids federal liens because they break his 120–150 day turnaround target [O6HhpnnQADM @ 00:11:55]. Dustin Hahn calls IRS liens a red flag for beginners while conceding the IRS often detaches them, so his warning is about skill level rather than a hard ban [vA4ImBMyenY @ 00:03:21]. Redemption clocks are not agreed on either: quotes across the field range from “typically 120 days” to one to two years, and Musa’s state grid runs 2 years in New Jersey, Iowa, and Florida against 3 years in Arizona, with lien life stretching from 3 years in Iowa to 20 in New Jersey [7ybooMbrE58 @ 00:07:52]. Supplemental-tax rights drew a live argument at Premier Wealth Builders, where a participant claimed outsiders could pay after 3 years and the speaker shot back “no, no, no,” holding that the lienholder keeps first right to pay supplementals in every state he knows except Mississippi, naming Alabama, Arizona, and Florida [AYiTxfuCWHk @ 00:00:57].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive lessons came from properties nobody looked at closely enough. The Ramsey host bought two and walked away calling them “a freaking nightmare,” flagging disrepair and the equity trap where a $250,000 house carrying a $270,000 mortgage is worth nothing to the lienholder, and a house with a $100k mortgage still has to be kept current through redemption [KytTy1-RC5I @ 00:03:36]. Dustin Hahn owned a former gas station with underground tanks and “gave it back to the county,” which is why he now refuses environmental sites and landlocked parcels and checks that the address actually matches the parcel; he adds that Google Earth misses fires, floods, and demolitions, so you drive the property [vA4ImBMyenY @ 00:02:08]. Ted Thomas has watched a burned-down house sell four times at auction, and Bill Williams treats inspection as a bid input: a popped Houston pool at about $30K went straight into his maximum bid, alongside roof, windows, green pools, and oak roots under the driveway [sXKw09ndbYg @ 00:31:26]. Hahn’s deed video lands the rule bluntly: “do your research and if you can’t have somebody go see the property or see it yourself, don’t get into tax deeds” [cI-GhiUY6pg @ 00:00:42].

Capital drag is the quiet killer. Hahn warns that about 5% of liens fail to redeem, and once foreclosure fees stack up a $300 lien becomes “a couple thousand,” with money tied up two to three years either way [vA4ImBMyenY @ 00:01:34]. Kyra at Rent To Retirement flags that liens throw off no recurring income and that subsequent liens demand more capital, because “new liens always take over old liens,” while money managers crowd the same auctions [iOoZ743spRo @ 00:02:02]. Premier Wealth Builders is harsher about that exact trap: skip a year of supplementals and another party can buy the subsequent-year lien, becoming a second lienholder or paying you off, and “if you don’t pay the supplemental, that’s your fault” [AYiTxfuCWHk @ 00:01:36]. On the deed side, Ted Thomas says $1K–5K bidding increments can erase the profit, that deposits are “really critical because not only must you send the money on time, it has to be received on time,” and that “sometimes the winning bidder is the biggest loser”; his team pays only 20–50 cents on the dollar and wins just “several percent” of the bids it places [sXKw09ndbYg @ 00:20:32]. Competition from banks and funds bidding rates down squeezes every one of these margins further.

The trap that survives every auction is the lien nobody recorded. Alex Goldovsky says “25% of the issues are related to unrecorded municipal liens,” meaning code violations and permits that run $100 a day in Arizona, plus utilities that attach to the property in Philadelphia for gas, Michigan for water, and about half the US; his shop ran about 160,000 searches in 2025 with human searchers because AI is “too dangerous” [O6HhpnnQADM @ 00:16:00]. The Florida title attorney behind Lien Clearing 101 reports rehabbers in blighted areas blocked “almost every time” by code enforcement, special assessment, and municipal liens, or by unclear title from absentee owners, defunct corporations, and estates where an heir still lives in the house [zPDMr-7eAOc @ 00:00:33]. When title has ghosts on it, Jennifer Felton of ReLaw puts the bill on the table: one client paid $25K to get people off title, uncontested quiet title runs a grand or two, court $10–15K, disputed $100K+, with one to four years on the clock [B0yvMIdmaaQ @ 00:23:16]. She also watched a client’s transfer into an entity void her title coverage, because title insurance only insures the past [B0yvMIdmaaQ @ 00:30:00].

callout.title: Four Kill Switches Before Any Bid Goes In
callout.body: Every item below comes from a loss, reversal, or near-miss a named practitioner reported firsthand. If any gate fails, the parcel comes off the bid list.
items: Physical eyes on the property: drive it or send someone, because Google Earth misses fires, floods, and demolitions, and a burned-down house has sold four times at auction [Dustin Hahn — vA4ImBMyenY @ 00:06:09].
Title pulled before bidding at $20–30 per report, about $2–3k for 100 deeds, with IRS and government liens flagged and sized against value [Dustin Hahn — vA4ImBMyenY @ 00:07:24].
Human search for unrecorded municipal and utility liens, since 25% of title issues sit off the record, including $100-per-day Arizona code fines [Alex Goldovsky — O6HhpnnQADM @ 00:16:00].
Hard maximum bid that already includes repairs like a $30K popped pool and stops before $1K–5K increments erase the profit [Ted Thomas — sXKw09ndbYg @ 00:19:17].

chapters.pull_quote: “Sometimes the winning bidder is the biggest loser.” — Ted Thomas (sXKw09ndbYg @ 00:20:32).
action_checklist: Map the four essentials for every target state before bidding: interest rate, bidding procedure, redemption period, and lien life, such as Iowa’s 3-year lien life that forces foreclosure to start right away [TaxLienLady — 7ybooMbrE58 @ 00:07:10].
Never bid blindly: confirm the address matches the parcel, and strike landlocked parcels and environmental sites from the list [Dustin Hahn — vA4ImBMyenY @ 00:00:56].
Reserve cash to pay every subsequent-year supplemental tax so no outside party can step in as a second lienholder or pay you off [Premier Wealth Builders — AYiTxfuCWHk @ 00:01:57].
Run the core lien workflow: buy the lien, record it, pay subsequent taxes where counties require it, and collect at redemption [TaxLienLady — 7ybooMbrE58 @ 00:10:33].
Negotiate every non-municipal lien, and pursue partial IRS releases by presenting the pending sale to a homebuyer [Alex Goldovsky — O6HhpnnQADM @ 00:11:23].
When strangers sit on title, offer a voluntary deed-back payout first, since a $20 grand sign-off beats a quiet title that runs years in court [Jose Luiz Morales — B0yvMIdmaaQ @ 00:13:24].

chapters.question_prompt: How do IRS federal tax liens interact with property, and how does the IRS right of redemption affect a tax sale buyer?
chapters.title: Federal Tax Liens and IRS Redemption
chapters.subtitle: Notices of Federal Tax Lien, the 30-Day Hearing, Credit Impact, Form 12277 Withdrawals, CNC Status, the $25,000 Threshold, Filing Statistics, and the IRS Right of Redemption at Foreclosure
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners agree a junior federal tax lien can follow a foreclosed property past the auction: the IRS holds a 120-day redemption right, or longer if state law allows, to buy the property back from the winning bidder and resell it. The payout is the bid plus 6% annual interest plus necessary preservation expenses, minus rent collected or rental value of occupancy, and Natalia Willette warns bidders have 15 days after the IRS redemption letter to submit proof. Cosmetic rehab inside the window is lost if the IRS redeems. On the debtor side, the NFTL attaches to all present and future property, vanished from credit reports in 2018 but still kills deals at title search, and practitioners split on whether bureaus still pick it up and how freely the IRS grants withdrawals beyond the $25,000 direct debit path.

sections.heading: 1. The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner who works the auction side agrees on the core threat: a junior federal tax lien sitting in the chain of title does not simply evaporate when the gavel drops. Global Estate Hub frames it as a fully legal trap that catches seasoned investors and flippers off guard, where the government can show up a month after the sale, hand the winning bidder a check, and take the house back [q4Kqh7Vleyg @ 00:00:46]. The stated motive is pure collection math: if a property sells for pennies on the dollar, the IRS loses its recovery, so it uses its statutory power to buy the property back from the bidder and resell it at a higher fair market value, effectively running its own flipping side hustle [q4Kqh7Vleyg @ 00:02:07]. Florida real estate attorney Natalia Willette of LCO Law confirms the same 120-day right of redemption applies across mortgage foreclosure auctions, tax deed auctions, and similar proceedings, and once the IRS exercises it the bidder is no longer the owner [GoBskUnMJ5k @ 00:00:00]. Willette adds a structural point bidders miss: the lien is only extinguished when the foreclosure actually goes all the way to sale; if the matter settles or ends in a deed in lieu, the federal lien survives intact [GoBskUnMJ5k @ 00:01:00].

On what a federal tax lien actually grips, the tax pros line up tightly. Logan Allec, a CPA who owns Choice Tax Relief, explains that the lien exists the moment an assessed bill goes unpaid, a so-called secret lien that attaches automatically to everything the taxpayer owns now and acquires later, including business property and the money customers owe the business [joIEfxnWZzE @ 00:02:01]. Anton of Stop IRS Problems quotes the same sweeping reach, all assets now owned and future acquired, recorded with the county recorder in the taxpayer's last known county [MLaWCy3MlMQ @ 00:01:13]. The Notice of Federal Tax Lien is just the public announcement of that claim, and Allec stresses it is a claim, not a seizure: a lien is a claim to property, while a levy is the actual taking of a bank account or paycheck [joIEfxnWZzE @ 00:04:57]. The former revenue officer behind Former IRS Agent Representation adds the operator reality check: technically the lien hits furniture, cars, and personal property, but in practice it only really affects real property, because that is what surfaces when someone runs a property search [Y2mRqIi8jqY @ 00:04:01]. For an auction bidder, that is the whole point: the lien lives on title, and title is exactly where it gets found.

The third consensus point is the one that blindsides people: the NFTL dropped off consumer credit reports, but it never left public record. Allec documents that Experian, Equifax, and TransUnion voluntarily stopped reporting tax liens as of April 2018 after errors linked liens to the wrong people with matching names, and stresses it was a voluntary bureau decision, not a law, so it could theoretically be reversed [_kLMdX9sR6Y @ 00:06:50]. Clarity Tax Relief puts the operator consequence bluntly: the FICO score looks clean and the refinance still dies at the title search, because lenders, title companies, and business creditors pull public records as a matter of course [oPKD4zP1XUQ @ 00:02:14]. Clarity also sizes the pipeline: IRS Data Book numbers show 214,099 NFTL filings in FY2025, up from 196,996 in FY2024 and 179,019 in FY2023, an 8.7% one-year jump and 19.6% over two, even as the agency lost roughly 27% of its workforce, because filing is automated and tied to account balance [oPKD4zP1XUQ @ 00:00:24]. Allec notes the IRS generally does not file when the unpaid balance is below $10,000, though someone at the agency typically makes a case-specific filing determination before the notice goes out [joIEfxnWZzE @ 00:03:34].

sections.heading: 2. Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The redemption clock runs on hard dates. Global Estate Hub lays out the sequence: for a non-judicial foreclosure to touch a federal tax lien, the foreclosing entity, usually the bank, must deliver written notice to the IRS at least 25 days before the sale; without that notice the lien survives completely intact, and with it the lien is discharged and the clock starts on day zero, the sale date, running 120 days or the period allowed under state law, whichever is longer, so some markets run past four months [q4Kqh7Vleyg @ 00:03:17]. Willette pins the authority to 28 US Code Section 2410, the provision under which the IRS subjects itself to junior lienholder status in mortgage and tax deed foreclosures and sets the notice it requires [GoBskUnMJ5k @ 00:00:40]. The core payout formula matches across both accounts: the IRS refunds the exact winning bid, adds 6% per year statutory interest from the sale date, and adds necessary expenses to secure and maintain the property, then subtracts any rent collected and, if the bidder lived there, the reasonable rental value of that occupancy [q4Kqh7Vleyg @ 00:04:05]. Willette adds that senior liens a bidder pays off during the window, such as another recorded mortgage, may also be reimbursable, subject to the notice requirement [GoBskUnMJ5k @ 00:01:56].

What counts as a reimbursable expense is where bidders bleed money. Global Estate Hub lists casualty insurance, changing the locks, paying property taxes, and fixing a burst pipe as reimbursable, while new kitchen cabinets, granite countertops, and hardwood floors are not; start the cosmetic flip before day 120 and a redemption wipes out every single cent of that spend [q4Kqh7Vleyg @ 00:05:08]. Willette draws the line even tighter: utilities, cleaning, cosmetic repairs, and current-year property taxes do not qualify, but outstanding property taxes that were already due and senior to the IRS lien do, as does a roof repair needed to preserve the condition of the structure [GoBskUnMJ5k @ 00:02:16]. Then comes the hard deadline: once the IRS sends a letter, which Willette identifies as a 5597, stating it will redeem, the bidder has 15 days from receipt to send back full expense documentation plus proof of release on any superior mortgages paid off, and Willette calls that 15-day period very key [GoBskUnMJ5k @ 00:02:57]. The silver lining Global Estate Hub flags is that capital parked in a redeemed house earns the guaranteed 6% statutory rate, which the channel jokes is probably the only time the IRS will happily pay an investor interest [q4Kqh7Vleyg @ 00:05:53].

The exit from a dead-money waiting period is paperwork, not patience. Global Estate Hub warns that trying to resell on day 30 hits a brick wall: title companies mandate an exception on the policy during the 120-day window, and no standard buyer's mortgage lender will fund a loan over that exception [q4Kqh7Vleyg @ 00:06:21]. The workaround is an application to the IRS Collection Advisory Group for a waiver of the redemption right, using documents such as Letter 5597 or a certificate of discharge; if the IRS runs the numbers and sees no equity to flip, the right is effectively valueless and the release is issued for free, while a decision to redeem triggers a certificate of redemption, the formula payout, and title transferring to the United States [q4Kqh7Vleyg @ 00:07:07]. On the owner-side mechanics that shape how much equity the IRS sees, Allec describes Form 14135 discharge as the house-sale tool that strips the lien off one specific property, usually in exchange for payment from proceeds or when there is not enough meat on the bone, filed at least 45 days before closing [joIEfxnWZzE @ 00:10:36]. Clarity adds the verification layer for any lien status check: transcript code 582 marks a lien filed and code 583 marks a later release [oPKD4zP1XUQ @ 00:04:09].

callout.title: Bidder Moves That Protect Capital During the IRS Window
callout.body: Auction-side practitioners converge on four habits that keep money recoverable and title clearable while the IRS decides whether to redeem.
items: Freeze the cosmetic flip until the window closes: cabinets, granite, and hardwood floors are not reimbursable, and a redemption wipes out every cent spent on them [Global Estate Hub LLC — q4Kqh7Vleyg @ 00:05:23]

Spend only on what preserves the asset and outranks the IRS, such as delinquent prior-year property taxes and roof repairs, and keep receipts ready for the 15-day claim [LCO Law LLC | Estate Planning & Real Estate Law — GoBskUnMJ5k @ 00:02:37]
When the property has thin equity, apply for a waiver of the redemption right; if the IRS sees no profit in flipping, the release is issued for free [Global Estate Hub LLC — q4Kqh7Vleyg @ 00:07:23]
After any payoff or release, confirm the Certificate of Release actually posted with the county recorder, because nobody calls to say the record cleared [Clarity Tax Relief — oPKD4zP1XUQ @ 00:07:18]

sop_steps.action: Calculate the exact 120-day window, or the longer state period, from the sale date.

sop_steps.action: Limit spending to preservation items and senior liens, and build the reimbursement file in advance.

sop_steps.action: Apply to the IRS Collection Advisory Group for a waiver of the redemption right, or hold until the window closes.

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The loudest split is whether a filed Notice of Federal Tax Lien still lands on a credit file. Logan Allec says Experian, Equifax and TransUnion voluntarily stopped reporting liens after a CFPB study found entries linked to the wrong people, and stresses that voluntarily means the bureaus could reverse course [_kLMdX9sR6Y @ 00:06:50]. IRS Notices Explained quotes Experian outright, tax liens are no longer a part of credit reports, and tells viewers the score itself is safe from this public record [B1e8xDSixVg @ 00:00:45]. Chad Silver of IRS FBAR Tax Attorney runs the opposite script, warning that a lien often drops a score 100 points and surfaces on background checks for employment and professional licenses [D-ia73OSPG0 @ 00:00:52]. Anton at Stop IRS Problems lands in the middle: the government no longer files liens with the bureaus, yet the bureaus still pick them up from county recorders through digital exchange, and some liens even get published in newspapers where a local school district might see them [MLaWCy3MlMQ @ 00:02:08]. Every camp agrees on one point that matters at the closing table: the notice is a recorded public document, so any lender or title examiner who searches county records will find it no matter what a bureau prints.

On getting the notice withdrawn without paying in full, the split is how rigid the $25,000 line is. Bob Jablonsky treats it as a hard checklist: $25,000 or less assessed including penalties and interest, a direct debit installment agreement that pays out within 60 months or before the ten-year statute, full filing compliance, then three consecutive direct debit payments before Form 12277 goes in [EpqtO6uiV_E @ 00:02:37]. Logan Allec runs the same playbook, telling clients to push the balance to $25,000 or below first, but reports beating the threshold: the firm has argued the notice was inhibiting a taxpayer's ability to earn income, mostly for real estate operators, and got the IRS to withdraw or never file even on balances above $50,000 [joIEfxnWZzE @ 00:13:42]. The Former IRS Agent Representation host, a former revenue officer, blurs the vocabulary, saying that getting under $25,000 and making three direct payments means they will release the lien, and adds a pre-filing move: when the 1058 letter arrives, tell the IRS not to file because something is pending, and many times they withhold the filing [Y2mRqIi8jqY @ 00:05:14]. Chad Silver is looser, saying a series of on-time direct debit payments may get the lien withdrawn, but one missed payment can collapse the agreement [D-ia73OSPG0 @ 00:02:27].

Inside the 120-day IRS redemption window, the two foreclosure-auction specialists disagree on what the government actually refunds. Global Estate Hub LLC lists casualty insurance, changing the locks, paying property taxes and fixing a burst pipe as reimbursable necessary expenses on top of the bid and 6% interest [q4Kqh7Vleyg @ 00:05:08]. Florida real estate attorney Natalia Willette at LCO Law is narrower: utilities, cleaning, cosmetic repairs and even current-year property taxes are out, while outstanding property taxes already due with lien position superior to the IRS, a roof repair, and payoffs of senior mortgages are in [GoBskUnMJ5k @ 00:02:16]. They also read Letter 5597 in opposite directions. Global Estate Hub frames 5597 as part of a waiver package filed with the IRS Collection Advisory Group, where a valueless redemption right gets released for free when there is not enough equity to flip [q4Kqh7Vleyg @ 00:07:07]. Willette treats a 5597 as the notice that the IRS is coming to redeem, triggering a 15-day deadline to send back every receipt and release of lien [GoBskUnMJ5k @ 00:02:57]. The length of the window splits too: Global Estate Hub says 120 days or the state-law period, whichever is longer, while Willette quotes a flat 120 days under 28 US Code section 2410.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: For auction buyers, the costliest mistake is treating the gavel as the finish line. Global Estate Hub LLC says that if you launch the cosmetic flip, granite countertops, hardwood floors, new cabinets, before the 120-day window closes and the IRS redeems, every cent of those upgrades is gone [q4Kqh7Vleyg @ 00:05:23]. The same channel flags a second wall: on day 30 a title company will mandate an exception for the redemption right, and no standard buyer's mortgage lender will fund over it, so a quick resale is dead until the clock runs or a waiver lands [q4Kqh7Vleyg @ 00:06:21]. Check the notice trail before bidding too, because if the foreclosing bank never delivered written notice to the IRS at least 25 days before a non-judicial sale, the federal lien survives intact [q4Kqh7Vleyg @ 00:03:01]. Natalia Willette adds that the lien only gets extinguished if the foreclosure actually goes to sale; a settlement or deed in lieu leaves it standing, and once the redemption letter arrives an investor who misses the 15-day window to submit expense proof and senior-lien releases is gambling with reimbursement [GoBskUnMJ5k @ 00:01:19]. The economics check is blunt: capital parks for four months earning the statutory 6% if the IRS redeems.

On the taxpayer side, the failure pattern practitioners keep repeating is silence. Chad Silver's client Richard ignored the lien notice for lack of money; six months later the IRS levied $59,000 from the bank account and started garnishing 30% of wages [D-ia73OSPG0 @ 00:01:07]. Read The Corner shows how one day kills leverage: a Form 12153 postmarked on Day 31 misses the window, and the fallback equivalent hearing, requested within one year, carries no Tax Court review and no required pause in collection [FEsG-qPFvMc @ 00:09:40]. Dan Britt, after 35 years of practice, says one or two taxpayers every year get the bad news that they lost their best opportunity to settle or resolve the debt [eZJCPENFp3o @ 00:03:26]. Logan Allec warns that chasing hardship status as an exit backfires: currently not collectible status will not withdraw an existing notice, and if no notice exists yet there is an almost guaranteed chance the IRS files one, because nothing else would stop someone owing $100,000 from selling a house with $200,000 of equity and pocketing roughly $150,000 after costs [Fl9ZtNoyzj8 @ 00:04:14]. Chad Silver also notes fewer than one in three offers in compromise get accepted, so a sloppy offer just burns time while the lien sits.

The real estate closing table is where sequencing errors quietly cost operators their deals. Clarity Tax Relief says the trap that blindsides homeowners is a clean FICO score paired with a refinance that dies at the title search, and that a subordination request filed late or framed badly can blow the closing outright [oPKD4zP1XUQ @ 00:06:29]. IRS Notices Explained puts the hard number on it: the certificate application goes in at least 45 days before the transaction, with a current title report that is mandatory for subordination, a proposed closing statement, and exact property descriptions down to a 15-character aircraft serial number [B1e8xDSixVg @ 00:05:53]. Logan Allec adds that the payoff demand usually exceeds the amount printed on the original notice because penalties and interest keep stacking, so budget off the payoff figure, not the lien face [joIEfxnWZzE @ 00:07:16]. Even the finish line leaks. Darrin Mish says liens are supposed to release automatically after payment, an accepted offer, or statute expiration, but from personal experience that does not always happen [1Ovbn9aeSCU @ 00:00:58]. Clarity's rule is to confirm, never assume, that the Certificate of Release actually posted with the county recorder, since nobody calls to tell you the record cleared.

callout.title: Four Hard Stops Before Capital Moves
callout.body: Each gate comes straight from losses and near-misses the practitioners reported. Clear every one before bidding, spending, or mailing.
items: Before bidding, confirm the foreclosing party delivered written notice to the IRS at least 25 days before sale and that the case actually went to sale rather than a deed in lieu [Global Estate Hub LLC — q4Kqh7Vleyg @ 00:06:35] [LCO Law LLC | Estate Planning & Real Estate Law — GoBskUnMJ5k @ 00:01:19].

chapters.question_prompt: How do court rulings and bankruptcy filings change what a tax sale investor can keep?
chapters.title: Tyler v. Hennepin, Bankruptcy, and Court Challenges
chapters.subtitle: Home Equity Theft and Surplus Rulings, Post-Tyler State Reforms in Nebraska and Illinois, the Automatic Stay, Owner Bankruptcy Myths, and Appellate Challenges to Defective Notice
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners agree Tyler v. Hennepin (9–0, May 2023) turned surplus retention into a Fifth Amendment taking: a roughly $2,300 bill grew to $15,000, the condo sold for $40,000, and Hennepin kept about $25,000. The rule is federal, reaches heirs, and per Matt Christ likely reaches tax lien buyers too. Street mechanics center on Illinois' 9%-to-0% interest auctions with 12–30 month redemptions, new court forms asking about equity, tolled certificates, and certified-mail surplus demands logged with dates. Pung (June 2026) pegs compensation to the auction price, $76,008 against a $194,000 assessment. Bankruptcy freezes sales instantly but never erases property taxes. Disagreement is sharp: Lynette Lowitz would not buy certificates now, Nebraska investors argue equity claims belong against the county, and John Bursch says shortfalls occur 90–95% of the time.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner tracking Tyler lands on the same core fact pattern and the same holding. Geraldine Tyler stopped paying on a Minneapolis condo in 2010, a roughly $2,300 tax bill swelled to about $15,000 through interest, penalties, and fees, and Hennepin County sold the unit for $40,000 and kept the roughly $25,000 difference [sb6T0Xe5siY @ 00:01:27]. The Supreme Court ruled 9–0 in May 2023 that keeping that surplus is a Fifth Amendment taking, with Gorsuch, joined by Jackson, flagging an Eighth Amendment excessive-fines problem the Court did not decide [9zlCqzr7-EA @ 00:06:24]. Matt Christ of the Center for Community Progress frames the operating rule plainly: tax foreclosure is a debt collection tool, and the government collects what it is owed, but no more, while local governments can still foreclose and sell or transfer delinquent property to satisfy the debt [SG5qy2A3jA0 @ 00:13:34]. Lynette Lowitz, a tax sale and tax deed attorney of about 19 years, restates the equity math with an Illinois example: a $100 lien on a $100,000 house means $99,900 of equity lost, and roughly 13 states ran on that model before Tyler [qAoyeFTuxms @ 00:04:27]. The rule also follows the property into heirs' hands, with claims routed to the county treasurer or probate depending on the state, because, as The Deed puts it bluntly, the rule is federal.

The second point of agreement is uncomfortable for lien buyers: the liability does not stay with the county. Matt Christ lists five questions Tyler left open, and on whether tax lien buyers carry exposure the answer is that liability is likely, yes, which is why the Center pushes lien states not to wait for case law to settle [SG5qy2A3jA0 @ 00:21:41]. Lowitz has already watched state-court class actions by homeowners against tax buyers appear, and warns that picking up assigned certificates now can mean buying liability rather than a yield [qAoyeFTuxms @ 00:18:34]. In Nebraska, Tax Sale Resources host Brian and attorney Greg walked through Continental Resources' Scotts Bluff County certificate: the investor took a tax deed, filed quiet title, beat the homeowners' takings and excessive-penalty counterclaims at trial and at the Nebraska Supreme Court, and then saw the U.S. Supreme Court hold the case and send it back for reconsideration consistent with Tyler [d67aVfAEUxg @ 00:02:03]. Community Living HQ adds that Nebraska now requires deed holders themselves to calculate surplus, while Minnesota, Maine, and Massachusetts rewrote their statutes [NZlx21J6n-c @ 00:06:08]. The consensus operator takeaway: a deed that strips equity is now a litigation asset for the former owner, and the investor holding that deed is a reachable defendant.

On bankruptcy, the speakers converge on the automatic stay as instant and blunt. LawShelf explains that the stay applies the moment a case is filed and binds even creditors with no notice, with violating acts treated as void [08d72pEpig4 @ 00:00:23]. Kyle Schumacher, a Texas bankruptcy lawyer, puts it in foreclosure terms: file before the sale date and the foreclosure stops, garnishments and levies stop, and collectors are bound even without notice [m1B_j8n-b9E @ 00:00:14]. Behind The Servicing pictures the guillotine: a 9:48 a.m. filing halts a 10:00 a.m. auction, and under In Re Schwartz, cited from the Ninth and First Circuits, stay violations are void ab initio — that auction sale never happened [au90-c2Pwvo @ 00:00:54]. For lien holders the consensus is calmer than the myth. Tax Sale Secrets says property taxes are never written off in bankruptcy; the one bankruptcy case that operator held paid out in $100 to $300 checks over six months, and the worst case is the debtor drags out getting paid by a few months, which a lien investor was already planning on [qEuYpfZ_Qgg @ 00:01:42]. The baseline prerequisite across these speakers: a bankruptcy filing freezes action against the property, but it does not erase the tax debt, and the stay does not cure a default.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Lowitz lays out the Illinois machine an investor actually operates. The county treasurer auctions unpaid taxes annually and bidders compete on interest rate, starting at a 9% ceiling and bidding down as far as 0%. The winning bid produces a certificate of purchase that becomes a lien, redemption runs 12 to 30 months depending on property type, and an unredeemed holder petitions the court for a tax deed and then moves for possession [qAoyeFTuxms @ 00:03:14]. Post-Tyler, the court application form now asks whether there is equity in the property, and the old adage that a certificate dies one year after final redemption no longer holds because certificates are being tolled, so the court file and county records must be checked directly [qAoyeFTuxms @ 00:15:05]. Lowitz calls the business an interest game where extra yield comes from paying subsequent taxes, with margins likely to shrink a little given the high cost of money [qAoyeFTuxms @ 00:13:48]. The Quiet Math shows the owner's side of that same compounding: a $3,000 delinquency becomes roughly $14,000 through $5,760 in subsequent taxes, $1,900 in interest at rates up to 18%, $600 in fees, and $2,500 in lawyer costs over a two-year redemption, ending in a $13,890 payoff [0FOLJutyMHY @ 00:06:23].

For the surplus claim itself, The Deed gives a paper-trail workflow: write the county treasurer and ask whether there was a surplus, how to claim it, and by what date; check the state Department of Revenue; send it certified, keep a copy, and log the date, because a verbal answer from a clerk is not proof [sb6T0Xe5siY @ 00:06:20]. Record the county name and the sale date, and lean on HUD housing counselors at 800-569-4287, which is free. Claims route to the county treasurer or to probate depending on the state, and heirs are covered. Community Living HQ adds a front-end checklist: open every notice, verify the address with both the assessor and the treasurer, ask about exemptions, request a distribution accounting, and contact legal aid before foreclosure [NZlx21J6n-c @ 00:09:07]. Notice mechanics cut both ways for investors. The Quiet Math cites Jones v. Flowers (2006): when certified mail comes back unclaimed, another reasonable step is required [0FOLJutyMHY @ 00:07:42]. The Florida tax deed challenge in Horn v. Miami-Dade turned partly on exactly that: §197.512 requires four weeks of publication, the trustee was left off the notice, Wells v. Thomas (1956) treats that as jurisdictional, and returned certified mail triggers additional reasonable steps [RlQwxNYiqok @ 00:15:33].

The valuation and timing numbers are where an operator models exposure. In Pung v. Isabella County, the Michigan family owed about $2,200 on a home assessed near $194,000 that auctioned for $76,008, and on June 23, 2026 the Court ruled 9–0, in an Alito opinion, that compensation is measured by the auction price, not market value — the garage-sale price [9zlCqzr7-EA @ 00:10:21]. Community Living HQ puts the precise debt at $2,241.93 with $73,766 returned, and notes three justices flagged that a fair auction was left unspecified [NZlx21J6n-c @ 00:07:13]. Matt Christ's mechanics for governments mirror that: public auction is the cleanest, safest valuation, appraisals invite challenge, the taking date is the later of sale or extinguishment of redemption, and distribution should copy mortgage foreclosure statutes with lienholders included and unclaimed surplus held in escrow [SG5qy2A3jA0 @ 00:15:05]. On the Nebraska clock, the Tax Sale Resources guest flags a 2-year limitations period on inverse condemnation that cuts off claims around December 2025, a roughly five-year exposure window, while the state moves to something close to judicial foreclosure starting in 2024 and remedies run through mandamus or judicial foreclosure followed by suing the county [d67aVfAEUxg @ 00:15:04].

callout.title: Post-Tyler Title and Stay Tactics From the Trenches
callout.body: Small procedural habits that practitioners use to keep deeds clean, redemptions confirmed, and bankruptcy hits contained.
items: Set a tickler for two and three weeks after a redemption closing and get actual proof of redemption, because Bob thought Stan sent the check is how certificates go sideways [The Devine Law Group — qAoyeFTuxms @ 00:16:45]
Keep the bankruptcy case number handy for every caller, since debt collectors are bound by the stay even without formal notice [Bankruptcy Explained — m1B_j8n-b9E @ 00:02:11]
Run the servicer 48-hour drill on any filing: bankruptcy hold, stop-work order, and dialers suppressed [Behind The Servicing — au90-c2Pwvo @ 00:01:28]

sop_steps.title: Pull the court file and county records
sop_steps.action: Verify certificate status directly before buying, assigning, or petitioning.
sop_steps.detail: Tolling has killed the old one-year-after-final-redemption adage, so check the court file and county records for every certificate instead of relying on dates alone [The Devine Law Group — qAoyeFTuxms @ 00:15:41]

sop_steps.title: Run the equity check
sop_steps.action: Compare the lien balance to property value and answer the equity question on the deed application.
sop_steps.detail: A $5,000 tax against a $55,000 value is $50,000 of equity, the exact math homeowners used in the Nebraska counterclaims, and the Illinois form now asks about equity outright [Tax Sale Resources — d67aVfAEUxg @ 00:06:14]

sop_steps.title: Audit every notice step
sop_steps.action: Confirm publication, every interest holder on the notice, and follow-up after returned mail.
sop_steps.detail: Horn v. Miami-Dade turned on four weeks of publication under §197.512, an omitted trustee, and the duty to take additional reasonable steps after returned certified mail [Florida Trust, Real Estate, Probate, & Foreclosure — RlQwxNYiqok @ 00:15:33]

sop_steps.title: Contain a bankruptcy hit
sop_steps.action: Freeze all collection and deed activity, then wait out the payment plan rather than over-research it.
sop_steps.detail: Property taxes are not written off; the one case reported paid $100 to $300 checks over six months, interest may stop, and the outcome is too unpredictable to justify heavy research [Tax Sale Secrets — qEuYpfZ_Qgg @ 00:01:15]

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over who eats the equity claim once a deed issues. Greg, defending investor Continental Resources in the Scotts Bluff County fight, argues the deed stays valid and any equity claim belongs against the county as grantor, because the bargain was immediate payment to the county with no risk, delay, or cost while the buyer takes interest or a deed [d67aVfAEUxg @ 00:07:36]. Matt Christ at Center for Community Progress lands on the opposite side of the risk ledger: asked whether tax lien buyers face liability, the answer is likely yes [SG5qy2A3jA0 @ 00:21:41]. Lynette Lowitz of Writer Law Offices sees that liability already arriving through state-court class actions by homeowners against tax buyers, and says buying assigned certificates now could mean buying liability [qAoyeFTuxms @ 00:18:34]. On the county side, John Bursch argues Tyler is the outlier, claiming shortfalls occur 90-95% of the time and that owners can pay the taxes, refinance, or sell the home themselves and keep the rest [I00OuoMBf3U @ 00:35:05]. The operator read: investor counsel is litigating to push equity exposure onto the county, policy counsel expects it to land on lien buyers, and a tax deed attorney with roughly 19 years in practice is sitting out new purchases right now.

The second fight is the valuation yardstick. In the 2026 Isabella County case, the debt was about $2,200, the assessed value about $194K, and the auction brought $76,008; the Court went 9-0 on June 23, 2026 that compensation is measured by the auction sale price, with Thomas leaning toward fair market value and counties pressing for an administrable number [9zlCqzr7-EA @ 00:10:54]. Community Living HQ adds that three justices noted 'fair auction' was left without a definition, so the quality of the sale itself becomes the next battleground [NZlx21J6n-c @ 00:07:13]. Lynette Lowitz flagged before the ruling that owners were pushing fair market value against the county's distressed-sale price, and that pending Illinois bills cite fair market value, meaning a state fix can still run on a different yardstick than the one the Court adopted [qAoyeFTuxms @ 00:12:22]. Matt Christ's guidance to governments sits with the auction camp: a public auction is the safest valuation method, an appraisal carries more challenge risk, and even an appraisal does not fully insulate a jurisdiction on demolition properties, where auctioning after demolition with the lien built into the minimum bid is the alternative [SG5qy2A3jA0 @ 00:15:05]. Operators bidding in post-Tyler auctions are buying into a price that now doubles as the constitutional measure of the owner's surplus.

Bankruptcy splits lien-side and servicer-side operators. Tax Sale Secrets tells lien holders property taxes are never written off in bankruptcy, reports that the speaker's one case paid out $100-$300 checks over six months, and calls the worst case a few months of drag on money the investor already planned to wait for, so researching the filing is not worth the effort [qEuYpfZ_Qgg @ 00:01:42]. Behind The Servicing treats the same stay as a guillotine: a 9:48 a.m. filing halts a 10:00 a.m. auction, violations are void ab initio, servicers run a 48-hour drill of bankruptcy hold, stop-work order, and suppressed dialers, and §362(k) exposes violators to actual damages, fees, and possible punitive damages [au90-c2Pwvo @ 00:02:22]. Jonathan Ginsburg of Personal Bankruptcy Law Atlanta reports the counterweight from an Eleventh Circuit decision: damages were denied where a stay-violating foreclosure was cancelled within a day, because the debtor lacked medical records or documented monetary loss [MoTnCzda1JA @ 00:03:11]. LawShelf notes creditors are bound even without notice, yet relief is available under §362(d)(1) for adequate protection and §362(d)(2) where there is no equity and the property is not needed for reorganization [08d72pEpig4 @ 00:02:57]. For a lien buyer, the filing mostly changes timing; for anyone pushing a sale through it, the auction simply never happened.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The first trap is assuming the deed comes at all. Greg warns 'don't assume' a deed will issue in Nebraska, where counties are split between issuing deeds, requiring foreclosure, and staying undecided, and the fallback remedies are a mandamus action or a judicial foreclosure followed by suing the county [d67aVfAEUxg @ 00:25:05]. Lynette Lowitz says the old Illinois adage that a certificate is dead one year after final redemption no longer holds because certificates are being tolled, so the court file and county records must be checked, and the court application form now asks whether there is equity in the property [qAoyeFTuxms @ 00:15:41]. Lowitz also reports the redemption-proof failure that bites after closing: 'Bob thought Stan sent the check,' which is why the fix is a tickler set for two and three weeks out plus proof of redemption [qAoyeFTuxms @ 00:16:45]. Matt Christ adds that moving property to an urban renewal agency does not absolve liability and that Michigan's right of first refusal is now riskier, so a transfer does not wash the surplus problem out of the chain [SG5qy2A3jA0 @ 00:51:59]. Every one of these is a step where an operator who ran the pre-Tyler playbook from memory loses the asset or inherits the claim.

Notice and auction mechanics are where deeds die in court. In the Florida challenge, §197.512 requires publication for four weeks, yet the trustee was omitted from the notice, and Wells v. Thomas (1956) treats that defect as jurisdictional [RlQwxNYiqok @ 00:02:00]. The same sale was closed so fast that a $53,000 bidder was cut off, colliding with the §197.542 requirement to sell to the highest bidder, and investor counsel Jones leaned on §197.552 prima facie validity while the court found no authenticated summary judgment evidence and the county conceded the record was insufficient [RlQwxNYiqok @ 00:07:42]. After certified mail comes back, 'additional reasonable steps' are required, and The Quiet Math traces the same rule to Jones v. Flowers (2006): when certified mail goes unclaimed, another reasonable step is owed [0FOLJutyMHY @ 00:07:42]. Community Living HQ names who falls through those gaps, elderly owners, heirs, and owners at outdated addresses, and pushes owners to verify their address with both the assessor and the treasurer [NZlx21J6n-c @ 00:02:50]. For a deed buyer, a returned certified letter, a missing trustee, or a truncated bidding window is a title defect waiting to be litigated, and the post-Pung 'fairly conducted' auction standard only raises the stakes on a rushed close.

The economics checks cut both ways. The Quiet Math shows how a $3,000 bill on a $210,000 paid-off house grows to about $14,000: $5,760 in subsequent taxes, $1,900 interest, $600 fees, and a $2,500 lawyer, with lien interest up to 18% over a 2-year redemption, ending in a $13,890 payoff funded by a daughter's early-withdrawal penalty [0FOLJutyMHY @ 00:06:23]. The owner's escrow ended with the loan, so automatic tax payment ended too, and the household applied for the senior tax freeze only after paying off. On the buyer side, the Tax Sale Resources host notes Nebraska has no premium bid, so no surplus is generated at sale, most liens redeem, and a New Jersey investor said they lose money on more than half of the deeds [d67aVfAEUxg @ 00:11:39]. Clocks kill claims on both sides: Nebraska inverse condemnation carries a 2-year limitations period that cuts off claims around December 2025 [d67aVfAEUxg @ 00:15:04], and a Michigan Court of Appeals ruling time-barred 2014 claims because 'a three-year limitations period therefore expired before Michigan created procedures' [NZlx21J6n-c @ 00:08:44]. Run the redemption math, the deed-loss rate, and the limitations calendar before bidding on any post-Tyler certificate, not after the owner's lawyer files a takings counterclaim.

callout.title: Four Gates Before Bidding, Petitioning, or Closing Post-Tyler
callout.body: Each gate below comes from a deal, case, or sale that practitioners watched go sideways. Clear all four before money moves or a deed petition is filed.
items: Confirm how the county actually handles deeds before buying; Greg's rule is 'don't assume' a deed will issue, with mandamus or judicial foreclosure plus suing the county as the fallback [Tax Sale Resources — d67aVfAEUxg @ 00:25:05].

Pull the court file and county records on every certificate and be ready for the court application form's new question on whether there is equity in the property [The Devine Law Group — qAoyeFTuxms @ 00:15:05].

Audit notice to every interest holder, including trustees, and document the additional reasonable steps taken after certified mail comes back [Florida Trust, Real Estate, Probate, & Foreclosure — RlQwxNYiqok @ 00:15:33].
Check for a bankruptcy filing up to the minute of sale, because a 9:48 a.m. filing halts a 10:00 a.m. auction and the sale is void [Behind The Servicing — au90-c2Pwvo @ 00:00:17].

chapters.pull_quote: "Right now, I wouldn't do it." Lynette Lowitz on buying tax lien certificates after Tyler, attributed to The Devine Law Group (qAoyeFTuxms @ 00:18:20).
action_checklist: Ask the treasurer in writing whether there was a surplus, how to claim it, and by what date, then send it certified, keep a copy, and log the date, because a verbal answer from a clerk is not proof [The Deed | Real Estate — sb6T0Xe5siY @ 00:06:20].
Before relying on certificate status, check the court file and county records, since certificates are being tolled and the one-year rule is dead [The Devine Law Group — qAoyeFTuxms @ 00:15:41].
After every redemption closing, set ticklers for two and three weeks out and collect proof of redemption [The Devine Law Group — qAoyeFTuxms @ 00:16:45].
In Nebraska, confirm whether the county issues deeds, requires foreclosure, or is undecided, and line up mandamus or judicial foreclosure as the remedy [Tax Sale Resources — d67aVfAEUxg @ 00:25:05].
When a bankruptcy filing hits, place the bankruptcy hold, issue a stop-work order, and suppress dialers within 48 hours [Behind The Servicing — au90-c2Pwvo @ 00:01:28].

On vacant-property deals, look for a fully loaded minimum bid that includes abatement and demolition liens, since a fully loaded bid with no other bidders means no surplus [Center for Community Progress — SG5qy2A3jA0 @ 00:33:09].

chapters.question_prompt: How do experienced practitioners fund, structure, and scale a tax lien portfolio?
chapters.title: Funding, Structuring, and Scaling the Portfolio
chapters.subtitle: Self-Directed IRAs and 401(k)s, LLC Structuring for Taxes, Portfolio Tools, and Long-Form Interviews With Veteran Lien Investors
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners funding tax lien portfolios converge on three engines: self-directed retirement money, entity wrappers, and other people's money. Custodians at Advanta, Next Generation, NuView, and CamaPlan route bids, certified checks, and redemptions entirely through the IRA, with fees such as NuView's $95 per purchase batch and Next Generation's $325 per asset per year. Ted Thomas sets a $20-25K entry floor, while Stephen Morel says matching bank-level 15-18% yields takes six to seven figures because institutions absorb roughly 80% of delinquent liens. Scaling tactics include CamaPlan's mixed IRA-and-cash pools earning 20% APR, Ross Budrakey's 10% unsecured notes funding 20% Georgia redemptions, and Clint Coons's single Wyoming lien LLC paired with one LLC per deed. Practitioners split on checkbook control versus custodian-issued checks, whether to chase big counties, and whether over-the-counter liens are junk or maximum-rate bargains.

key_metrics.label: Minimum Starting Bankroll
key_metrics.value: At least $20,000-$25,000; $500 is not enough
key_metrics.context: Ted Thomas, in their 33rd year, sets the floor for a new investor buying liens and defaulted property, paired with keeping the day job and getting a coach.

key_metrics.label: Capital to Match Institutional Yield
key_metrics.value: Six to seven figures to earn 15-18% year over year
key_metrics.context: Stephen Morel reports about 80% of delinquent liens go to institutional investors and that bank-level returns require six- to seven-figure capital.

key_metrics.label: OPM Spread on Georgia Redemptions
key_metrics.value: Borrow at 10%, earn 20%; 120% annualized on a one-month redemption
key_metrics.context: Friends lend to the LLC on unsecured notes at 10% while the LLC earns the 20% Georgia penalty; lenders are refunded if the bid strikes out.

key_metrics.label: Custodian Fee Drag vs. Taxable Account
key_metrics.metric: Custodian Fee Drag vs. Taxable Account
key_metrics.value: $390 first-year fees, $1,193 over 5 years vs. $2,700/year interest on $15K; about 50% more net
key_metrics.context: CamaPlan walks a $15K lien account through five years of fees against interest earned and compares the IRA result to a taxable account.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every custodian on the circuit describes the same plumbing: the retirement account, not the investor, is the buyer, payer, and payee. Jared of Next Generation has contracts titled 'Next Generation TS FBO client name plus IRA number' and insists that every due diligence cost and every dollar of income flow through the IRA [l9-Us7KWWPM @ 00:12:43]. Advanta's Reneka Lightbourne runs the same rule through a checkbook-control LLC: the operating agreement names the IRA as owner, Advanta signs it, a check lands in the LLC's own bank account, bids are paid from that account, and interest and profits flow back into it [c3YDDPR5wVo @ 00:06:23]. CamaPlan's co-founder bids in the name 'CamaPlan FBO name IRA number,' pulls a TIN for the IRA, and now pushes an entity with its own bank account because bidding sites demand one [U08uLxrDVE4 @ 00:36:29]. NuView frames itself as a custodian like Schwab or Fidelity that gives no advice and does not lock clients into stocks, bonds, and mutual funds, so liens and deeds can sit inside the account [Hqqt5H7mS3o @ 00:03:22]. The operator takeaway is blunt: the capital stack starts with paperwork. If the bidder registration, the bank account, and the redemption payee do not all match the IRA or its LLC, the deal is structured wrong before the first bid.

On how much money it takes, the veterans agree the floor is higher than the guru pitch. Ted Thomas, 85 and in their 33rd year, says $500 is not enough and tells newcomers to start with at least $20-25K, keep their job, and get a coach [jDYlxXpw-e4 @ 00:36:45]. Stephen Morel of Juristdeed says roughly 80% of delinquent liens now go to institutional investors and that matching bank-level returns takes six to seven figures, with institutions pulling 15-18% year over year [UyiZp8ocowM @ 00:13:10]. Kessler, the PropertyOnion tax deed professor, reports banks putting $100M into Florida to earn $5M in 90 days and Capital One pushing about $150M a year into the state, which is why they call Florida auctions not even worth participating in anymore [vD0IitWLjZE @ 00:17:32]. Ross Budrakey's answer is the same: banks and funds own the big counties, a $1M fund in Fulton County paid above retail, so the small operator should not compete with those guys and should instead work smaller counties in the path of progress [VmzztAnZ71w @ 00:09:40]. Scaling, in this consensus, is a capital-allocation problem first. The small check wins where institutional money does not bother to show up, and the big check only competes on yield.

Structure consensus among the lawyers and custodians lands on separating the lien book from anything that carries owner liability. Clint Coons runs every lien, say 20 certificates, through one Wyoming LLC that is disregarded for federal tax purposes and files no return; redemption funds pay into the LLC and get distributed out, and Coons says there is no lawsuit risk because a lien holder does not own the property [bzu0eYCEXNg @ 00:02:10]. Stephan Hild of Provident Trust Group recommends a checkbook-control LLC specifically for tax lien investing [AcKbZeNuPr4 @ 00:56:15], and Advanta's host says the IRA can either send funds before the sale or the investor can run checkbook control through an IRA-owned LLC [RDk1Gksh9R4 @ 00:51:16]. Morel adds the out-of-state wrinkle: bidders working another state register an LLC there, and the work itself is the most non-passive passive investment in the passive investments [UyiZp8ocowM @ 00:35:01]. Coons then layers one Wyoming LLC per deed property under a Wyoming holding LLC parent for anything kept long term. The operator rule: one clean entity holds the paper, retirement dollars enter it only through the custodian or an IRA-owned LLC, and every property that can generate a lawsuit gets its own shell.

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Sale-day cash logistics decide whether IRA money can even bid, and the custodians teach exact routines. NuView's online workflow: open the account, register as a county bidder, fund the bidding account with, say, $20,000, win $14,000 across five liens, return the $6,000 balance, then send purchase details so the temporary asset can be split into individual liens [Hqqt5H7mS3o @ 00:13:23]. Online sales often want only a 10% deposit with the balance due in about 24 hours, but NuView prefers full funding upfront. For live sales, NuView issues certified checks, for example four $5,000 checks; on a $14,000 win the bidder hands over three and waits weeks for the $1,000 refund [Hqqt5H7mS3o @ 00:29:28]. Next Generation does the same with cashier's checks payable to the township, and unused checks go back into the IRA [l9-Us7KWWPM @ 00:58:36]. Chantelle Owens adds the Georgia ground truth: pay at the tax commissioner's office within an hour or two after the auction, no personal checks, and most counties cannot take wires [RDk1Gksh9R4 @ 00:59:37]. The refund example is telling: a $50K check against a $49K bid leaves cash stranded at the county until it comes back. Break the stake into blocks so unused capital returns to the account intact.

Carrying costs are small but they compound against small liens, so practitioners quote exact numbers. Next Generation charges $50 at setup, $325 per asset per year, $100 per purchase, and $5 per check or $30 per wire; Jared calls the per-asset structure usually the best fee arrangement [l9-Us7KWWPM @ 00:16:07]. NuView flips the model: $95 for every batch of liens bought in one process and $300 a year for all liens held, which the speaker contrasts with Schwab and TD fees that are baked in [Hqqt5H7mS3o @ 00:36:44]. CamaPlan runs $275 a year above $40K invested and $150-275 below it, and walks a $15K account through the math: $390 in first-year fees and $1,193 over five years against $2,700 a year, $13,500 total, in interest, netting about 50% more than a taxable account; a $250K account comes out about 22% ahead [U08uLxrDVE4 @ 00:49:01]. Provident quotes a $50 activation fee halved in the first year and warns that transfers out of Equity Trust take two to three weeks [AcKbZeNuPr4 @ 00:50:34]. The unit-economics check: a $325 per-asset fee on $1-2K liens eats a large slice of the yield, so per-asset custodians fit fewer, larger certificates while batch pricing fits volume buyers.

Once personal capital is deployed, the scaling playbooks shift to pooled and borrowed money. CamaPlan's pool example puts $250K into one entity: Bill's traditional IRA holds 50%, Bill's Roth 10%, Cheryl 15%, and Jim personally 25%; the pool throws off $2,400 interest and $2,000 principal monthly, Bill receives $1,200 plus $1,000, the pool earns 20% APR, and only Jim's personal share is taxed [U08uLxrDVE4 @ 00:19:42]. The passive alternative is lending to an operator at a fixed 10-12% while the operator earns 12-24% [U08uLxrDVE4 @ 00:22:45]. Ross Budrakey ran the street version: friends lend to the LLC at 10% on unsecured notes while the LLC earns Georgia's 20%, so a one-month redemption annualizes to 120%, and lenders are refunded if the bid strikes out [VmzztAnZ71w @ 01:24:13]. That OPM engine produced the Sherwood deal in Florida, bought at $60,300 with $25K of rehab and a $125K resale, for $30K profit in four months. Clint Coons keeps scaled holdings clean by never foreclosing inside the lien LLC; the certificate gets assigned to Wyoming LLC number two, which takes title, and flips run through a Wyoming LLC taxed as a C Corp to avoid dealer status and the loss of investor benefits [bzu0eYCEXNg @ 00:04:24].
